  • A decoder has \(n\) inputs and \(2^n\) outputs and asserts exactly one, output \(i\) being minterm \(m_i\). With OR gates it realises any function with no simplification (use NAND gates with an active-low decoder, and use the complement when the function has more than \(2^{n-1}\) minterms).
  • The enable input makes expansion possible: two \(k\)-to-\(2^k\) decoders and one extra address line make a \((k+1)\)-to-\(2^{k+1}\) decoder; \(2^{n-k}\) modules build an \(n\)-to-\(2^n\) decoder.
  • An encoder is the inverse of a decoder. The simple encoder assumes one active input and is ambiguous otherwise; a priority encoder resolves several active inputs in favour of the highest and adds a valid output \(V\) to separate "code 0" from "no input".
  • A multiplexer selects one of \(2^n\) inputs with \(n\) select lines. It implements any \(n\)-variable function on a \(2^n\):1 multiplexer directly, and with input reduction any \((n+1)\)-variable function on a \(2^n\):1 multiplexer, using \(0\), \(1\), \(x\) or \(x'\) on the data inputs. A \(2^n\):1 multiplexer is built from a tree of smaller ones.
  • A demultiplexer is a decoder with an enable: feed the data into the enable. With \(D = 1\) it is a decoder. A MUX at one end and a DEMUX at the other, with a shared select counter, is a time-division link.
Component Inputs \(\to\) outputs Key equations Decoder \(n \to 2^n\) \(D_i = m_i\) (or \(E\cdot m_i\)) Encoder (octal) \(8 \to 3\) \(A_2 = D_4{+}D_5{+}D_6{+}D_7\), \(A_1 = D_2{+}D_3{+}D_6{+}D_7\), \(A_0 = D_1{+}D_3{+}D_5{+}D_7\) Priority encoder (4-to-2) \(4 \to 2 + V\) \(x = D_2{+}D_3\), \(y = D_3{+}D_1D_2'\), \(V = D_0{+}D_1{+}D_2{+}D_3\) Multiplexer (4:1) \(4 + 2 \to 1\) \(Y = S_1'S_0'I_0 + S_1'S_0I_1 + S_1S_0'I_2 + S_1S_0I_3\) Demultiplexer (1-to-4) \(1 + 2 \to 4\) \(Y_i = D\cdot m_i\) MUX tree \(M:1\) from \(k:1\) \((M-1)/(k-1)\) modules

docs.title: 5.13 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 5.1. (Multiple choice) An \(n\)-to-\(2^n\) decoder with all outputs active-high asserts, for each input combination: (A) all outputs; (B) exactly one output, its minterm; (C) no output; (D) exactly two outputs.

Answer

(B). Output \(i\) is the minterm \(m_i\), so exactly one output is 1 for each input combination.

Exercise 5.2. Draw the truth table and the AND-gate logic of a 3-to-8 decoder with an active-high enable, and state the output equation for \(D_5\).

Answer

The truth table is Table 5.1 with an extra enable column: when \(E = 0\) all eight outputs are 0, and when \(E = 1\) exactly the output whose number equals the binary value of \(ABC\) is 1. Each output is one 4-input AND gate taking \(E\) and one minterm. For input \(101\): \(D_5 = E \cdot A \cdot B' \cdot C\) (that is \(A\,B'\,C\) when enabled).

Exercise 5.3. Using a 3-to-8 decoder and OR gates implement \(F_1(A,B,C) = \sum m(0,2,4,6)\) and \(F_2(A,B,C) = \sum m(1,3,5,7)\). Give the OR-gate connections. Is there an even cheaper way?

Answer

\(F_1 = D_0 + D_2 + D_4 + D_6\) (the even lines) and \(F_2 = D_1 + D_3 + D_5 + D_7\) (the odd lines): two 4-input OR gates. A cheaper way exists: \(F_1 = C'\) and \(F_2 = C\), because the even minterms are exactly those with \(C = 0\). No decoder is needed at all, only one inverter; simplification should come before choosing hardware.

Exercise 5.4. Implement \(F(A,B,C) = \sum m(0,2,5,7)\) using a 3-to-8 decoder and one OR gate, and say what the connections would be if the decoder had active-low outputs.

Answer

\(F = D_0 + D_2 + D_5 + D_7\): one 4-input OR gate on the corresponding decoder outputs. With an active-low decoder the outputs are \(D_k'\), so the OR gate is replaced by a 4-input NAND gate on the same four lines, because \((D_0' D_2' D_5' D_7')' = D_0 + D_2 + D_5 + D_7\).

Exercise 5.5. Show how to build a 3-to-8 decoder from two 2-to-4 decoders with enable inputs, and explain the role of the most-significant address bit.

Answer

Feed \(A_1A_0\) to the address inputs of both 2-to-4 decoders. Connect the most-significant bit \(A_2\) through an inverter to the enable of the first decoder (outputs \(D_0\) to \(D_3\)) and directly to the enable of the second (outputs \(D_4\) to \(D_7\)). When \(A_2 = 0\) the first decoder is enabled and the second is disabled (all outputs inactive); when \(A_2 = 1\) the roles are exchanged. \(A_2\) thus chooses which decoder is active while \(A_1A_0\) choose the line inside it. Cost: two 2-to-4 decoders and one inverter.

Exercise 5.6. How many 3-to-8 decoders with enable are needed to build a 6-to-64 decoder? How many 2-to-4 decoders are needed to build a 4-to-16 decoder, counting the decoder that generates the enables?

Answer

A 6-to-64 decoder from 3-to-8 modules needs \(2^{6-3} = 8\) output decoders, plus one more 3-to-8 decoder (driven by the top three address bits) to generate the eight enables, so 9 modules in two levels. A 4-to-16 decoder from 2-to-4 modules needs \(2^{4-2} = 4\) output decoders plus one 2-to-4 decoder for the enables: 5 modules.

Exercise 5.7. An active-low 3-to-8 decoder is enabled and \(ABC = 110\). Which output is 0? Which gate type is used to implement \(F = \sum m(3,5,6,7)\) from the outputs?

Answer

\(110\) is decimal 6, so only \(D_6 = 0\) and the other seven outputs are 1. \(F = D_3 + D_5 + D_6 + D_7\) is formed by a 4-input NAND gate on the outputs \(D_3', D_5', D_6', D_7'\).

Exercise 5.8. Design an octal-to-binary encoder: give the output equations, state the two limitations of the simple encoder and how a priority encoder overcomes them.

Answer

\(A_2 = D_4 + D_5 + D_6 + D_7\), \(A_1 = D_2 + D_3 + D_6 + D_7\), \(A_0 = D_1 + D_3 + D_5 + D_7\). Limitations: (1) if two inputs are active the output is the OR of their codes and is wrong (for example \(D_3\) and \(D_6\) give \(111\)); (2) output \(000\) is ambiguous between "\(D_0\) active" and "nothing active". A priority encoder encodes only the highest-priority active input, ignoring lower ones, and adds a valid output \(V = D_0 + \cdots + D_7\) that distinguishes "\(D_0\)" from "no input".

Exercise 5.9. For the 4-to-2 priority encoder of Table 5.4, give the outputs \(x\), \(y\) and \(V\) for the inputs \(D_0 = 1\), \(D_1 = 0\), \(D_2 = 1\), \(D_3 = 0\). Also, if \(D_1\) and \(D_3\) are both 1, what is \(xy\)?

Answer

The highest active input is \(D_2\), so \(xy = 10\) and \(V = 1\): \(x = D_2 + D_3 = 1\), \(y = D_3 + D_1D_2' = 0 + 0\cdot 0 = 0\). For \(D_1 = D_3 = 1\) the winner is \(D_3\), so \(xy = 11\): \(x = 1 + \ldots = 1\) and \(y = D_3 + \ldots = 1\).

Exercise 5.10. Design a decimal-to-BCD encoder (10-to-4). Write the four output equations and explain why \(D_0\) is not connected to any gate.

Answer

\(A_3 = D_8 + D_9\); \(A_2 = D_4 + D_5 + D_6 + D_7\); \(A_1 = D_2 + D_3 + D_6 + D_7\); \(A_0 = D_1 + D_3 + D_5 + D_7 + D_9\). Decimal 0 is encoded as \(0000\), so \(D_0\) contributes a 1 to no output column. The encoder therefore outputs \(0000\) both when \(D_0\) is active and when nothing is active; \(D_0\) is used only in \(V = D_0 + D_1 + \cdots + D_9\), which tells "digit zero" (\(V=1\)) from "no key" (\(V=0\)).

Exercise 5.11. Implement \(F(A,B,C) = \sum m(0,2,3,5,7)\) (a) on an 8:1 multiplexer and (b) on a 4:1 multiplexer with \(A, B\) on the select lines. Give the data-input table for each.

Answer

(a) \(I_k = 1\) for the minterms in \(F\): \(I_0 \ldots I_7 = 1,0,1,1,0,1,0,1\). (b) \(AB = 00\): \(m_0, m_1 = 1, 0\), so \(I_0 = C'\). \(AB = 01\): \(m_2, m_3 = 1, 1\), so \(I_1 = 1\). \(AB = 10\): \(m_4, m_5 = 0, 1\), so \(I_2 = C\). \(AB = 11\): \(m_6, m_7 = 0, 1\), so \(I_3 = C\).

Exercise 5.12. Implement \(F(A,B,C) = \sum m(0,2,3,5)\) on a 4:1 multiplexer with \(A, B\) as the selects.

Answer

\(AB = 00\): \(m_0, m_1 = 1, 0\), so \(I_0 = C'\). \(AB = 01\): \(m_2, m_3 = 1, 1\), so \(I_1 = 1\). \(AB = 10\): \(m_4, m_5 = 0, 1\), so \(I_2 = C\). \(AB = 11\): \(m_6, m_7 = 0, 0\), so \(I_3 = 0\). One 4:1 multiplexer and one inverter.

Exercise 5.13. Implement \(F(A,B,C) = \sum m(1,2,4,7)\) on a 4:1 multiplexer with \(A, B\) as the selects and say which familiar function this is.

Answer

\(AB = 00\): \(m_0, m_1 = 0, 1\), so \(I_0 = C\). \(AB = 01\): \(m_2, m_3 = 1, 0\), so \(I_1 = C'\). \(AB = 10\): \(m_4, m_5 = 1, 0\), so \(I_2 = C'\). \(AB = 11\): \(m_6, m_7 = 0, 1\), so \(I_3 = C\). The alternating pattern shows that \(F = A \oplus B \oplus C\), the odd-parity function (the full-adder sum).

Exercise 5.14. A 3-to-8 decoder (inputs \(A, B, C\)) has its outputs \(D_1\), \(D_2\), \(D_4\) and \(D_7\) tied to one OR gate. What function does the OR gate compute? (Multiple choice: majority, odd parity, AND, OR.)

Answer

Odd parity of \(A, B, C\), which is the three-input XOR \(A \oplus B \oplus C\): the minterms 1, 2, 4 and 7 are exactly the ones with an odd number of 1s. This is the full-adder sum.

Exercise 5.15. Construct a 16:1 multiplexer from 4:1 multiplexers only. How many are required and how are the select lines distributed?

Answer

Five: four first-level multiplexers \(M_0\) to \(M_3\), taking \(I_0\) to \(I_3\), \(I_4\) to \(I_7\), \(I_8\) to \(I_{11}\) and \(I_{12}\) to \(I_{15}\) with common selects \(S_1S_0\), and a fifth multiplexer \(M_4\) that takes their four outputs and is driven by \(S_3S_2\). Check: \((16-1)/(4-1) = 5\).

Exercise 5.16. (a) State what appears on the three unselected outputs of a 1-to-4 demultiplexer. (b) State in one sentence how a demultiplexer relates to a decoder with an enable. (c) A demultiplexer's data input is tied to 1. What does it now behave as?

Answer

(a) They sit at 0 (for an active-high design), because each unselected output is \(D \cdot m_i\) with \(m_i = 0\). (b) A demultiplexer is exactly a decoder with an enable, with the data line used as the enable. (c) A decoder: output \(i\) is then \(1\cdot m_i = m_i\).

Exercise 5.17. (True or false) (a) A \(2^n\)-input multiplexer needs \(n\) select lines. (b) A simple 8-to-3 encoder gives the correct code whenever two inputs are active. (c) Decoder expansion is impossible without an enable input.

Answer

(a) True. (b) False; it gives the OR of the two codes, which is wrong. (c) True; without an enable every decoder output would be active whenever its own address bits matched.

Exercise 5.18. (Short answer) (a) Why is a multiplexer a better way to select a source for a bus than connecting all the sources to the same wire? (b) Four sensors are read over one wire with a MUX/DEMUX pair. What goes wrong if the two select buses are one count out of step?

Answer

(a) Directly connecting outputs together causes bus contention: several drivers fight, giving undefined levels and possible short circuits. A multiplexer connects exactly one source at a time, so the line has one well-defined driver. (b) Every sensor is delivered to the wrong destination (the channels are permuted cyclically, for example sensor 0 arrives at \(Y_1\)), and nothing looks broken. It is a framing error, prevented by a common clock or a frame marker.

Exercise 5.19. Show how a single 2:1 multiplexer realises the OR function, and explain why that, together with NOT and AND, makes the multiplexer a universal building block.

Answer

Use \(Y = S'I_0 + SI_1\) with \(S = A\), \(I_0 = B\), \(I_1 = 1\): \(Y = A'B + A = A + B\). NOT (with \(I_0 = 1, I_1 = 0\)) and AND (with \(I_0 = 0, I_1 = B\)) are obtained the same way. Since NOT, AND and OR can build any Boolean function, a 2:1 multiplexer with suitable constants on its data inputs is a universal building block.

Exercise 5.20. (Discussion) A designer must realise a function (i) that is fixed and rarely used, (ii) that might need changing after the board is built, and (iii) that is selected at run time by a control input. Choose among a decoder with OR gates, a ROM and a multiplexer for each case and justify the choice.

Answer

(i) A few gates, or a decoder with an OR gate: cheapest for a one-off function that never changes. (ii) A ROM, preferably an EEPROM or flash device: it stores the whole truth table and can be reprogrammed without rewiring. (iii) A multiplexer: its select lines are the run-time control. Weigh gate count against flexibility and speed, and note that a ROM's decoder grows as \(2^k\) and is wasteful for very wide inputs.

docs.title: Chapter 21: Direct Memory Access and I/O Processors
docs.text:
Taking the CPU out of the data path altogether: bus request and grant, the DMA controller, burst and cycle stealing, and the I/O processor

The previous chapter ended with two modes of transfer and a problem. In programmed I/O the CPU wastes its time waiting. With interrupts it no longer waits, but it still handles every single word, and for a fast device that is too much: each word costs a context switch into a service routine and back. The transfer of data between a fast storage device such as a magnetic disk and memory is often limited by the speed of the CPU, not of the device.

The answer is to remove the CPU from the path and let the device manage the memory buses directly. This is direct memory access (DMA). A small controller, which needs far less intelligence than a processor, moves a whole block between the device and memory by itself, and the CPU is involved exactly twice: once at the start, to set the transfer up, and once at the end, when a single interrupt says it is done. This chapter explains how the CPU hands over the buses, what the DMA controller contains, the two ways it can use the bus, how much time and CPU effort DMA saves, and how the idea is taken one step further in the I/O processor, which executes whole I/O programs of its own.

What you will learn

  • Explain why DMA is needed and compare the CPU effort of interrupt-driven I/O and DMA for a block.
  • Describe the bus request / bus grant handshake, including why the CPU finishes its bus cycle and floats its lines.
  • Describe the DMA controller: address register, word-count register, control register and its signals, and how a transfer is set up and completed.
  • Distinguish burst transfer from cycle stealing and choose between them.
  • Compute DMA transfer times, register contents and interrupt counts.
  • Compare programmed I/O, interrupt-initiated I/O and DMA, and describe the I/O processor (channel).

docs.title: 21.1 Why DMA?
docs.text:
Consider a disk that delivers 4 million words a second. With interrupt-driven I/O each word costs a context switch of perhaps 50 instructions. That is 200 million instructions a second spent purely on overhead, most of a processor, to move data it is not even using. Worse, every word makes two trips: from the device into a CPU register, and from the register out to memory. DMA stops routing the data through the CPU at all.

Example 21.1: Comparing the I/O overhead for one block

Problem. A disk delivers a 4 KB block. Under interrupt-initiated I/O each 2-byte word causes one interrupt. How many interrupts does the block cause, and how does DMA improve on that?

Solution. The block has \(4096/2 = 2048\) words, so there are 2048 interrupts, that is, 2048 context switches into the service routine. With DMA the controller moves all 2048 words directly and raises a single interrupt at completion.

Answer. 2048 interrupts against 1: a reduction of about 2000 times in CPU interruptions.

Example 21.2: The cost of one interrupt per word at disk speed

Problem. A disk delivers 4 million words per second, and interrupt-driven I/O costs about 50 instructions of overhead per word. How many instructions per second go on overhead?

Solution. \(4 \times 10^6 \text{ words/s} \times 50 \text{ instructions/word} = 2 \times 10^8\) instructions per second.

Answer. 200 million instructions per second, most of the capacity of an ordinary processor, spent on moving data it is not itself using. DMA removes all of it except the setup and the one completion interrupt.

This is why copying a large file does not freeze your game. The DMA controller shovels the data straight into memory while the CPU keeps rendering frames. The CPU only set up the transfer (source, destination, count) and will get one interrupt when it finishes. Without DMA, every few bytes would drag the processor into an interrupt service routine, and the whole machine would stutter. DMA is the reason bulk data movement and interactive work coexist smoothly.

There is, however, a cost. The DMA controller and the CPU both want the memory bus. Since peripheral transfers are slower than processor transfers, DMA cycles are relatively infrequent, but they do delay the CPU when they occur.

docs.title: 21.2 Handing over the buses: bus request and bus grant
docs.text:
To let the DMA controller drive memory, the CPU must first release the address, data and control buses. Two control signals do this, and the exchange has five steps (Figure 21.1).

Figure 21.1. The CPU and the DMA controller joined by the two signals BR and BG, with the address, data and control buses below them; the CPU's lines are floated to the high-impedance state.
  1. BR, bus request. The DMA controller asserts Bus Request to ask the CPU for control of the buses.
  2. The CPU finishes its bus cycle. It completes the transfer in progress; it never abandons one half-done.
  3. The CPU floats its lines. It places its address, data and read/write lines in the high-impedance (tri-state) condition, effectively disconnecting itself from the buses.
  4. BG, bus grant. The CPU asserts Bus Grant. The DMA controller now owns the buses and drives memory directly.
  5. Release. When the transfer is done, the controller disables BR; the CPU disables BG and takes the buses back.

Two details deserve a word. First, why must the CPU finish its bus cycle before granting the bus? A memory access already under way cannot be interrupted half-way: the address is on the lines and the data is in flight. The CPU therefore honours BR at the next cycle boundary, exactly as it recognises interrupts only between instructions. Second, why float the lines? Two drivers on one bus would short-circuit. Floating the CPU's outputs makes it electrically safe for the DMA controller to drive the same lines.

The CPU is not stopped during DMA

It gives up the bus, and often only for the cycles DMA actually uses. It can keep executing instructions out of its cache, which needs no bus, the entire time, and it stalls only when it itself needs the bus while DMA holds it. DMA steals bus cycles, not the processor's ability to compute. The controller is said to become the bus master for as long as it needs, and the CPU is a bystander.

docs.title: 21.3 The DMA controller
docs.text:
The DMA controller is, in effect, a very simple processor with just enough logic to count and to drive an address. Figure 21.2 shows its block diagram. It looks to the CPU like any other I/O interface: the CPU selects it and reads or writes its registers through the data bus, using the DS (device select) and RS (register select) lines together with the RD and WR lines. BR and BG are its two connections to the CPU's bus arbitration, and two further wires, DMA request and DMA acknowledge, run to the I/O device: the device says it has a word ready (or needs one), and the controller tells the device that the transfer is happening now. When the transfer is finished it also raises an interrupt to the CPU.

Figure 21.2. The DMA controller: the address register, the word-count register and the control register, with input lines DS, RS, RD, WR, BR and BG, an output to the address and data bus, DMA request and acknowledge lines to the I/O device, and an interrupt to the CPU on completion.

It holds three registers.

Register Holds What happens to it Address register the memory address of the next word incremented (automatically) after every word Word-count register the number of words still to move decremented after every word; zero ends the transfer Control register the direction (read or write) and the mode (burst or cycle stealing); the start bit written once by the CPU at setup

Table 21.1. The three registers of a DMA controller.

The word count is a countdown, and the address is a bookmark: two counters do all the work. One says where the next word goes and steps forward automatically; the other says how many are left and steps down to zero. When the countdown reaches zero the controller raises its interrupt and stops. No intelligence is needed beyond that, which is why a DMA controller is far simpler and cheaper than a processor.

A transfer is carried out in five steps:

  1. The CPU programs the controller like any other I/O interface: it writes the starting memory address, the number of words and the direction into the three registers, and issues the start command. Then it goes back to its own work.
  2. The controller raises BR.
  3. The CPU finishes its current bus cycle and replies BG, releasing the buses.
  4. The controller moves words between device and memory, stepping the address up and the count down.
  5. When the count reaches zero, the controller releases the buses and interrupts the CPU to say the block is complete.

Example 21.3: What the registers hold after 100 words

Problem. A DMA controller is set up with address 2000 and word count 512. What are the two registers holding after 100 words have moved, and when does the transfer end?

Solution. The address register increments once per word: \(2000 + 100 = 2100\). The word-count register decrements once per word: \(512 - 100 = 412\). The transfer ends when the count reaches 0, after the 512th word, when the address register will hold \(2000 + 512 = 2512\), just past the block.

Answer. Address 2100, word count 412; the transfer ends when the count reaches 0.

A footnote on caches: because DMA reads and writes main memory directly, it cares whether main memory is up to date. A write-back cache leaves memory temporarily stale, so a DMA read could fetch an old value; this is one reason write-through is required whenever a DMA controller reads memory, and one source of the cache-coherence problems that arise whenever more than one device can see the same data.

docs.title: 21.4 Burst transfer and cycle stealing
docs.text:
Once the controller owns the bus there are two ways to use it.

Burst (block) transfer. The controller keeps the bus and transfers the entire block in one go. It is the fastest possible transfer, but the CPU is locked out of memory for the whole burst, and so is every other device that might need the bus.

Cycle stealing. The controller transfers one word, returns the bus to the CPU, then requests it again for the next word. It "steals" occasional memory cycles, in cycles the CPU was not using or can spare, so the CPU stays responsive and is only slowed a little. The transfer is slightly slower overall.

Point Burst transfer Cycle stealing Bus use held until the whole block is transferred one word, then released CPU during the transfer cannot use the bus for the whole block runs between words, slightly delayed each time Transfer speed fastest for the block (no re-arbitration) slower (the bus must be requested for each word) Latency imposed on the CPU one long, large gap many short, tiny gaps Suits fast devices: a disk sector, a network frame slower devices, and systems that must stay responsive

Table 21.2. Burst transfer and cycle stealing.

If burst is the fastest, why would any system choose cycle stealing? Because "fastest for the transfer" is not "best for the whole system". A long burst can lock the CPU, and every other device, off the bus for a noticeable stretch, hurting responsiveness and, worse, risking data loss for another real-time device that needed the bus meanwhile. Cycle stealing trades a slightly slower transfer for a system that stays responsive and fair, which is the right call whenever the device can tolerate it. Burst is normal for disk block reads, where the block must arrive as one unit; cycle stealing suits devices that produce words at a steady, moderate rate. A slow device in burst mode would hold the bus idle between its own words, stalling the CPU for no gain. The word "stealing" is exactly right: the CPU is not stopped, it is merely slowed, as though someone had taken the occasional cycle from it.

docs.title: 21.5 Putting numbers on DMA
docs.text:
Example 21.4: A DMA transfer, with numbers

Problem. A DMA controller transfers 512 words to memory. Its address register starts at 2000 and the memory cycle time is 100 ns. How long does the transfer take in burst mode, what is the final value of the address register, and how many interrupts does the CPU receive?

Solution.

  • Time: burst mode moves one word per memory cycle with no arbitration between words, so \(512 \times 100 \text{ ns} = 51\,200 \text{ ns} = 51.2\) µs.
  • Address register: incremented once per word, so \(2000 + 512 = 2512\).
  • Interrupts: one, when the word count reaches zero. Interrupt-driven I/O would have caused 512 of them.

For comparison, with interrupt-driven I/O at 2 µs per context switch the same block would cost about \(512 \times 2 = 1024\) µs of CPU time, twenty times as much, all of it the CPU's.

Answer. 51.2 µs; address register 2512; one interrupt.

Example 21.5: DMA against interrupts at 3 µs per word

Problem. A DMA controller moves 1024 words with a memory cycle of 80 ns. Give the burst-mode transfer time and the number of interrupts, and compare with interrupt-driven I/O that costs 3 µs of CPU time per word.

Solution. Burst: \(1024 \times 80 \text{ ns} = 81\,920 \text{ ns} \approx 82\) µs, with one interrupt. Interrupt-driven: \(1024 \times 3\) µs \(= 3072\) µs of CPU time and 1024 interrupts. The ratio is \(3072/82 \approx 37\).

Answer. 82 µs and one interrupt, against 3072 µs of CPU time and 1024 interrupts: about 37 times as much CPU time for interrupts, none of it doing the machine's real work.

Example 21.6: How much of the memory bandwidth does cycle stealing take?

Problem. A disk moves 2048 words by cycle stealing, one word every 2 µs, and a memory cycle is 100 ns. What fraction of the memory bandwidth does the transfer take, how long does it last, and how does that compare with a burst transfer?

Solution. Each word steals exactly one memory cycle of 100 ns, once every 2 µs \(= 2000\) ns, so the fraction taken is \(100/2000 = 0.05 = 5\%\). The whole transfer lasts \(2048 \times 2\) µs \(= 4096\) µs \(= 4.096\) ms. Under burst transfer the same 2048 words would move in \(2048 \times 100 \text{ ns} = 204.8\) µs, far faster, but the CPU would be shut out of memory for the whole of it.

Answer. 5 per cent of the bandwidth for 4.096 ms. The CPU keeps 95 per cent of the memory bandwidth throughout and simply runs a little slower. That is the trade the designer has to make.

Example 21.7: Fraction of cycles stolen

Problem. A device transfers data at 2 MB/s using DMA in cycle-stealing mode. Each DMA memory cycle is 500 ns and moves 2 bytes. What fraction of the memory cycles are stolen from a CPU that would otherwise use the bus every 500 ns continuously?

Solution. 2 MB/s at 2 bytes per cycle is \(10^6\) transfers per second, one every 1 µs. The CPU would use the bus every 500 ns, that is, \(2 \times 10^6\) cycles per second. The DMA takes \(10^6\) of them, so it takes every second 500-ns cycle.

Answer. \(10^6 / (2 \times 10^6) = 50\%\) of the cycles are stolen.

Example 21.8: Streaming from an SSD

Problem. Streaming a 4K video from an SSD moves hundreds of megabytes per second into memory. Explain why the system uses DMA rather than interrupt-initiated I/O, roughly how many interrupts each approach would generate, and what the CPU is free to do meanwhile. Assume 200 MB/s, 2-byte words, and DMA blocks of 64 KB.

Solution. At 200 MB/s and 2 bytes per word the stream is \(10^8\) words per second. Interrupt-initiated I/O would need about \(10^8\) interrupts per second, each a context switch, which would swamp the CPU. With DMA in 64 KB blocks there is one interrupt per block: \(200 \times 10^6 / 65\,536 \approx 3000\) interrupts per second, about \(30\,000\) times fewer. During each transfer the CPU is free to decode and render the video, run other programs, and respond to the user.

Answer. About \(10^8\) interrupts per second without DMA against about 3000 with it. The CPU is left free for decoding and rendering. The exact figures depend on the assumed word and block size; the ratio does not.

docs.title: 21.6 The three modes of transfer compared
docs.text:
We can now compare all three modes of transfer, the table that examinations ask for.

Feature Programmed I/O Interrupt-initiated I/O DMA Who controls and moves the data the CPU, word by word the CPU inside the ISR, word by word the DMA controller, the whole block CPU while waiting busy-waiting: it polls the flag free: it runs other programs free; it only releases bus cycles CPU interventions every word, plus all the polling every word (one interrupt each) once per block Data path device, CPU register, memory device, CPU register, memory device to memory directly Speed slowest use of the CPU moderate fastest Hardware cost lowest interrupt logic needed a DMA controller and bus arbitration Best for simple, slow devices; small systems moderate-speed devices: keyboards, printers high-speed block devices: disks, network cards, graphics

Table 21.3. The three modes of transfer.

In one sentence: each mode buys the CPU more freedom at the price of more hardware. Programmed I/O costs nothing but the CPU's entire attention; interrupts cost some logic and free it from waiting; DMA costs a controller and frees it from the data itself. When asked to compare them, give the table, then the one-line reason: the three modes differ in how often the CPU must intervene: every word plus waiting, every word without waiting, or once per block.

Note that programmed I/O is not "slow" in the transfer itself, which is as fast as any other method; what it wastes is the CPU's time. Nor is DMA entirely interrupt-free: it still needs one interrupt, at completion.

docs.title: 21.7 The input-output processor
docs.text:
A DMA controller must be told what to do for every block: where it starts, how many words, in which direction. The next step in freeing the CPU is the input-output processor (IOP), a processor in its own right, with direct memory access, that executes I/O programs of its own. The CPU tells it where its program is, and it then carries out whole sequences of transfers by itself. A DMA controller is a porter: you say "carry these 2048 words to that shelf", one job, fully specified. An IOP is a dispatch manager: you hand over the day's job list, and they organise it all, reporting back only when everything is done.

Figure 21.3. A computer with an IOP: the memory unit on a memory bus shared by the central processing unit and the input-output processor, with the IOP connected through an I/O bus to several peripheral devices.

In Figure 21.3 the CPU and the IOP share the memory bus, and the IOP drives the I/O bus to which the peripheral devices (PD) are attached. The CPU is the master and the IOP a slave processor: it is assigned the task of initiating all operations, but the I/O instructions are executed in the IOP. The cooperation between the two follows five steps.

  1. The CPU sends an instruction to test the IOP path.
  2. If the status is OK, the CPU sends a start I/O instruction naming the IOP program in memory.
  3. The CPU continues with another program; the IOP fetches and executes its own commands, using DMA for the data.
  4. When the whole operation is complete, the IOP writes a status word to memory and interrupts the CPU.
  5. The CPU checks that status word for a correct transfer.

The IOP handles the data formatting, the error checking and the transfers, and interrupts the CPU only when it has finished. In IBM mainframes the IOP is called a channel, the I/O program it runs is a channel program held in memory, and the CPU-IOP conversation uses commands such as "send status", "start I/O" and "transfer completed". Because it can execute several transfers, to several devices, with its own conditions and branches, an IOP moves still more of the decision-making away from the processor. The progression to remember is this: with programmed I/O the CPU does the waiting; with interrupts it stops once per word; with DMA it stops once per block; with an IOP it stops once per sequence of blocks.

docs.title: 21.8 Summary
docs.text:
Key points

  • DMA removes the CPU from the data path. The controller moves a whole block between device and memory, and the CPU is involved only to set it up and when one interrupt reports completion.
  • The CPU hands over the buses with BR and BG: it finishes its bus cycle, floats its address, data and read/write lines to high impedance, and asserts BG. The CPU is not stopped; it loses only the bus cycles DMA uses.
  • The DMA controller has an address register (incremented per word), a word-count register (decremented per word, zero ends the transfer) and a control register (direction, mode, start), plus DMA request and acknowledge lines to the device.
  • Burst transfer holds the bus for the whole block (fastest, locks out the CPU); cycle stealing takes one cycle per word (slower, CPU stays responsive).
  • Programmed I/O: CPU intervenes on every word and waits. Interrupt-initiated: every word, no waiting. DMA: once per block.
  • An IOP is a processor that executes its own I/O programs (channel programs), and interrupts the CPU only when a whole operation is complete.
Topic Rule or figure Bus handover BR, finish cycle, float lines, BG, release DMA registers address (up), word count (down), control (direction, mode) Burst time words \(\times\) memory cycle time Cycle-stealing share memory cycle time \(/\) time between words Interrupts one per block (DMA), one per word (interrupts) Burst vs cycle stealing fastest, CPU locked out vs slower, CPU runs between words IOP executes its own program; interrupts once per whole operation

docs.title: 21.9 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 21.1. Describe DMA. List the registers in a DMA controller and explain the bus-request / bus-grant handshake.

Answer

DMA lets an I/O device transfer a block of data directly to or from memory without passing it through the CPU. The CPU programs a DMA controller with a starting address, a word count and a direction, and then grants it the buses on request. Registers: the address register (next memory address, incremented per word), the word-count register (words left, decremented; zero ends the transfer) and the control register (direction and mode). Handshake: the controller asserts BR; the CPU finishes its current bus cycle, puts its address, data and read/write lines in the high-impedance state and asserts BG; the controller then owns the buses; when done it disables BR and the CPU disables BG and resumes. The CPU is interrupted once, when the count reaches zero.

Exercise 21.2. Why must the CPU float its address and data lines before asserting bus grant?

Answer

Two devices driving the same bus lines simultaneously would short-circuit. Tri-stating (floating) the CPU's outputs makes it electrically safe for the DMA controller to drive them.

Exercise 21.3. During a DMA transfer the CPU: (a) executes the transfer word by word (b) releases the system bus to the controller (c) halts permanently (d) polls the status flag.

Answer

(b). It gives up the bus (and need not stop: it can run from its cache), while the controller moves the data.

Exercise 21.4. A DMA controller's word-count register is used to: (a) store the data being transferred (b) hold the memory address (c) count words remaining and end the transfer at zero (d) select the device.

Answer

(c). It is decremented after every word, and when it reaches zero the controller stops and interrupts the CPU. (The memory address is in the address register.)

Exercise 21.5. A DMA controller is set up with address 2000 and word count 512. What do the two registers hold after 100 words have moved?

Answer

Address register \(2000 + 100 = 2100\); word-count register \(512 - 100 = 412\). The transfer ends when the count reaches 0.

Exercise 21.6. Differentiate burst-mode and cycle-stealing DMA.

Answer

Burst mode: the controller keeps the bus and transfers the whole block; fastest for the block, but the CPU is locked out of memory for the whole burst. Cycle stealing: the controller takes the bus for one word and then releases it; slower for the block, but the CPU runs between words and is only slightly delayed each time.

Exercise 21.7. Under what circumstances would you choose cycle stealing rather than a burst transfer? A real-time sensor shares the bus with the CPU during a long block transfer. To keep the CPU and the sensor responsive you would choose: (a) burst-mode DMA (b) programmed I/O (c) cycle-stealing DMA (d) disabling all interrupts.

Answer

Choose cycle stealing when the CPU or other devices must stay responsive during a long transfer, or the device is slow: a burst can lock everyone else off the bus, risking data loss for a second real-time device, and a slow device in burst mode would hold the bus idle between its own words. The answer to the multiple-choice question is (c): cycle stealing returns the bus between words.

Exercise 21.8. True or false: cycle-stealing DMA locks the CPU out of memory for the entire block.

Answer

False. That describes burst mode. Cycle stealing takes only an occasional cycle, one per word, and returns the bus between words.

Exercise 21.9. Why is DMA preferred over interrupt-driven I/O for disk transfers?

Answer

DMA moves the whole block directly between the disk and memory with a single interrupt at the end, whereas interrupt-driven I/O needs about one interrupt and context switch per word. For a disk delivering thousands of words that overhead would swamp the CPU.

Exercise 21.10. A DMA controller transfers 512 words to memory with an address register starting at 2000 and a memory cycle of 100 ns. Give the burst-mode time, the final address-register value and the number of interrupts.

Answer

\(512 \times 100 \text{ ns} = 51.2\) µs; address register \(2000 + 512 = 2512\); one interrupt (when the word count reaches zero).

Exercise 21.11. A DMA controller moves 1024 words with a memory cycle of 80 ns. Give the burst-mode time and the number of interrupts, and compare with interrupt-driven I/O at 3 µs of CPU time per word.

Answer

\(1024 \times 80 \text{ ns} = 81\,920\) ns \(\approx 82\) µs and one interrupt. Interrupt-driven: \(1024 \times 3\) µs \(= 3072\) µs of CPU time and 1024 interrupts, about 37 times as much CPU time.

Exercise 21.12. A device transfers data at 2 MB/s using DMA in cycle-stealing mode. If each DMA memory cycle is 500 ns and moves 2 bytes, what fraction of memory cycles are stolen from a CPU that would otherwise use the bus every 500 ns continuously?

Answer

2 MB/s at 2 bytes per cycle is \(10^6\) transfers per second, one every 1 µs, which is every second 500-ns cycle: 50 per cent of the cycles are stolen.

Exercise 21.13. A disk moves 2048 words by cycle stealing, one word every 2 µs, with a 100 ns memory cycle. What fraction of the memory bandwidth is taken, and how long does the transfer last?

Answer

\(100/2000 = 5\%\) of the bandwidth. Duration \(2048 \times 2\) µs \(= 4.096\) ms.

Exercise 21.14. A disk delivers 4 KB in a block of 2-byte words, interrupt-driven. How many interrupts, and how many with DMA?

Answer

\(4096/2 = 2048\) words, so 2048 interrupts without DMA and 1 with DMA, about a 2000-fold reduction.

Exercise 21.15. Compare programmed I/O, interrupt-initiated I/O and DMA in a table: who moves the data, CPU during the transfer, interventions, best use.

Answer Programmed Interrupt-initiated DMA Who moves data CPU, per word CPU in the ISR, per word DMA controller, whole block CPU during transfer busy-waiting (polls) free until interrupted free; releases bus cycles Interventions every word plus polling every word once per block Best use simple, slow devices moderate-speed devices high-speed block devices (disk)

Exercise 21.16. Streaming a 4K video from an SSD moves hundreds of megabytes per second. Why does the system use DMA instead of interrupt-initiated I/O, and what is the CPU free to do?

Answer

At hundreds of MB/s, with 2-byte words, that is of the order of \(10^8\) words per second, so interrupt-driven I/O would need about \(10^8\) interrupts per second, each a context switch, swamping the CPU. DMA moves the stream and raises essentially one interrupt per block, leaving the CPU free to decode and render the video.

Exercise 21.17. What is an I/O processor? How does it differ from a DMA controller, and what are the steps of a CPU-IOP exchange?

Answer

An IOP is a processor with direct memory access that executes I/O programs (channel programs) held in memory. A DMA controller executes a single transfer set by its three registers; an IOP executes a whole program, several blocks to several devices, with its own conditions and branches. Steps: the CPU tests the IOP path; if the status is OK it sends a start I/O instruction naming the IOP program; the CPU continues with other work while the IOP executes its commands, using DMA; on completion the IOP writes a status word to memory and interrupts the CPU; the CPU checks the status word.

Exercise 21.18. True or false: during a DMA transfer the CPU is stopped. Explain.

Answer

False. The CPU gives up only the bus, often only for the cycles DMA actually uses, and can keep executing out of its cache. It stalls only when it needs the bus while DMA holds it.

Exercise 21.19. Open-ended. DMA lets a device controller write directly to any memory address without the CPU checking each write. What reliability or security risk does this create, and how might hardware reduce it?

Answer

A faulty or malicious device (or a corrupted driver programming the controller) can overwrite any part of memory, including the operating system, bypassing the protection the CPU's page tables provide. Hardware can reduce this by translating and bounding the addresses a device may use, as an IOMMU does: it gives each device its own address space, like virtual memory for devices, so a transfer outside its permitted region is blocked.

Exercise 21.20. Self-test. (a) Name the three registers of a DMA controller and say what each holds. (b) Differentiate burst transfer from cycle stealing and say which suits a slow device. (c) Compare programmed I/O, interrupt-initiated I/O and DMA on CPU involvement and speed.

Answer

(a) Address register: the memory address the next word will go to or come from, incremented after each word. Word-count register: how many words are left, decremented each time; at zero the transfer ends and an interrupt is raised. Control register: the direction of the transfer and the mode. (b) Burst: the controller keeps the bus until the whole block has moved, fastest for the device, but the CPU is stalled throughout. Cycle stealing: one bus cycle at a time, handing the bus back, so the CPU continues at slightly reduced speed. A slow device suits cycle stealing, since otherwise it would hold an idle bus for a long time. (c) Programmed: the CPU moves every word and busy-waits, slowest. Interrupt: the CPU moves every word but does not wait, moderate. DMA: the controller moves the whole block and the CPU intervenes once, fastest.

docs.title: Chapter 14: General Register Organization and Stacks
docs.text:
One shared ALU, a bank of registers, a fourteen-bit control word, and the last-in first-out store that makes expressions and subroutines possible

The basic computer of the previous unit was deliberately small. It had one working register, the accumulator, and every calculation had to pass through it. That is a good machine for learning how an instruction cycle works, but it is a poor machine for doing arithmetic quickly: each time the program needs a second intermediate value, the first one has to be parked in memory and fetched back later, and memory is much slower than a register. A real processor attacks this problem in three ways. It keeps a whole bank of general-purpose registers inside the CPU; it provides a stack, a store with a very simple access rule that suits subroutine calls and expression evaluation; and it chooses carefully how many operands an instruction names. This chapter deals with the first two ideas and with the instruction formats that go with them. The next chapter takes up addressing modes and the instruction set, and the two chapters after that compare the RISC and CISC philosophies and look at multicore processors and GPUs.

The chapter follows one thread. We first draw the register-bank datapath: seven registers, two multiplexers, one ALU and a decoder. We show that everything the datapath does in one clock pulse is described by a single fourteen-bit control word, and we learn the mechanical method for writing that word. We then turn to the stack, built first from registers and then from ordinary memory, and see how reverse Polish notation lets a stack evaluate any arithmetic expression in one left-to-right pass. Finally we compare instruction formats with three, two, one and zero addresses by writing the same programs in each.

What you will learn

  • Draw the general register datapath and explain what the two multiplexers, the decoder and the ALU each contribute.
  • Encode any register-to-register microoperation into the 14-bit control word SELA, SELB, SELD, OPR, and decode a control word back into a microoperation.
  • Perform PUSH and POP on a register stack and on a memory stack, with correct SP, FULL and EMTY handling, and state which convention a question is using.
  • Convert infix expressions to reverse Polish notation and evaluate them with a stack trace.
  • Write the same program for three-, two-, one- and zero-address machines and compare the formats.
  • Count the instructions available in a fixed-length format using an expanding opcode.

docs.title: 14.1 From one accumulator to many registers
docs.text:
The central processing unit has three parts. The register set stores operands, intermediate results, addresses and status while an instruction executes. The arithmetic logic unit (ALU) performs the arithmetic, logic and shift microoperations on data taken from the registers. The control unit supervises the transfer of information among the registers and tells the ALU which operation to perform. Together the registers, the ALU and the buses that join them form the datapath; the control unit supplies, at every clock pulse, the bits that steer it.

Consider what one accumulator costs. To compute X = (A + B) × (C + D) the basic computer must load A, add B, and then store the partial result in a temporary memory word T, because it needs the accumulator for C + D. Only after that can it load C, add D, multiply by the saved value and store X. Seven instructions, four of which touch memory only because there was nowhere else to put a number. With a bank of registers the same work becomes

R1 ← R2 + R3
R4 ← R5 + R6
R7 ← R1 × R4

and the partial results never leave the processor. Memory is touched only for values that genuinely live there. A register is also much faster than main memory: a register-to-register microoperation takes one clock pulse, while a memory access takes many. Keeping the working set on the bench beside you, rather than fetching every tool from the store room, is the single biggest reason a modern CPU is fast, and it is why the RISC designs of Chapter 16 insist on having many registers.

Single accumulator General registers Intermediate results must be stored in memory stay in registers Instruction length short (one address) register fields are only 3 to 5 bits, so still short Speed limited by memory access register to register, one clock pulse Example the basic computer of Unit 4 IBM 360, ARM, x86, every modern CPU

There is a design problem, however. If seven registers must all be able to supply an ALU and receive its result, do we connect each register to every other with its own dedicated path? The number of paths grows as the square of the number of registers: seven people who each want a private telephone line to every other person need 21 lines, and a hundred people need nearly five thousand. The sensible answer is to share one meeting room, the ALU, reached by two corridors, the A bus and the B bus, and to let a receptionist, the control word, decide who walks down each corridor and what they do in the room. Sharing turns an exploding wiring problem into a small, cheap and reusable datapath, and this is the whole reason register files exist.

docs.title: 14.2 The register-bank datapath
docs.text:
The general register organization is a CPU organization in which a set of general-purpose registers is connected through two common buses, A and B, to a shared ALU, whose output is returned to a selected destination register through a decoder. In the course text's example there are seven registers, R1 to R7. Figure 14.1 shows the arrangement.

Figure 14.1. General register organization: two multiplexers select the registers that drive the A and B buses, the ALU computes, and the output is loaded into the register chosen by the destination decoder.

Read the figure from top to bottom. The output of every register in the register file goes to two multiplexers, MUX A and MUX B. A multiplexer is a selector: it has n inputs, one output, and a select code that decides which input gets through. MUX A, driven by the selector SELA, chooses which register's contents appear on the A bus, the first ALU input. MUX B, driven by SELB, chooses the register for the B bus, the second ALU input. The ALU performs the operation named by the code OPR (arithmetic, logic or shift) and produces its result on the output bus. That output travels back to the inputs of all the registers, but only one of them is told to accept it: a 3 × 8 decoder, driven by the selector SELD, activates the load input of exactly one register, and that register latches the ALU result at the next clock edge. The external input can be selected in place of a register by code 000 on SELA or SELB, and the ALU result is always visible on the output lines as the CPU's output data. The ALU also sets the status bits that we meet in Chapter 15.

Two multiplexers are enough to let any register reach either side of the ALU without wiring every register to every other. The decoder is needed on the destination side for the opposite reason: a source selector must pick one of many values and pass it on, while a destination selector must pick one of many registers and let only that one load. Selecting is the job of a multiplexer; enabling is the job of a decoder.

One consequence deserves attention. All of this happens within a single clock cycle. SELA puts a register on the A bus, SELB puts one on the B bus, OPR tells the ALU what to compute and SELD picks the register that latches the result, and all four happen in the same cycle. This is possible because registers are edge-triggered: during the cycle the old values are read out onto the buses and ripple through the ALU, and only at the end of the cycle, at the clock edge, is the result latched. Reading and writing are separated in time by the clock, so a register may safely be both a source and the destination of the same microoperation. The basic computer of Unit 4 had one common bus and no register file; here there are two buses and seven registers, the same idea widened.

docs.title: 14.3 The control word
docs.text:
The datapath is governed by a control word of 14 bits, divided into four fields: three 3-bit selectors, SELA, SELB and SELD, and one 5-bit operation field OPR. Whatever value the control unit places in these fourteen bits, that single microoperation happens at the next clock edge.

Figure 14.2. The 14-bit control word: SELA (3 bits), SELB (3 bits), SELD (3 bits) and OPR (5 bits).

Figure 14.2 shows the four fields. Read left to right they say: take these two, do this, put it there. SELA names the register that feeds the A side, SELB the register that feeds the B side, SELD the register that receives the answer, and OPR the operation the ALU performs. The three selection fields use the same code, which is simply the register number in binary.

Register selection codes (Table 14.1)

Binary SELA SELB SELD 000 Input Input None 001 R1 R1 R1 010 R2 R2 R2 011 R3 R3 R3 100 R4 R4 R4 101 R5 R5 R5 110 R6 R6 R6 111 R7 R7 R7

The code 000 is not a register called R0. On the source side it selects the external input; on the destination side it means no destination: nothing is loaded and the result simply appears on the output lines. A microoperation that should discard its result (for example one run only for its effect on the status bits) uses SELD = 000. Students sometimes lose a mark by writing an operand into "R0"; the seven registers are R1 to R7, encoded 001 to 111.

The ALU operations are encoded in the 5-bit OPR field. The course uses the following sample encoding.

ALU operation codes (Table 14.2)

OPR Microoperation Symbol 00000 Transfer A TSFA 00001 Increment A INCA 00010 A + B ADD 00101 A − B SUB 00110 Decrement A DECA 01000 A AND B AND 01010 A OR B OR 01100 A XOR B XOR 01110 Complement A COMA 10000 Shift right A SHRA 11000 Shift left A SHLA

Notice that the table says nothing about clear. There is no OPR code for it and none is needed: XOR of a register with itself gives zero, because \(x \oplus x = 0\). Notice also which operations use both inputs (ADD, SUB, AND, OR, XOR) and which use only A (transfer, increment, decrement, complement, shifts). A unary operation ignores the B bus, so SELB is a don't care for it, and by convention it is written 000.

Use the codes the question supplies

The OPR codes of Table 14.2 follow the course text's sample encoding, but a question may give its own table (for example ADD = 10010, OR = 01011, or ADD = 00011). Use the codes you are given. Only the order of the fields and the register selection codes stay fixed.

docs.title: 14.4 From microoperation to control word
docs.text:
Encoding a microoperation is a purely mechanical translation, and it is by far the most frequently examined item in this unit. The method never changes.

  1. Write the microoperation out as Rd ← Ra op Rb.
  2. SELA is the binary code of Ra.
  3. SELB is the binary code of Rb.
  4. SELD is the binary code of Rd; OPR is the code for op from the table in use.

Then assemble the four fields in the fixed order SELA, SELB, SELD, OPR and check that you have 3 + 3 + 3 + 5 = 14 bits. The word is "take what is in Ra, take what is in Rb, apply op, put the answer in Rd", written in binary, one field per blank on an order form.

The classic slip

Writing the fields in the wrong order. The microoperation reads destination first (R1 ← R2 − R3) but the control word reads sources first, destination third: SELA, SELB, SELD, OPR. Fix it in memory with one sentence: A and B are the two you take, D is the one you put it in, and A and B come first.

Example 14.1: The control word for R2 ← R4 + R3

Problem. In a general register organization a 14-bit control word has fields SELA, SELB, SELD (3 bits each) and OPR (5 bits). Show how to implement the microoperation R2 ← R4 + R3, given that the OPR code for addition is 00011.

Working.

  1. Destination is R2, first source is R4, second source is R3.
  2. Register codes: R4 = 100, R3 = 011, R2 = 010.
  3. Assemble in the fixed order: SELA = 100 (R4), SELB = 011 (R3), SELD = 010 (R2), OPR = 00011 (ADD).

Answer. The control word is 100 011 010 00011, that is 10001101000011, and 3 + 3 + 3 + 5 = 14 bits. Writing 010 100 011 00011 (destination first) would be the commonest lost mark in the unit.

Example 14.2: Two control words with a supplied OPR table

Problem. Assume the OPR codes are 00000 = transfer, 01011 = OR, 10010 = ADD, 10100 = complement. Give the control words for (i) R1 ← R2 + R3 and (ii) R1 ← R2 ∨ R3.

Working. The registers are the same in both: SELA = R2 = 010, SELB = R3 = 011, SELD = R1 = 001. Only the OPR field changes.

Answer. (i) 010 011 001 10010. (ii) 010 011 001 01011.

The two words differ only in OPR. That is the whole idea of a general register organization: the datapath is fixed and the control word reconfigures it, so one piece of hardware performs every operation in the instruction set.

Example 14.3: Reading a control word backwards

Problem. A control word is 101 010 111 10010, and 10010 is ADD. State the microoperation.

Working. Cut the word into 3, 3, 3 and 5 bits: 101, 010, 111, 10010. SELA = 101 = R5, SELB = 010 = R2, SELD = 111 = R7, OPR = ADD. The destination is the third field, so the microoperation is destination ← A op B.

Answer. R7 ← R5 + R2. The common error is to read the fields destination first and answer R5 ← R2 + R7.

The method works equally well for the eight microoperations that the course text tabulates for this CPU.

Example 14.4: A table of control words, and two special rows

Problem. Using Tables 14.1 and 14.2, give the control word for each microoperation.

Working and answer.

Microoperation SELA SELB SELD OPR Control word R1 ← R2 − R3 R2 R3 R1 SUB 010 011 001 00101 R4 ← R4 ∨ R5 R4 R5 R4 OR 100 101 100 01010 R6 ← R6 + 1 R6 — R6 INCA 110 000 110 00001 R7 ← R1 R1 — R7 TSFA 001 000 111 00000 Output ← R2 R2 — None TSFA 010 000 000 00000 Output ← Input Input — None TSFA 000 000 000 00000 R4 ← shl R4 R4 — R4 SHLA 100 000 100 11000 R5 ← 0 R5 R5 R5 XOR 101 101 101 01100

Two rows deserve a second look. Output ← Input is the all-zeros control word: the external input goes through the multiplexer, through the ALU untouched (transfer A), and out, into no register, a pure pass-through. R5 ← 0 clears a register by XOR-ing it with itself, since there is no clear operation in the table. A dash in the SELB column means that the operation uses only the A input.

Example 14.5: Doubling a register, and why the same register may sit on both buses

Problem. Encode R3 ← R3 + R3, and explain why it is safe even though R3 is both source and destination. Also say what is wrong with the control word 001 000 110 00010, written by a student to double R1 into R6 with the argument "ADD only needs one source, so SELB can be 000".

Working. For the first part: SELA = SELB = SELD = R3 = 011 and OPR = ADD = 00010, giving 011 011 011 00010. It is safe because the register is edge-triggered: R3's old value is read onto both the A and B buses during the cycle, the ALU adds them, and only at the clock edge is the sum latched back into R3. The read and the write are separated in time, so there is no race.

For the second part: ADD uses both ALU inputs, so SELB is not a don't care. With SELB = 000 the CPU would compute R1 + (external input), not R1 + R1. To double R1 into R6, select R1 on both buses.

Answer. 011 011 011 00010 for the first; the corrected word for the student is 001 001 110 00010. A don't-care SELB is valid only for single-operand operations such as complement, increment, decrement, transfer or shift.

How many different microoperations?

The form Rd ← Ra + Rb can be written with any of 7 sources for A, any of 7 for B and any of 7 destinations, so this CPU can express 7 × 7 × 7 = 343 different register-to-register additions, and the same number for each other two-input operation.

docs.title: 14.5 Stack organization
docs.text:
A stack is a storage device that stores information in such a manner that the item stored last is the first item retrieved. It is a last-in first-out (LIFO) list. Only the top of the stack is accessible. The register that holds the address of the top is the stack pointer (SP). Insertion of an item is called push and deletion is called pop; the standard picture is a pile of canteen trays, to which you add on top and from which you take the top one. Nothing is physically moved: pushing and popping change SP, and the data stays where it was written.

The restriction, that you may not reach into the middle, is the whole point. It makes the hardware very cheap, because the only address you ever need is the address of the top, and it happens to be exactly the discipline that function calls and expression evaluation require. Stacks are used for four jobs.

  • Subroutine calls and returns. If f calls g, which calls h, the return addresses pile up, and as each routine finishes the most recent one is popped first. The stack unwinds the calls in perfect reverse order, which is what lets calls nest and lets a subroutine call itself.
  • Expression evaluation, in one pass, with no brackets and no precedence rules (Section 14.8).
  • Saving the processor state during an interrupt without reserving a fixed place for it.
  • Passing parameters to procedures and holding local data.

A pop does not erase anything. It reads the top word and moves SP; the old value stays in its cell until something is pushed over it. That is why a stack looks "dirty" in a memory dump, and why leftover data on a stack can be a security concern. A stack machine, one whose arithmetic instructions take their operands from the stack, uses zero-address instructions: ADD pops two items, adds them and pushes the sum.

There are two ways to build a stack, and they differ in where the words live. A register stack is a small bank of registers with a stack pointer. It is fast but small and of fixed size, so it needs flags to report FULL and EMPTY. A memory stack is a region of ordinary memory with SP pointing at the top. It is effectively unlimited and is what real machines use, at the price of a memory access for every push and pop.

docs.title: 14.6 The register stack
docs.text:
Figure 14.3 shows the course text's 64-word register stack. SP is a 6-bit register, because \(2^6 = 64\), and holds the address of the top item. Two 1-bit flip-flops record the state of the stack: FULL is 1 when the stack is full and EMTY is 1 when it is empty. DR is the data register that exchanges words with the stack.

Figure 14.3. A 64-word register stack: SP points at the top item; FULL and EMTY distinguish the two meanings of SP = 0.

The initial state is SP = 0, EMTY = 1, FULL = 0. The operations are

PUSH (allowed only if FULL = 0):
    SP ← SP + 1
    M[SP] ← DR
    if (SP = 0) then (FULL ← 1)
    EMTY ← 0

POP (allowed only if EMTY = 0):
    DR ← M[SP]
    SP ← SP - 1
    if (SP = 0) then (EMTY ← 1)
    FULL ← 0

Note the order of the first two lines of each operation, because it is different for push and pop, and that difference is what the examiner checks. A push moves the pointer first and then writes; otherwise it would overwrite the item already on top. A pop reads first and then gives the room back by moving the pointer. The first item is stored at address 1: the first push makes SP = 1 and writes into location 1.

The flags are needed because SP is only six bits wide and wraps around. Incrementing 63 (111111) gives 1 000000, and only the low six bits are kept, so SP becomes 0. The design uses this wrap-around as the "full" signal: when a push makes SP return to 0, the 64th word has just been written and the stack is FULL. On the other hand, a pop that leaves SP = 0 has just removed the last item, so the stack is EMPTY. The value SP = 0 therefore has two meanings, and FULL and EMTY tell them apart. The two flags can never both be 1: every push clears EMTY and every pop clears FULL.

Pushing when FULL = 1 would overwrite the oldest item, and popping when EMTY = 1 would return rubbish; these are stack overflow and stack underflow. A real register stack checks the flags before acting.

Example 14.6: How many items are in the stack, and a short trace

Problem. (a) In the 64-word register stack let SP = 000000. How many items are in the stack if (i) FULL = 1 and EMTY = 0, and (ii) FULL = 0 and EMTY = 1? (b) The stack starts with SP = 0, EMTY = 1, FULL = 0. Trace PUSH A, PUSH B, PUSH C, POP, and then PUSH D.

Working. (a)(i) SP wrapped from 63 back to 0 on a push, and FULL was set: every word holds an item, so the stack contains 64 items. (ii) SP was decremented to 0 by pops and EMTY was set: nothing is left, so 0 items.

(b) Apply the micro-operations step by step.

Operation SP Top word M[SP] EMTY FULL start 0 — 1 0 PUSH A 1 A 0 0 PUSH B 2 B 0 0 PUSH C 3 C 0 0 POP (returns C) 2 B 0 0 PUSH D 3 D (C overwritten) 0 0

Answer. (a) 64 items; 0 items. (b) The POP returned C (last in, first out). At the end SP = 3, the top is D, and the stack holds A, B, D. The overwriting of C is exactly right: it had been popped.

docs.title: 14.7 The memory stack
docs.text:
A stack does not need dedicated registers. A portion of main memory can be assigned to it, with a processor register acting as the stack pointer. In the course text's layout, memory is partitioned into a program segment (addressed by PC), a data segment (addressed by AR) and a stack segment (addressed by SP). The stack segment occupies locations 3000 to 4001, and it grows towards lower addresses; Figure 14.4 shows the layout and a stack of three items.

Figure 14.4. A memory stack: the stack is an ordinary segment of memory plus one register that remembers the top. With the stack starting at 4001 and growing downwards, three pushes of A, B and C leave SP = 3998.

In this convention SP initially holds 4001, the address just beyond the last word of the segment, and each push first decrements it, so that the first item goes into location 4000. The operations are

PUSH:   SP ← SP - 1
        M[SP] ← DR

POP:    DR ← M[SP]
        SP ← SP + 1

Overflow and underflow are detected not by flags but by two limit registers. After a push, SP is compared with the upper limit, 3000; after a pop it is compared with the lower limit, 4001. The basic hardware provides no such check on its own, which is why the comparison with the limit registers is needed.

Read the convention before you answer

Two things vary between books and questions, and both change the micro-operations: which way the stack grows, and whether SP points at the top item or at the next free slot.

Convention Push Pop Register stack, grows up, SP at the top item SP ← SP + 1; M[SP] ← DR DR ← M[SP]; SP ← SP − 1 Memory stack, grows down, SP at the top item SP ← SP − 1; M[SP] ← DR DR ← M[SP]; SP ← SP + 1 Memory stack, grows down, SP at the next free slot M[SP] ← DR; SP ← SP − 1 SP ← SP + 1; DR ← M[SP]

The third row is why the two lines swap order: when SP points at free space instead of at the top item, a push must write first and then move, and a pop must move first and then read. Always state the growth direction and the meaning of SP before writing the micro-operations.

Why do real machines grow the stack downwards? On x86, ARM and almost every modern machine the stack grows towards lower addresses, and a push decrements SP. The reason is a space-sharing trick: the program's heap grows upwards from low memory while the stack grows downwards from high memory, so the two share one region and collide only if the program genuinely runs out of space. That collision is the stack overflow that gave a well-known programming website its name.

Example 14.7: A stack traced by hand

Problem. A memory stack has SP = 3000 and the stack grows upwards (towards higher addresses), with SP pointing at the top item. Show SP and the stack after PUSH 25, PUSH 40, POP, PUSH 60, POP, POP.

Working. Push: SP ← SP + 1 then M[SP] ← DR. Pop: DR ← M[SP] then SP ← SP − 1.

PUSH 25   SP ← 3001, M[3001] ← 25         stack [25]
PUSH 40   SP ← 3002, M[3002] ← 40         stack [25, 40]
POP       DR ← M[3002] = 40, SP ← 3001    stack [25]
PUSH 60   SP ← 3002, M[3002] ← 60         stack [25, 60]  (40 overwritten)
POP       DR ← 60,  SP ← 3001             stack [25]
POP       DR ← 25,  SP ← 3000             stack empty

Answer. The three pops return 40, 60 and 25, and the final SP is 3000 with the stack empty. A common mistake is to write M[SP] ← DR before SP ← SP + 1 on a push, which overwrites the item currently on top and loses it.

Example 14.8: Counting items in the downward stack

Problem. A memory stack grows downwards from 4001 with SP pointing at the top item. Initially SP = 4001. (a) Write the first three pushes and give SP. (b) If SP = 3998, how many items are on the stack, and where was the first item stored?

Working. (a) The first push: SP ← 4000; M[4000] ← DR. The second: SP ← 3999; M[3999] ← DR. The third: SP ← 3998; M[3998] ← DR, so SP = 3998. (b) The first item went to 4000, and 4000, 3999 and 3998 are occupied, so there are 3 items.

Answer. SP = 3998 after three pushes; 3 items, the first stored at location 4000.

docs.title: 14.8 Reverse Polish notation
docs.text:
Ordinary algebra writes the operator between its operands: A + B. This is infix notation. A machine cannot evaluate infix in one left-to-right pass, because it has to honour parentheses and precedence, and on reading A + it still does not know what is being added. The Polish logician Łukasiewicz showed that putting the operator before its operands (prefix, + A B) or after them (postfix, or reverse Polish notation, RPN, A B +) removes the need for parentheses altogether. The order of the symbols already encodes the order of operations, so there is exactly one way to read an expression and no bracket in sight.

Infix Prefix (Polish) Postfix (reverse Polish) A + B + A B A B + A * B + C * D + * A B * C D A B * C D * + (A + B) * C * + A B C A B + C *

Read A B + aloud as instructions: get A, get B, now add. Every symbol is an action you can perform the moment you reach it, using only what you have already collected. That is precisely a stack: operands pile up, and an operator consumes the top two. Scientific calculators convert what you type into RPN internally, and so do compilers: an expression tree walked in postorder is reverse Polish notation.

docs.title: Converting infix to RPN
docs.text:
Work outwards from the innermost parentheses, honouring the normal precedence (multiplication and division before addition and subtraction; equal precedence associates left to right). Each time you resolve a sub-expression, write its operator after its two operands; its RPN string then counts as a single operand for the next level. When no brackets are given you must supply the precedence yourself, by putting the brackets in first: A + B * C - D / E means (A + (B * C)) - (D / E).

Convert with precedence, not left to right

In A + B * C the multiplication binds first, so the RPN is A B C * +, not A B + C *. Writing A B + C * converts (A + B) * C, a different expression.

A quick check: an expression with n operands has n − 1 binary operators, and, scanning left to right, the number of operands seen so far must never fall below what the operators need. If a conversion breaks either rule it is wrong.

Example 14.9: Infix to reverse Polish notation

Problem. Convert to RPN: (a) A * B + C * D + E * F; (b) A + B * C - D / E; (c) (A + B) * [C * (D + E) + F]; (d) A * [B + C * (D + E)] / [F * (G + H)].

Working.

(a) Products first: A B *, C D *, E F *. Then add left to right: A B * C D * +, then ... E F * +.

(b) Bracketed: (A + (B * C)) - (D / E). B * C → B C *; A + that → A B C * +; D / E → D E /; then the minus goes at the end.

(c) Innermost first: (A + B) → A B +; (D + E) → D E +; C * (D + E) → C D E + *; + F → C D E + * F +; finally the outer * joins the two halves.

(d) D + E → D E +; C * (...) → C D E + *; B + ... → B C D E + * +; A * [...] → A B C D E + * + *; G + H → G H +; F * (...) → F G H + *; finally divide.

Answer.

(a) A B * C D * + E F * +

(b) A B C * + D E / -

(c) A B + C D E + * F + *

(d) A B C D E + * + * F G H + * /

docs.title: Evaluating RPN with a stack
docs.text:
Scan the expression left to right. If the symbol is an operand, push it. If it is an operator, pop the top two items, apply the operator, and push the result. When the scan ends, exactly one value is left on the stack: the answer. For the non-commutative operators there is one detail to get right. In A B - the value pushed first, A, is the left operand and the result is A − B. Since the stack gives you B first, the rule is: the item popped second is the left operand. So 8 2 - is 6, not −6.

Example 14.10: Evaluating RPN with a stack trace

Problem. Evaluate (a) 3 4 * 5 6 * + (the postfix form of (3 × 4) + (5 × 6)) and (b) 15 7 - 2 /, showing the stack after every token.

Working. The top of the stack is at the right.

(a)

Token Action Stack 3 push 3 4 push 3, 4 * pop 4 and 3, push 12 12 5 push 12, 5 6 push 12, 5, 6 * pop 6 and 5, push 30 12, 30 + pop 30 and 12, push 42 42

(b)

Token Action Stack 15 push 15 7 push 15, 7 - pop 7 (right), pop 15 (left); 15 − 7 = 8 8 2 push 8, 2 / pop 2 (right), pop 8 (left); 8 ÷ 2 = 4 4

Answer. (a) 42. (b) 4, which agrees with the infix check \((15 - 7)/2 = 4\). Had the operands been swapped at the minus, the result would have been \(7 - 15 = -8\) and the division nonsense.

Example 14.11: A longer conversion and evaluation

Problem. Convert \((3 + 4)\,[\,10\,(2 + 6) + 8\,]\) to RPN and evaluate it on a stack.

Working. Work outwards. \(3 + 4\) becomes 3 4 + and \(2 + 6\) becomes 2 6 +; multiplying that by 10 gives 2 6 + 10 *; adding 8 gives 2 6 + 10 * 8 +; the outer product then joins the two halves. The RPN is

3 4 + 2 6 + 10 * 8 + *

Trace (top of stack at the right):

Token Action Stack 3, 4 push both 3, 4 + 3 + 4 7 2, 6 push both 7, 2, 6 + 2 + 6 7, 8 10 push 7, 8, 10 * 8 × 10 7, 80 8 push 7, 80, 8 + 80 + 8 7, 88 * 7 × 88 616

Answer. 616. Check: \((3+4) imes (10 imes 8 + 8) = 7 imes 88 = 616\). The stack is empty but for the answer, which is the check that the expression was well formed.

Two further checks round out the picture. First, the expression A * (B + C) - D / (E + F) converts to A B C + * D E F + / -; with A = 6, B = 2, C = 3, D = 12, E = 1, F = 2 the trace is: push 6, 2, 3 (stack 6, 2, 3); + gives 6, 5; * gives 30; push 12, 1, 2 gives 30, 12, 1, 2; + gives 30, 12, 3; / gives 30, 4; - gives 26. At the division the stack holds 12 below 3, so the division is 12 ÷ 3 and not 3 ÷ 12. Second, the order of symbols carries the whole meaning: 8 2 / 3 - is \((8/2) - 3 = 1\), whereas 8 2 3 - / is \(8/(2-3) = -8\). Moving one operator changes the expression completely.

docs.title: 14.9 Instruction formats: three, two, one and zero addresses
docs.text:
An instruction format is the layout of the bits of an instruction. The most common fields are an operation code (opcode), a mode field that says how to find the operand, and one or more address fields, each holding a memory address or a register number. How many address fields an instruction has depends on the internal organization of the CPU.

Organization Typical instruction Address fields Single accumulator ADD X 1 (AC is implied) General register ADD R1, R2, R3 2 or 3 Stack ADD 0 (the top two items are implied)

The best way to compare the formats is to write the same program in each. The course text does this with X = (A + B) × (C + D), where A, B, C, D and X are memory words, R1 and R2 are registers, T is a temporary memory word and TOS is the top of the stack.

Example 14.12: X = (A + B) × (C + D) in all four formats

Problem. Write programs to evaluate X = (A + B) × (C + D) for a three-address, a two-address, a one-address and a zero-address machine.

Working and answer.

Three-address (3 instructions):

ADD R1, A, B       R1 ← M[A] + M[B]
ADD R2, C, D       R2 ← M[C] + M[D]
MUL X, R1, R2      M[X] ← R1 × R2

Two-address (6 instructions). The destination is always one of the two named operands, so a MOV is needed first to avoid destroying a memory word.

MOV R1, A          R1 ← M[A]
ADD R1, B          R1 ← R1 + M[B]
MOV R2, C          R2 ← M[C]
ADD R2, D          R2 ← R2 + M[D]
MUL R1, R2         R1 ← R1 × R2
MOV X, R1          M[X] ← R1

One-address (7 instructions). There is one accumulator, so the temporary T exists only because there is nowhere else to park the first sum.

LOAD A             AC ← M[A]
ADD B              AC ← AC + M[B]
STORE T            M[T] ← AC
LOAD C             AC ← M[C]
ADD D              AC ← AC + M[D]
MUL T              AC ← AC × M[T]
STORE X            M[X] ← AC

Zero-address (8 instructions). This is just the postfix expression A B + C D + * with PUSH written in front of the operands and a POP to store the answer.

PUSH A             TOS ← A
PUSH B             TOS ← B
ADD                TOS ← (A + B)
PUSH C             TOS ← C
PUSH D             TOS ← D
ADD                TOS ← (C + D)
MUL                TOS ← (C + D) × (A + B)
POP X              M[X] ← TOS

The program lengths are 3, 6, 7 and 8: the programs get longer as the instructions get shorter.

The trade-off is summarised in the table below. More addresses per instruction mean shorter programs but longer instructions; fewer addresses mean longer programs but shorter, more regular instructions, which are easier to pipeline. That single trade-off is the RISC and CISC argument in miniature.

Format Advantage Disadvantage Three-address shortest programs longest instructions (three addresses to encode) Two-address the most common in commercial computers one operand is overwritten by the result One-address short instructions; simple hardware long programs; temporaries go to memory Zero-address shortest instructions; expressions map directly from RPN longest programs; PUSH and POP still need an address

A RISC machine uses a restricted form of the three-address format in which only LOAD and STORE touch memory and every other instruction is register to register; Chapter 16 returns to this.

Example 14.13: X = (A − B) × (C + D × E) in four formats

Problem. Write programs for X = (A - B) × (C + D × E) with the instructions ADD, SUB, MUL, MOV, LOAD, STORE, PUSH, POP.

Working and answer. The RPN is A B - C D E * + *.

Three-address (4 instructions):

SUB R1, A, B
MUL R2, D, E
ADD R2, C, R2
MUL X, R1, R2

Two-address (7 instructions):

MOV R1, A
SUB R1, B
MOV R2, D
MUL R2, E
ADD R2, C
MUL R1, R2
MOV X, R1

One-address (8 instructions). Computing A - B first loses it when C + D × E is loaded, so do the bracket that needs a temporary first.

LOAD D
MUL E
ADD C
STORE T
LOAD A
SUB B
MUL T
STORE X

Zero-address (10 instructions), following the RPN:

PUSH A   PUSH B   SUB
PUSH C   PUSH D   PUSH E   MUL   ADD
MUL
POP X

The counts are 4, 7, 8 and 10. In zero-address code SUB pops B then A and pushes A − B. Counting the stack after every instruction: A and B bring it to 2 items, the SUB reduces it to 1, the three pushes of C, D and E raise it to 4, and the MUL, ADD and final MUL bring it down to 1 again. The deepest the stack gets is 4 items.

docs.title: Counting instructions: the expanding opcode
docs.text:
If an instruction has n bits and the address (and mode) fields use a of them, the opcode has n − a bits and there can be \(2^{n-a}\) instructions. When the instruction set mixes formats, an expanding opcode reuses an unused opcode value as an escape: the bits of the missing address field become extra opcode bits, exactly as the opcode 111 did in the basic computer.

Example 14.14: How many one-address and zero-address instructions?

Problem. A computer has 16-bit instructions and 6-bit addresses. There are 14 two-address instructions. How many one-address instructions can be formulated, and how many zero-address instructions if there are 100 one-address instructions?

Working. Two-address. The two addresses take 2 × 6 = 12 bits, so the opcode is 4 bits: 16 codes, of which 14 are used, leaving 2 as escapes.

One-address. Each escape code extends the opcode by the 6 bits freed by the missing address: 2 × \(2^6\) = 128 possible codes.

Zero-address. With 100 of the 128 used, 28 remain; each gains another 6 bits: 28 × \(2^6\) = 1792.

Answer. At most 128 one-address instructions; with 100 of them, 1792 zero-address instructions.

docs.title: 14.10 Summary
docs.text:
Key points
