Problem. Perform \((-68)_{10} + (+95)_{10}\) using 10's complement arithmetic on three-digit numbers. State what is done with the end carry and why.

Solution. A negative operand is represented by its 10's complement; for a three-digit number this is \(1000\) minus the number. So \(-68\) is stored as \(1000 - 068 = 932\). Add the representation of \(+95\):

  932    (this stands for -68)
+ 095    (this is +95)
-----
 1027
 ^
 end carry

The end carry is discarded. Discarding it is not an approximation: the representation of \(-68\) is \(1000 - 68\), so the sum is \(1000\) too large, and the carry is that \(1000\). That a carry occurred tells us the result is positive, and the remaining three digits are the answer in ordinary form.

Answer. \(027\), that is \(+27\). Check: \(95 - 68 = 27\).

A last remark before we move on. In every example above the working used one fixed width, and the sign of the result came from the end carry. In the next chapter we will give the leftmost bit a permanent meaning as a sign bit and ask the hardware to cope with numbers that are not limited to the positive half of the wheel. Everything there is built on the two procedures just described.

docs.title: 7.7 Summary
docs.text:
Key points

  • A positional numeral of base \(r\) has value \(N = \sum a_i r^i\); the digit gives "how many", the position gives "of what".
  • Base \(r\) to decimal: multiply each digit by its place value and add. Decimal to base \(r\): divide repeatedly for the integer part (read remainders bottom-up) and multiply repeatedly for the fraction (read integer parts top-down).
  • A fraction that terminates in decimal may repeat forever in binary (\(0.1\) is the typical case), so a finite machine stores only an approximation.
  • One octal digit is exactly 3 bits and one hexadecimal digit exactly 4 bits. Group outwards from the radix point; pad the integer part on the left and the fraction on the right. Octal-to-hex goes through binary.
  • The \((r-1)\)'s complement of \(N\) is \((r^n - 1) - N\) (invert every bit in binary, subtract each digit from 9 in decimal); the \(r\)'s complement is that plus 1. The 2's complement can also be formed by copying bits up to and including the first 1 from the right and inverting the rest.
  • \(M - N\) with the \(r\)'s complement: add the complement of \(N\) to \(M\). End carry: discard it, the result is positive. No end carry: the result is negative; complement the sum to read the magnitude.
  • With the \((r-1)\)'s complement an end carry is added back into the least significant digit (end-around carry). That extra step is why 2's complement is preferred.
  • Always fix the word length first and keep every value at that width.
Topic Rule Positional value \(N = \sum a_i r^i\) Base \(r\) to decimal digit \(\times\) weight, then add Decimal integer to base \(r\) divide by \(r\), remainders read bottom-up Decimal fraction to base \(r\) multiply by \(r\), integer parts read top-down Binary to octal / hex group in 3s / 4s from the point; pad int. left, frac. right 1's / 9's complement invert each bit / subtract each digit from 9 2's / 10's complement 1's / 9's complement plus 1 2's complement shortcut copy up to and including first 1 from the right; invert the rest \(r\)'s-complement subtraction add; end carry: discard (positive); none: negative, recomplement \((r-1)\)'s-complement subtraction add; end carry: add back to LSB; none: negative, recomplement

Table 7.6: Chapter summary.

docs.title: 7.8 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 7.1. The binary numeral \((1011.1)_2\) is equal in decimal to: (A) 11.1, (B) 11.5, (C) 13.5, (D) 23.0.

Answer

B. \(8 + 2 + 1 + 0.5 = 11.5\).

Exercise 7.2. The 2's complement of \(01100100\) is: (A) 10011011, (B) 10011100, (C) 10011010, (D) 01100011.

Answer

B. Invert to get \(10011011\), then add 1 to get \(10011100\). (Check: \(100 + 156 = 256\).)

Exercise 7.3. Two multiple-choice items. (i) \((57)_8\) equals which hexadecimal value? (A) 2F, (B) 3F, (C) 2E, (D) 4F. (ii) The 9's complement of the decimal number \(4085\) is: (A) 5914, (B) 5915, (C) 6085, (D) 4914.

Answer

(i) A. \((57)_8 = 101\,111_2 = 0010\,1111_2 = (2F)_{16}\), which is \(47\) in decimal. (ii) A. \(9999 - 4085 = 5914\) (5915 is the 10's complement).

Exercise 7.4. In \((r-1)\)'s-complement subtraction, an end carry means you must: (A) discard it, (B) add it back to the least significant digit, (C) treat the result as negative, (D) prefix a minus sign.

Answer

B. The end-around carry is added back to the least significant digit. Discarding it is the rule for the \(r\)'s complement.

Exercise 7.5. True or false: the \(r\)'s complement of a non-zero number equals its \((r-1)\)'s complement plus 1.

Answer

True. \(r^n - N = [(r^n - 1) - N] + 1\).

Exercise 7.6. Convert (a) \((101101.011)_2\) and (b) \((3A7)_{16}\) to decimal, showing the place-value expansion.

Answer

(a) \(32 + 8 + 4 + 1 + 0.25 + 0.125 = 45.375\). (b) \(3 \times 256 + 10 \times 16 + 7 = 768 + 160 + 7 = 935\).

Exercise 7.7. Convert \((89.625)_{10}\) to binary, showing the repeated division for the integer part and the repeated multiplication for the fraction.

Answer

Integer 89: remainders \(1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1\) (from \(89/2 = 44\) r 1, \(44/2 = 22\) r 0, \(22/2 = 11\) r 0, \(11/2 = 5\) r 1, \(5/2 = 2\) r 1, \(2/2 = 1\) r 0, \(1/2 = 0\) r 1), read upward: \(1011001\). Fraction: \(0.625 \times 2 = 1.25\) (1), \(0.25 \times 2 = 0.5\) (0), \(0.5 \times 2 = 1.0\) (1), so \(.101\). Answer: \((1011001.101)_2\).

Exercise 7.8. Convert \((741)_{10}\) to (a) octal and (b) hexadecimal by repeated division.

Answer

(a) Remainders upward give \((1345)_8\). (b) Remainders upward give \((2E5)_{16}\). Check: \(2 \times 256 + 14 \times 16 + 5 = 741\).

Exercise 7.9. Using only the grouping shortcut (no decimal step), convert \((3C5.E)_{16}\) to binary and then to octal.

Answer

\(3C5.E = 0011\,1100\,0101.1110\), so the binary value is \(1111000101.111\). Regroup in threes about the point: \(001\,111\,000\,101 . 111\) (the integer part is padded on the left, the fraction already fits), giving \((1705.7)_8\).

Exercise 7.10. Convert \((657)_8\) to hexadecimal via binary grouping.

Answer

\(657_8 = 110\,101\,111_2\). Regroup in fours from the right: \(1\,1010\,1111 = 0001\,1010\,1111\). Answer: \((1AF)_{16}\).

Exercise 7.11. Explain why memory is organised in 8-bit bytes, yet programmers write memory dumps in hexadecimal rather than octal. Would octal ever align neatly to a byte boundary?

Answer

A byte is 8 bits, which is exactly two hexadecimal digits of four bits each, so hex aligns cleanly with byte and nibble boundaries and a byte is always two characters. Octal groups three bits, and three does not divide eight: a byte needs three octal digits (000 to 377), and the leftmost digit holds only two of the byte's bits, so byte boundaries fall inside an octal digit. Octal aligns only with word lengths that are multiples of three bits (such as 12, 24 or 36), never with an 8-bit byte.

Exercise 7.12. Find the 1's and 2's complement of (a) \(10110100\) and (b) \(01101000\). Use the copy-and-flip method for at least one and check it with invert-and-add-1.

Answer

(a) 1's: \(01001011\); 2's: \(01001100\). Copy-and-flip: from the right copy \(100\) (two zeros and the first 1), then invert the remaining bits \(10110\) to \(01001\), giving \(01001100\). (b) 1's: \(10010111\); 2's: \(10011000\) (copy \(1000\), invert \(0110 \to 1001\) gives \(10011000\)).

Exercise 7.13. Find the 9's and 10's complement of (a) \(250100\) and (b) \(009900\).

Answer

(a) 9's: \(749899\); 10's: \(749900\). (b) 9's: \(990099\); 10's: \(990100\).

Exercise 7.14. Using the 2's-complement method, compute (a) \(1101011 - 1001010\) and (b) \(1001010 - 1101011\) in seven-bit binary. State the sign of each result and how you determined it.

Answer

(a) The 2's complement of \(1001010\) is \(0110110\). \(1101011 + 0110110 = 1\,0100001\). An end carry is present, so it is discarded and the result is positive: \(+0100001 = +33\). (b) The 2's complement of \(1101011\) is \(0010101\). \(1001010 + 0010101 = 1011111\), with no end carry, so the answer is negative. The 2's complement of \(1011111\) is \(0100001 = 33\), so the answer is \(-33\). Check: \(107 - 74 = 33\).

Exercise 7.15. Using the 1's-complement method, compute \(1010100 - 1000110\) and show the end-around carry.

Answer

The 1's complement of \(1000110\) is \(0111001\). \(1010100 + 0111001 = 1\,0001101\). The end carry is added back: \(0001101 + 1 = 0001110 = +14\). Check: \(84 - 70 = 14\).

Exercise 7.16. Compute \(62574 - 28376\) by (a) the 10's-complement method and (b) the 9's-complement method, and confirm that both agree.

Answer

(a) The 10's complement of \(28376\) is \(71624\); \(62574 + 71624 = 1\,34198\), so discard the carry: \(34198\). (b) The 9's complement is \(71623\); \(62574 + 71623 = 1\,34197\); add the end-around carry: \(34198\). Check: \(62574 - 28376 = 34198\).

Exercise 7.17. In your own words, explain why an end carry in \(r\)'s-complement subtraction of \(M - N\) means the result is positive and its absence means the result is negative.

Answer

Adding the \(r\)'s complement of \(N\) adds \(r^n - N\), so the raw sum is \(M + r^n - N\). If \(M \ge N\) the sum is at least \(r^n\), which produces an end carry (that carry is the \(r^n\) term, and discarding it leaves \(M - N \ge 0\)). If \(M < N\) the sum is below \(r^n\), so there is no carry, and what is left is \(r^n - (N - M)\), the \(r\)'s complement of the magnitude of a negative result, which must be re-complemented to be read.

Exercise 7.18. A student computes \(1000011 - 1010100\) (\(67 - 84\)) in seven-bit 2's complement as follows: "The 2's complement of \(1010100\) is \(0101100\). Adding \(1000011 + 0101100 = 1101111\). There is no end carry, so the answer is \(+1101111 = +111\)." Find the flaws and give the right answer.

Answer

There are two flaws. First, no end carry means the result is negative, not positive. Second, a negative result is in complement form and must be re-complemented to read its magnitude. The 2's complement of \(1101111\) is \(0010001 = 17\), so the answer is \(-17\). Check: \(67 - 84 = -17\).

Exercise 7.19. (a) Convert \((B6F.4C)_{16}\) to octal. (b) Convert \((2413)_5\) to decimal. (c) Convert \((58.375)_{10}\) to binary and to hexadecimal.

Answer

(a) \(1011\,0110\,1111.0100\,1100 \to 101\,101\,101\,111 . 010\,011\,000 = (5557.23)_8\). (b) \(2 \times 125 + 4 \times 25 + 1 \times 5 + 3 = 358\). (c) Integer 58: \(111010\); fraction \(0.375\): \(0.375 \times 2 = 0.75\) (0), \(\times 2 = 1.5\) (1), \(0.5 \times 2 = 1.0\) (1), so \(.011\). Binary: \(111010.011\). Grouping in fours: \(0011\,1010.0110 = (3A.6)_{16}\).

Exercise 7.20. Self-test. (a) Convert \(137_{10}\) to binary, octal and hexadecimal. (b) Convert \(0.34375_{10}\) to binary, showing the repeated multiplication. (c) Compute \(1010\,0110 - 0111\,0011\) on eight bits using 2's complement.

Answer

(a) \(137 = 1000\,1001_2 = 211_8 = 89_{16}\) (group the bits in threes and in fours). (b) \(0.34375 \times 2 = 0.6875\) (0), \(\times 2 = 1.375\) (1), \(0.375 \times 2 = 0.75\) (0), \(\times 2 = 1.5\) (1), \(0.5 \times 2 = 1.0\) (1). So \(0.34375 = (0.01011)_2\). (c) The 2's complement of \(0111\,0011\) is \(1000\,1101\). \(1010\,0110 + 1000\,1101 = 1\,0011\,0011\); discard the carry: \(0011\,0011 = 51\). Check: \(166 - 115 = 51\).

docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
Who this book is for, how it follows the syllabus, and how to use it

This book follows the course Computer System Architecture (DSC02 / DSC03 / GE2c) taught in the first semester of the B.Sc. (Hons) Computer Science programme at the University of Delhi. It starts from a logic gate and ends at a processor talking to memory and to input-output devices, and it tries to keep one thread running through the whole journey: every component that appears late in the book is assembled from parts that were built earlier. The adder of Chapter 4 reappears inside the arithmetic unit of the basic computer; the flip-flop of Chapter 3 becomes the register of Chapter 6, and then the program counter and accumulator of Chapter 9; the decoder of Chapter 5 becomes the instruction decoder and the address decoder of the memory system.

The text is written for a student who has finished school mathematics and has never opened a computer. No electronics is assumed. What is assumed is willingness to work with small tables of zeros and ones, and to follow a procedure one step at a time. The prerequisite for the course is nothing more than that.

docs.title: How the book maps to the course
docs.text:
The syllabus has six units totalling 45 hours. Each unit is one or more chapters here.

Unit Syllabus hours Chapters 1. Digital Logic Circuits 6 1. Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra; 2. Karnaugh Maps and Minimisation; 3. Sequential Circuits and Flip-Flops 2. Digital Components 9 4. Adders, Subtractors and Code Converters; 5. Decoders, Encoders and Multiplexers; 6. Registers, Shift Registers and Memory 3. Data Representation and Arithmetic 6 7. Number Systems and Complements; 8. Signed Numbers, Floating Point and Binary Codes 4. Basic Computer Organization and Design 9 9. The Basic Computer: Registers, Bus and Instruction Codes; 10. Timing, Control and the Instruction Cycle; 11. Register-Reference, Input-Output and Interrupts; 12. The Complete Computer and Control Unit Design; 13. Instruction Pipelining 5. Processors 6 14. General Register Organization and Stacks; 15. Addressing Modes and the Instruction Set; 16. RISC and CISC; 17. Multicore Processors and GPUs 6. Memory and Input-Output Organization 9 18. Memory Hierarchy, Main Memory and Auxiliary Memory; 19. Cache Memory and Virtual Memory; 20. Input-Output Interface and Modes of Transfer; 21. Direct Memory Access and I/O Processors

The course text is M. Morris Mano, Computer System Architecture (3rd edition); the references named by the course are listed under Further Reading at the end of the book. This book is a self-contained account of the same topics, in the order in which the units teach them.

docs.title: How a chapter is built
docs.text:
Every chapter opens by saying what it covers and why it matters, and then proceeds in numbered sections. Three kinds of box recur.

  • Worked examples show every step of a problem, from the statement to the final answer. Read the problem, cover the working, try it yourself, and only then compare.
  • Definitions and cautions pick out the precise statements you must be able to reproduce, and the slips that students most often make.
  • Answers to the exercises at the end of each chapter are folded away. Open one only after you have an answer of your own.

Each chapter closes with a Summary of the key points, often with a compact table to revise from, and with Exercises: short conceptual questions, numerical problems, true-or-false items with reasons, and design problems, every one with an answer. Quick-reference tables for all six units are gathered at the end of the book, followed by a glossary and a short list of further reading.

docs.title: A word on method
docs.text:
Computer architecture is learned by doing. In the first three units that means filling in truth tables, drawing maps and converting numbers by hand. From the fourth unit onward it means tracing instructions through registers, clock pulse by clock pulse, and the book gives many such traces. Do them with a pencil. Where the text writes a register transfer such as AR ← PC, say aloud what it means: copy the contents of the program counter into the address register. A student who can narrate a trace of the instruction cycle without looking at the page has understood the basic computer.

Notation follows the course: a prime denotes complement (A'), a plus sign in a Boolean expression is OR, a dot or juxtaposition is AND, and numbers in the basic-computer chapters are hexadecimal unless a subscript says otherwise.

docs.title: Quick Reference
docs.text:
Tables and formulas of the six units, for revision

These pages gather the tables and formulas of the six units. Each block agrees with the chapter that develops it; look there for the reasoning.

docs.title: Gates and truth tables
docs.text:
Gate Expression Output is 1 when AND \(A\cdot B\) all inputs are 1 OR \(A + B\) any input is 1 NOT \(A'\) the input is 0 NAND \((AB)'\) not all inputs are 1 NOR \((A+B)'\) all inputs are 0 XOR \(A \oplus B = A'B + AB'\) the inputs differ (odd number of 1s) XNOR \((A\oplus B)'\) the inputs are equal

An \(n\)-input truth table has \(2^n\) rows. NAND and NOR are universal: NOT \(= A\) NAND \(A\), AND needs 2 NANDs, OR needs 3. XOR is not universal. A positive-logic AND is a negative-logic OR. Any two-level SOP maps to all-NAND, any two-level POS to all-NOR.

docs.title: Boolean algebra
docs.text:
Law OR form AND form Identity / null \(x + 0 = x\), \(x + 1 = 1\) \(x\cdot 1 = x\), \(x\cdot 0 = 0\) Idempotent / complement \(x + x = x\), \(x + x' = 1\) \(xx = x\), \(xx' = 0\) Distributive \(x(y+z) = xy + xz\) \(x + yz = (x+y)(x+z)\) Absorption \(x + xy = x\), \(x + x'y = x + y\) \(x(x+y) = x\), \(x(x'+y) = xy\) Combining \(xy + xy' = x\) \((x+y)(x+y') = x\) Consensus \(xy + x'z + yz = xy + x'z\) \((x+y)(x'+z)(y+z) = (x+y)(x'+z)\)

DeMorgan: \((x+y)' = x'y'\), \((xy)' = x' + y'\) ("break the bar, change the sign"). Precedence: parentheses, NOT, AND, OR. Dual: swap \(\cdot \leftrightarrow +\) and \(0 \leftrightarrow 1\) (variables unchanged); complement: DeMorgan, so variables are inverted too.

docs.title: Canonical forms
docs.text:
• Minterm \(m_i\): unprimed if the bit is 1, primed if 0. Maxterm \(M_i\): the opposite. \(M_i = m_i'\).
  • SOP: \(F = \sum m(\text{rows where } F=1)\). POS: \(F = \prod M(\text{rows where } F=0)\). The two index lists are complements within \(0 \dots 2^n - 1\).
  • Expand a missing variable by multiplying by \((x + x') = 1\); write a repeated minterm once.
  • Design procedure: state the problem, assign variables, truth table, simplify, draw the diagram. The truth table is the design.

docs.title: Karnaugh maps
docs.text:
• Rows and columns in Gray order 00, 01, 11, 10; edges wrap round (the four corners of a 4-variable map form a group). Diagonals are not adjacent.
  • Groups: only 1s, rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 cells, as large as possible, as few as possible, may overlap and wrap.
  • Reading a group: keep the constant variables (1 as unprimed, 0 as primed); a group of \(2^k\) cells removes \(k\) variables.
  • Prime implicant: cannot be enlarged. Essential: only cover of some 1. Find the essentials first; a minimal cover need not be unique.
  • POS: group the 0s to get \(F'\), then complement (or write each group as a sum, 0 unprimed and 1 primed).
  • Don't-cares: use an X only if it enlarges a group; never a group of Xs alone; never assume all Xs are 1. BCD codes 1010 to 1111 are don't-cares.
  • Beyond four variables: paired maps for 5 or 6 variables, Quine-McCluskey (group by number of 1s, combine pairs differing in one bit, prime-implicant chart) beyond.
  • Static-1 hazard: two adjacent 1s in different groups. Cure: add the consensus term (logically redundant, electrically essential).

docs.title: Combinational versus sequential
docs.text:
Combinational Sequential Output function of present inputs function of inputs and state Memory, clock none flip-flops, usually clocked Examples adder, MUX register, counter

Latch: level-triggered (transparent while enabled). Flip-flop: edge-triggered. Master-slave: two latches on opposite clock phases.

docs.title: Flip-flops
docs.text:
Flip-flop Characteristic equation Excitation, \(Q \to Q(t+1)\) = 00, 01, 10, 11 SR \(Q(t+1) = S + R'Q\), \(SR = 0\) \(SR\) = 0X, 10, 01, X0 D \(Q(t+1) = D\) \(D\) = 0, 1, 0, 1 JK \(Q(t+1) = JQ' + K'Q\) \(JK\) = 0X, 1X, X1, X0 T \(Q(t+1) = T \oplus Q\) \(T\) = 0, 1, 1, 0

SR: 00 holds, 01 resets, 10 sets, 11 forbidden. JK: 00 holds, 01 resets, 10 sets, 11 toggles. Characteristic: inputs to next state (analysis). Excitation: required transition to inputs (design).

Conversions: JK to D: \(J = D\), \(K = D'\). D to T: \(D = T \oplus Q\). JK to T: \(J = K = T\). SR to D: \(S = D\), \(R = D'\). Recipe: wanted next-state table, then the available flip-flop's excitation table, then K-maps.

docs.title: Timing and counters
docs.text:
• \(f = 1/T\); duty cycle \(= t_{HIGH}/T\). Setup \(t_{su}\) before the edge and hold \(t_h\) after it; clock period \(T \ge t_{cq} + t_{logic} + t_{su}\). Violations cause metastability.
  • A toggling flip-flop divides the clock by 2; \(n\) stages give \(f_{in}/2^n\). A mod-\(N\) counter needs the smallest \(n\) with \(2^n \ge N\) (decade: 4, mod-60: 6).
  • Ripple counter: delay grows with the number of stages. Synchronous counter: one common clock, \(T_i = Q_{i-1}\cdots Q_0\) for an up-counter built from T flip-flops.
  • Race-around (\(J=K=1\), level-triggered) is cured by master-slave or edge triggering.

docs.title: Adders and subtractors
docs.text:
Circuit Equations Half adder \(S = A \oplus B\), \(C = AB\) Full adder \(S = A \oplus B \oplus C_{in}\), \(C_{out} = AB + C_{in}(A \oplus B) = AB + AC_{in} + BC_{in}\) (two half adders + OR, 5 gates) Full subtractor \(D = A \oplus B \oplus B_{in}\), \(B_{out} = A'B + A'B_{in} + BB_{in}\)
  • Sum is parity (odd number of 1s); carry is majority (at least two 1s).
  • Ripple-carry adder: \(n\) full adders, carry of stage \(i\) is the carry-in of stage \(i+1\); worst-case delay about \(2n\) gate delays, so it grows with \(n\).
  • Carry look-ahead: \(G_i = A_iB_i\), \(P_i = A_i \oplus B_i\), \(C_{i+1} = G_i + P_iC_i\), \(S_i = P_i \oplus C_i\); carries are formed in parallel at the price of high fan-in, so real adders use blocks.
  • Adder-subtractor: XOR on each \(B_i\) and \(M\) into \(C_0\). \(M = 0\): \(A + B\). \(M = 1\): \(A + B' + 1 = A - B\).
  • Overflow: unsigned \(\Rightarrow\) carry-out \(C_n = 1\). Signed \(\Rightarrow\) \(V = C_n \oplus C_{n-1}\); possible only when both operands have the same sign. Range of \(n\) bits signed: \(-2^{n-1}\ldots 2^{n-1}-1\). A signed carry-out alone means nothing.
  • Arithmetic microoperations: R3 ← R1 + R2 (add), R3 ← R1 + R2' + 1 (subtract), R2 ← R2' (1's complement), R2 ← R2' + 1 (2's complement), R1 ← R1 + 1 (increment), R1 ← R1 - 1 (decrement), add with carry R3 ← R1 + R2 + C.

docs.title: Code converters and detectors
docs.text:
Converter Result BCD to Excess-3 (don't-cares 10-15) \(w = A + B(C+D)\), \(x = B'C + B'D + BC'D' = B \oplus (C+D)\), \(y = (C \oplus D)'\), \(z = D'\) Binary to Gray \(G_{n-1} = B_{n-1}\), \(G_i = B_{i+1} \oplus B_i\); one XOR level Gray to binary \(B_{n-1} = G_{n-1}\), \(B_i = B_{i+1} \oplus G_i\); chain of \(n-1\) XORs
  • 2-bit comparator: \(x_i = A_i \odot B_i\); \(E = x_1x_0\), \(G = A_1B_1' + x_1A_0B_0'\), \(L = A_1'B_1 + x_1A_0'B_0\), \(E = (G+L)'\).
  • 3-bit prime detector: \(F = \sum m(2,3,5,7) = A'B + AC\). BCD prime detector with don't-cares: \(F = B'C + BD\).

docs.title: Decoders, encoders, multiplexers, demultiplexers
docs.text:
Block In \(\to\) out Rule Decoder \(n \to 2^n\) \(D_i = m_i\) (with enable: \(E\cdot m_i\)); decoder + OR gates = any function Encoder \(2^n \to n\) octal: \(A_2 = D_4{+}D_5{+}D_6{+}D_7\), \(A_1 = D_2{+}D_3{+}D_6{+}D_7\), \(A_0 = D_1{+}D_3{+}D_5{+}D_7\) Priority encoder \(2^n \to n + V\) 4-to-2: \(x = D_2{+}D_3\), \(y = D_3{+}D_1D_2'\), \(V = \sum D_i\); \(V\) separates code 0 from no input MUX \(2^n + n \to 1\) \(Y = \sum m_i I_i\); \(2^n\):1 gives any \(n\)-variable function, \(2^{n-1}\):1 with residue (\(0\), \(1\), \(x\), \(x'\)) DEMUX \(1 + n \to 2^n\) \(Y_i = D\cdot m_i\) = decoder with enable (data on \(E\))
  • Decoder expansion: \(n\)-to-\(2^n\) from \(k\)-to-\(2^k\) modules needs \(2^{n-k}\) modules (plus an enable decoder); low-order bits to every module, high-order bits to the enables.
  • NAND (active-low) decoder: selected line = 0; use NAND gates for the OR. A function with more than \(2^{n-1}\) minterms is cheaper from its complement (NOR).
  • Column rule for MUX input reduction: \((0,0) \to 0\), \((1,1) \to 1\), \((0,1) \to x\), \((1,0) \to x'\).
  • MUX tree: \(M\):1 from \(k\):1 modules needs \((M-1)/(k-1)\) modules (16:1 from 4:1 = 5). DEMUX tree puts the high-order selects at the first level.
  • A decoder + OR, an 8:1 MUX and an \(8\times 1\) ROM all realise the same truth table.
  • Simple encoder wrong if two inputs are 1 (\(D_3 + D_6 \to 111\)); use a priority encoder for interrupts.

docs.title: Registers, shift registers and memory
docs.text:
• Register = \(n\) flip-flops, one clock. Parallel load: \(D_i = \text{Load}\cdot I_i + \text{Load}'\cdot Q_i\); Load = 0 holds by feedback. Never gate the clock (clock skew).
  • Shift registers: SISO (delay), SIPO (serial to parallel), PISO (parallel to serial), PIPO (storage). Left shift multiplies by 2, right shift divides by 2.
  • Universal shift register (\(s_1s_0\)): 00 hold, 01 shift right, 10 shift left, 11 parallel load.
Memory facts \(m\) words \(\times\) \(n\) bits \(k = \log_2 m\) address lines, \(n\) data lines, capacity \(m\cdot n\) bits \(1\text{K} = 1024\) \(8\to 256\), \(10 \to 1\text{K}\), \(12 \to 4\text{K}\), \(16 \to 64\text{K}\), \(20 \to 1\text{M}\) address lines to words Chip count \((M/m)\times(N/n)\); depth selected by a decoder on the high-order address lines, width by chips in parallel ROM \(2^k \times n\) \(k\)-to-\(2^k\) decoder + \(n\) OR gates = stored truth table (combinational) SRAM DRAM Cell latch, 4-6 transistors 1 transistor + 1 capacitor Refresh no yes Speed / density fast / low slower / high Use cache main memory
  • ROM types: mask (factory, fixed), PROM (user once), EPROM (UV erase, whole chip), EEPROM (electrical, byte), flash (electrical, block). ROM is non-volatile; RAM is volatile.

docs.title: Q.3 Unit 3: Data Representation and Arithmetic
Number systems and conversion
docs.text:
System Base Digits Bits per digit Binary 2 0, 1 1 Octal 8 0 to 7 3 Decimal 10 0 to 9 - Hexadecimal 16 0 to 9, A to F 4
  • Positional value: \(N = \sum a_i r^i\); positions count from 0 at the radix point and go negative to the right.
  • Base \(r\) to decimal: multiply each digit by its weight and add.
  • Decimal to base \(r\): integer part by repeated division (remainders read bottom-up); fraction part by repeated multiplication (integer parts read top-down).
  • Binary to octal or hex: group in 3s or 4s outwards from the point; pad the integer part on the left, the fraction on the right. Octal to hex goes through binary.
  • \(0.1_{10}\) is \(0.000110011\ldots_2\) (never terminates), hence rounding in floating point.
  • Handy values: \(2^8 = 256\), \(2^{10} = 1024\), \(2^{16} = 65536\), \(255 = \text{FF} = 377_8\), \(1000 = \text{3E8}\).

docs.title: Complements and subtraction
docs.text:
\((r-1)\)'s complement \(= (r^n-1)-N\) \(r\)'s complement \(= r^n - N\) Binary 1's: invert every bit 2's: invert, then add 1 Decimal 9's: subtract each digit from 9 10's: 9's complement plus 1
  • 2's complement shortcut: from the right copy bits up to and including the first 1, invert the rest.
  • \(M - N\) with the \(r\)'s complement: add the complement of \(N\) to \(M\). End carry: discard it, result positive. No end carry: result negative; take the \(r\)'s complement of the sum.
  • With the \((r-1)\)'s complement: an end carry is added back to the LSB (end-around carry); no end carry means negative.
  • Work to a fixed width \(n\); the \(r\)'s complement of 0 is 0; taking the complement twice returns the number.

docs.title: Signed numbers
docs.text:
Scheme Range (\(n\) bits) Zeros Negative of \(x\) Signed-magnitude \(\pm(2^{n-1}-1)\) two flip the sign bit Signed 1's complement \(\pm(2^{n-1}-1)\) two invert all bits Signed 2's complement \(-2^{n-1}\) to \(2^{n-1}-1\) one invert all bits, add 1
  • 8-bit 2's complement: \(-128\) to \(+127\); 16-bit: \(-32768\) to \(+32767\). The MSB has weight \(-2^{n-1}\). Sign-extend by replicating the sign bit.
  • Add: add with the sign bits, discard the carry out. Subtract \(A - B\): add \(A\) to the 2's complement of \(B\).
  • Overflow: \(V = C_{in} \oplus C_{out}\) of the sign bit. Only like-signed operands can overflow (positive + positive = negative, or negative + negative = positive). Opposite signs never overflow. A carry out alone is not overflow (for unsigned numbers it is).
  • Subtraction \(A - B\) overflows when \(A\) and \(B\) have opposite signs and the result sign differs from the sign of \(A\).
  • Shifts: left \(\times 2\); arithmetic right \(\div 2\) (sign kept). Multiply = shift-and-add; divide = shift-and-subtract; result sign = XOR of operand signs.

docs.title: Floating point
docs.text:
• Value \(= \pm\, m \times 2^e\); normalised mantissa (leading digit non-zero), biased exponent \(E = e + \text{bias}\), hidden leading 1.
  • IEEE-754 single: 1 + 8 + 23 bits, bias 127, \(V = (-1)^S \times 1.F \times 2^{E-127}\) (about 7 decimal digits). Double: 1 + 11 + 52, bias 1023 (about 16 digits).
  • \(E = 0\): zero or denormal; \(E = 255\): infinity or NaN; \(E = 1\) to \(254\): normal.
  • Encode in four steps: binary; normalise to \(1.x \times 2^e\); \(E = e + 127\), fraction padded to 23 bits; assemble. Example: \(13.625 = 1.101101 \times 2^3 \to\) 0x415A0000; \(-6.5 \to\) 0xC0D00000.
  • More exponent bits: wider range, coarser precision. Never test floating-point values for exact equality.

docs.title: Binary codes
docs.text:
Code Type Property BCD (8421) weighted one digit per 4 bits; 1010 to 1111 illegal Excess-3 non-weighted BCD + 0011; self-complementing 2421 weighted self-complementing Gray non-weighted one bit changes per step; cyclic ASCII character 7 bits; '0' = 30H, 'A' = 41H, 'a' = 61H
  • Binary to Gray: \(G = B \oplus (B \gg 1)\), i.e. \(g_i = b_{i+1} \oplus b_i\) with the MSB copied. Gray to binary: \(b_i = b_{i+1} \oplus g_i\) (running XOR from the MSB).
  • A parity bit makes the number of 1s even (or odd); it detects single-bit errors only.
  • BCD addition: add digits in binary; if a digit sum exceeds 1001 or produces a carry, add 0110 (6, the six unused codes) and carry into the next digit. Example: \(7 + 5 = 1100 + 0110 = 1\,0010\), digit 2 and carry 1.

docs.title: Q.4 Unit 4: Basic Computer Organization and Design
Basic computer: parameters and registers
docs.text:
Memory 4096 × 16 (12 address lines, 16 data lines, 65 536 bits = 8 KB). Instruction word = I (bit 15) + opcode (bits 14-12) + address (bits 11-0) = 1 + 3 + 12 = 16. Instructions: 7 memory-reference + 12 register-reference + 6 input-output = 25. Stored program: instructions and data share one memory; a word is an instruction only because it is fetched as one.

Register Bits Function AR 12 memory address (the only register wired to the memory address lines) PC 12 address of the next instruction DR 16 operand read from or written to memory AC 16 accumulator IR 16 instruction being executed TR 16 temporary (control unit scratch) INPR 8 input character OUTR 8 output character

Flip-flops: I (indirect), S (run/halt), E (carry / extended AC), R (interrupt), IEN (interrupt enable), FGI, FGO (device flags). Field sizing: address = \(\lceil\log_2 \text{words}\rceil\), mode = \(\lceil\log_2 \text{modes}\rceil\), register = \(\lceil\log_2 \text{registers}\rceil\), opcode = remainder; always add back to the word length.

docs.title: Common bus and control signals
docs.text:
S2S1S0 000 001 010 011 100 101 110 111 Source none AR PC DR AC IR TR memory M[AR]
  • Template for X ← Y: S2S1S0 = code of Y (the source), LD(X) = 1, Read if Y is memory, Write if X is memory.
  • Each register has LD, INR, CLR; INR and CLR act locally and need no bus.
  • Rules: one bus source per pulse; memory only through AR; AC loaded only through the adder-and-logic circuit (inputs AC, DR).
  • IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1 shares one pulse because PC increments locally.

docs.title: Instruction formats and decoding
docs.text:
Class Opcode I Hex Count Memory-reference 000-110 0 / 1 0xxx-6xxx / 8xxx-Exxx 7 Register-reference 111 0 7xxx (one-hot, 12 bits) 12 Input-output 111 1 Fxxx (one-hot, 6 bits) 6

Memory-reference opcodes: AND 0, ADD 1, LDA 2, STA 3, BUN 4, BSA 5, ISZ 6; I = 1 adds 8 to the leading hex digit. Leading hex digit: 0-6 direct, 8-E indirect, 7 register-reference, F input-output. Direct: EA = address field. Indirect: EA = M[address field], once only (one extra memory read).

docs.title: Timing and the instruction cycle
docs.text:
SC (4 bits) → 4-to-16 decoder → T0-T15; IR(12-14) → 3-to-8 decoder → \(D_0\)-\(D_7\); control logic gates AND them (D3T4). SC ← 0 ends every instruction.

T0: AR ← PC
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1
T2: D0..D7 ← decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)
D7'IT3:  AR ← M[AR]          (memory-reference, indirect)
D7'I'T3: nothing             (memory-reference, direct)
D7I'T3:  register-reference, execute, SC ← 0
D7IT3:   input-output, execute, SC ← 0

PC is incremented at T1, not after execution. Memory-reference instructions execute from T4. Indirect uses the T3 slot for one extra memory read; the clock-pulse count is the same as for direct.

docs.title: Memory-reference microoperations
docs.text:
Instruction Microoperations Pulses AND D0T4: DR ← M[AR]; D0T5: AC ← AC ∧ DR, SC ← 0 6 ADD D1T4: DR ← M[AR]; D1T5: AC ← AC + DR, E ← Cout, SC ← 0 6 LDA D2T4: DR ← M[AR]; D2T5: AC ← DR, SC ← 0 6 STA D3T4: M[AR] ← AC, SC ← 0 5 BUN D4T4: PC ← AR, SC ← 0 5 BSA D5T4: M[AR] ← PC, AR ← AR + 1; D5T5: PC ← AR, SC ← 0 6 ISZ D6T4: DR ← M[AR]; D6T5: DR ← DR + 1; D6T6: M[AR] ← DR, if (DR = 0) PC ← PC + 1, SC ← 0 7

Only AND, ADD, LDA, ISZ read the operand into DR. BSA returns with an indirect BUN through the first word (BSA 470 at 30 saves 31 at 470 and jumps to 471; return C470). ISZ with a counter of \(-N\) runs a loop body \(N\) times.

docs.title: Trace checklist
docs.text: Build the instruction word; fetch (AR, IR, PC one past the instruction); decode (AR = address field, I, D); if I = 1 do AR ← M[AR] once; execute; SC ← 0. Final AR = effective address (for memory-reference), PC = instruction address + 1 unless branched. Common slips: PC left at the instruction's own address, AR left at the instruction's own address, S2S1S0 set for the destination instead of the source.

docs.title: Register-reference instructions (7xxx)
docs.text:
Executed when \(r = D_7I'T_3\); each instruction is selected by one bit \(B_i\) of the address field, and every one ends with \(SC \leftarrow 0\).

Sym Hex Bit Microoperation CLA 7800 \(B_{11}\) AC ← 0 CLE 7400 \(B_{10}\) E ← 0 CMA 7200 \(B_9\) AC ← AC' CME 7100 \(B_8\) E ← E' CIR 7080 \(B_7\) AC ← shr AC, AC(15) ← E, E ← AC(0) CIL 7040 \(B_6\) AC ← shl AC, AC(0) ← E, E ← AC(15) INC 7020 \(B_5\) AC ← AC + 1 SPA 7010 \(B_4\) skip if AC(15) = 0 SNA 7008 \(B_3\) skip if AC(15) = 1 SZA 7004 \(B_2\) skip if AC = 0 SZE 7002 \(B_1\) skip if E = 0 HLT 7001 \(B_0\) S ← 0

Skip means PC ← PC + 1. CMA then INC negates AC. Circulates rotate the 17-bit ring AC + E: the count of 1s is unchanged. CMA does not touch E; INC does not touch E.

docs.title: Input-output instructions (Fxxx)
docs.text:
Executed when \(p = D_7IT_3\).

Sym Hex Microoperation INP F800 AC(0-7) ← INPR, FGI ← 0 OUT F400 OUTR ← AC(0-7), FGO ← 0 SKI F200 skip if FGI = 1 SKO F100 skip if FGO = 1 ION F080 IEN ← 1 IOF F040 IEN ← 0

Polling: LOOP, SKI / BUN LOOP / INP (wastes the CPU). INPR and OUTR are 8 bits; FGI and FGO tell the CPU when the slow device is ready.

docs.title: Interrupt
docs.text:
Set R:  T0'T1'T2'(IEN)(FGI + FGO) :  R ← 1        (only between instructions)
RT0:  AR ← 0,  TR ← PC
RT1:  M[AR] ← TR,  PC ← 0
RT2:  PC ← PC + 1,  IEN ← 0,  R ← 0,  SC ← 0

Return address saved at word 0; service routine starts at word 1; routine ends with ION then BUN I 0. IEN is cleared so that a second interrupt cannot overwrite word 0. With interrupts, fetch is \(R'T_0\), \(R'T_1\), \(R'T_2\).

docs.title: Control-gate design (hardwired)
docs.text:
Each control input is the OR of every control function in the table that changes the register.

Register Expressions AR \(LD = R'T_0 + R'T_2 + D_7'IT_3\); \(CLR = RT_0\); \(INR = D_5T_4\) PC \(LD = D_4T_4 + D_5T_5\); \(CLR = RT_1\); \(INR = R'T_1 + RT_2 +\) skip conditions Memory \(Read = R'T_1 + D_7'IT_3 + (D_0 + D_1 + D_2 + D_6)T_4\); \(Write = RT_1 + D_3T_4 + D_5T_4 + D_6T_6\)

Bus select: \(S_0 = x_1 + x_3 + x_5 + x_7\), \(S_1 = x_2 + x_3 + x_6 + x_7\), \(S_2 = x_4 + x_5 + x_6 + x_7\) (encoder of the source lines \(x_1 \ldots x_7\) = AR, PC, DR, AC, IR, TR, memory); \(x_1 = D_4T_4 + D_5T_5\), \(x_2 = T_0 + D_5T_4\), \(x_7 = Read\). Only one \(x_i\) is 1 at a time.

Hardware: memory 4096 × 16; nine registers; seven flip-flops (I, S, E, R, IEN, FGI, FGO); 3 × 8 and 4 × 16 decoders; 16-bit bus; control gates; adder and logic circuit at AC.

docs.title: Control unit styles
docs.text:
Hardwired Microprogrammed Built from gates, decoders, flip-flops control memory of microinstructions (CAR sequences it) Speed faster slower (a control-memory read per step) Change redesign the circuit rewrite the microcode Suits RISC, the basic computer CISC, emulation

20-bit microinstruction: F1 (3) F2 (3) F3 (3) CD (2) BR (2) AD (7); control memory up to \(2^7 = 128\) words. Microoperation = one register transfer in one clock; microinstruction = one control word; microprogram = all the microinstructions that implement the instruction set.

docs.title: Pipelining
docs.text:
Segments: FI fetch instruction, DA decode and effective address, FO fetch operand, EX execute. Clock period = slowest segment (plus register delay).

Quantity Formula Cycles, pipelined / unpipelined \(k + n - 1\) / \(k \cdot n\) Time, pipelined / unpipelined \((k + n - 1)\,t_p\) / \(n\,t_n\) Speedup \(S = n\,t_n / ((k + n - 1)\,t_p)\) Ceiling \(t_n/t_p\) (\(= k\) if \(t_n = k\,t_p\)) Efficiency, throughput \(S/k\); \(n\) over pipelined time

Pipelining raises throughput, not latency. Hazards insert bubbles: structural (same hardware, for example FI and FO both need memory; separate instruction and data memories), data (result not ready; forwarding, stalls), control (branch makes fetched instructions wrong; prediction, delayed branch, flush).

docs.title: The control word (general register organization)
docs.text:
Datapath: register file R1 to R7, MUX A (SELA) and MUX B (SELB) feed the A and B buses, the ALU (OPR) computes, a 3 × 8 decoder (SELD) loads the destination, all in one clock pulse.

Field Bits Selects SELA 3 register on the A bus SELB 3 register on the B bus SELD 3 destination register OPR 5 ALU operation

Register codes: 000 = external input (SELA, SELB) or none (SELD); 001 to 111 = R1 to R7. Sample OPR codes: TSFA 00000, INCA 00001, ADD 00010, SUB 00101, DECA 00110, AND 01000, OR 01010, XOR 01100, COMA 01110, SHRA 10000, SHLA 11000. Always use the codes a question supplies.

Method for Rd ← Ra op Rb: SELA = Ra, SELB = Rb, SELD = Rd, OPR = op, written in the order SELA SELB SELD OPR (14 bits). Unary operations leave SELB = 000. Clear a register by XOR with itself. Example: R1 ← R2 − R3 is 010 011 001 00101.

docs.title: Stacks and reverse Polish notation
docs.text:
Stack Push Pop Register stack (64 words) SP ← SP + 1; M[SP] ← DR; if SP = 0 then FULL ← 1; EMTY ← 0 DR ← M[SP]; SP ← SP − 1; if SP = 0 then EMTY ← 1; FULL ← 0 Memory stack (grows down, SP at top) SP ← SP − 1; M[SP] ← DR DR ← M[SP]; SP ← SP + 1

State the growth direction and whether SP points at the top item or the next free slot. Memory stack limits are checked with limit registers.

RPN: operand, push; operator, pop two (the second popped is the left operand), apply, push. (A + B) × (C + D) is A B + C D + *; A + B × C is A B C × +. An expression with n operands has n − 1 binary operators.

Instruction formats for X = (A + B) × (C + D): three-address 3 instructions, two-address 6, one-address 7, zero-address (stack) 8. Expanding opcode: each unused code gains the freed address bits (16-bit word, 6-bit addresses, 14 two-address instructions: 2 × 64 = 128 one-address, then (128 − 100) × 64 = 1792 zero-address).

docs.title: Addressing modes and the instruction set
docs.text:
Mode EA Mano's example (A = 500, PC = 202, R1 = 400, XR = 100) Immediate none (operand = field) 500 Direct A 500, AC = 800 Indirect M[A] 800, AC = 300 Relative PC + A 702, AC = 325 Indexed XR + A 600, AC = 900 Register none AC = 400 Register indirect R 400, AC = 700 Autoincrement R, then R + 1 400, AC = 700 Autodecrement R − 1 first, then used 399, AC = 450

PC is the updated PC (a two-word instruction at 200 and 201 gives PC = 202). Indexed: field = array base, register varies; base-register: register = base, field = displacement. Relative addressing gives relocatable code. Notation: # immediate, @ indirect, $ relative, (R) register indirect, ADR(X) indexed, (R)+ autoincrement.

Instruction families: data transfer (LD, ST, MOV, XCH, IN, OUT, PUSH, POP); arithmetic (INC, DEC, ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, ADC, SBB, NEG); logical (CLR, COM, AND, OR, XOR; with a mask AND clears, OR sets, XOR complements); shifts (logical, arithmetic, rotate, rotate through carry); program control (BR, JMP, SKP, CALL, RET, CMP, TST). CALL: SP ← SP − 1; M[SP] ← PC; PC ← EA; RET: PC ← M[SP]; SP ← SP + 1.

Status bits: C = C8, S = F7, Z = all-zero result, V = C7 ⊕ C8. After A − B: unsigned A ≥ B iff C = 1 (BHI: C = 1 and Z = 0, BLO: C = 0); signed A < B iff S ⊕ V = 1 (BLT). An interrupt saves the PC and the PSW; a subroutine call saves only the PC.

docs.title: RISC and CISC
docs.text:
Point RISC CISC Instructions few, simple (under 100) many, complex (100 to 250) Length fixed variable Memory access LOAD and STORE only most instructions Cycles per instruction about 1 several Registers many (windows) few Control hardwired microprogrammed Addressing modes 3 to 5 5 to 20 Complexity in the compiler the hardware Examples ARM, MIPS, SPARC, RISC-V x86, VAX, 68000

Register windows: window size = L + 2C + G; register file = (L + C)W + G (G = 10, L = 10, C = 6, W = 4 gives 32 and 74; W = 8 gives 138). The caller's output registers are the callee's input registers. Berkeley RISC I: 31 instructions, three 32-bit formats (opcode 8 bits). RISC-V: x0 = 0, six formats R, I, S, B, U, J; opcode bits 6 to 0, rd 11 to 7, rs1 19 to 15, rs2 24 to 20; add x5, x6, x7 = 0x007302B3; addi x5, x6, 100 = 0x06430293; sub x10, x11, x12 = 0x40C58533.

CPU time = instruction count × CPI × clock period (period = 1/frequency). Pipeline of k segments: n instructions take (k + n − 1) clock periods. Example: 800 × 6 × 2 ns = 9600 ns (CISC) against 1600 × 1.2 × 1 ns = 1920 ns (RISC), a factor of 5.

docs.title: Multicore, Amdahl's law and GPUs
docs.text:
Power wall: dynamic power ≈ C·V²·f; higher f needs higher V, so clocks stopped rising around 2005. Multicore: private L1 and L2, shared L3, cache coherence keeps copies consistent. Flynn: SISD, SIMD (GPU), MISD, MIMD (multicore).

Amdahl: S = 1 / ((1 − p) + p/n); ceiling 1/(1 − p); p = (1 − 1/S)/(1 − 1/n).

p n = 2 n = 4 n = 8 n = 16 ceiling 0.50 1.33 1.60 1.78 1.88 2 0.75 1.60 2.29 2.91 3.37 4 0.80 1.67 2.50 3.33 4.00 5 0.90 1.82 3.08 4.71 6.40 10 0.95 1.90 3.48 5.93 9.14 20

"25% cannot be parallelised" means p = 0.75.

CPU GPU Goal low latency high throughput Cores few (4 to 64), complex thousands, simple Model MIMD SIMD or SIMT (warp of 32) Cache and control large small; area goes to ALUs Best for serial, branchy code data-parallel work (matrices, pixels, deep learning)

Branch divergence: a warp whose threads take different branches runs both paths in turn (32-way divergence is 32 times slower). A GPU hides memory latency by switching warps.

docs.title: Q.6 Unit 6: Memory and Input-Output Organization
Memory hierarchy and chips
docs.text:
Level Technology Access time Capacity Cost per bit Registers flip-flops about 1 ns bytes highest Cache SRAM 1-10 ns KB-MB high Main memory DRAM, ROM 50-100 ns GB medium SSD / disk / tape flash, magnetic 50 µs / 10 ms / seconds TB lowest
  • Going down: access time rises, cost per bit falls, capacity grows. It works because of locality of reference.
  • RAM is volatile (SRAM for cache, DRAM for main memory); ROM is non-volatile and holds the bootstrap loader. ROM family: mask ROM, PROM, EPROM (UV erase), EEPROM, flash.
  • A chip of \(2^k \times n\) has \(k\) address lines and \(n\) data lines. K = 1024.
  • Chips \(=\) (words needed / words per chip) \(\times\) (bits needed / bits per chip), each factor rounded up. The decoder has \(\log_2(\text{rows})\) inputs.
  • Memory map: low-order lines go to every chip; high-order lines feed the decoder. Block sizes in hex: 256 B = 100, 512 B = 200, 1 KB = 400, 4 KB = 1000, 8 KB = 2000.

docs.title: Disk
docs.text:
• Capacity \(=\) surfaces \(\times\) tracks \(\times\) sectors per track \(\times\) bytes per sector.
  • Access time \(= T_{seek} + T_{rot} + T_{transfer}\), with average \(T_{rot} = \tfrac12 \times 60/\text{RPM}\) s. At 7200 RPM one revolution is 8.33 ms and the latency 4.17 ms.
  • Tape is sequential and cheapest (backup); an SSD has no seek or rotational latency.

docs.title: Cache
docs.text:
• \(t_{avg} = h\,t_c + (1-h)\,t_m\); hit ratio \(h\) = hits / references.
  • Address split: word bits \(= \log_2(\text{block size})\); lines \(=\) cache size / block size; direct index \(= \log_2(\text{lines})\); \(k\)-way set bits \(= \log_2(\text{lines}/k)\); tag \(=\) the rest.
Mapping Fields Block may go in Tags compared Direct TAG, INDEX, WORD one line 1 Associative TAG, WORD any line all \(k\)-way set-associative TAG, SET, WORD any of \(k\) lines of one set \(k\)
  • More associativity at fixed size: fewer sets, index shrinks, tag grows, word unchanged.
  • Write-through: memory always consistent, heavy traffic. Write-back: dirty bit, light traffic, memory stale. Replacement (FIFO, LRU, random, LFU) only for associative and set-associative caches.
  • Misses: compulsory, capacity, conflict. Virtual memory: page number translated, offset copied; presence bit 0 means a page fault.

docs.title: I/O interface and transfer
docs.text:
• Interface registers: port (data), control, status; selected by CS, RS1, RS0. Isolated I/O: separate space, IN/OUT. Memory-mapped I/O: one space, load/store, reduces memory, must be non-cacheable.
  • Strobe: one line, no reply. Handshake: two lines (data valid / data accepted or ready for data), timeout detects failure.
  • Serial frame: start 0, data LSB first, optional parity, stop 1. Characters per second \(=\) baud / bits per frame (11 bits at 9600 baud: 872).

docs.title: Modes of transfer
docs.text:
Programmed I/O Interrupt-initiated DMA Who moves data CPU CPU in ISR DMA controller CPU waits? yes (polls) no no CPU interventions every word + polling every word once per block Speed slowest moderate fastest
  • Daisy chain: acknowledge passes through PI/PO; the device with PI = 1, PO = 0 is served; nearest the CPU wins.
  • Parallel priority: interrupt register AND mask register, priority encoder; \(x = I_0'I_1'\), \(y = I_0'I_1 + I_0'I_2'\), IST \(= I_0+I_1+I_2+I_3\).
  • Polling cost: checks per word \(=\) time per word / time per check.

docs.title: DMA
docs.text:
• BR: controller asks; CPU finishes its bus cycle, floats its lines (high impedance), asserts BG.
  • Registers: address (incremented), word count (decremented, zero ends), control (direction, mode). One interrupt at completion.
  • Burst: whole block, fastest, CPU locked out. Cycle stealing: one word per cycle, CPU slowed slightly. Burst time \(=\) words \(\times\) memory cycle.
  • IOP (channel): executes its own I/O program; interrupts the CPU once per whole operation.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Register-Reference, Input-Output and Interrupts
docs.text:
The instructions that finish in a single step, the way the computer talks to slow devices, and the interrupt that lets it stop waiting

In the previous two chapters we built the machine piece by piece: the registers, the common bus, the 16-bit instruction format, the timing signals produced by the sequence counter, the fetch and decode steps, and the seven memory-reference instructions that need an operand from memory. One whole family of instructions has been left to one side until now. When the three opcode bits are 111, the instruction does not refer to memory at all. Either it works on a register that already sits inside the processor (clear the accumulator, complement it, rotate it, test it) or it talks to the outside world through a pair of small registers and a pair of flags. These instructions are the simplest in the machine, because the whole of their work can be done in one timing step, \(T_3\).

The second half of the chapter uses those input-output instructions to ask a question that every real computer must answer: what should a processor do while it waits for a device that is millions of times slower than itself? The first answer, programmed input-output, is to look at a flag over and over again, which is correct and wasteful. The second answer, the program interrupt, is to carry on with other work and let the device announce itself. We will see exactly how this is added to the basic computer with one extra flip-flop, three microoperations and a small change to the fetch phase, and why the designers made the choices they did.

What you will learn

  • Decode the twelve register-reference and six input-output instructions from their one-hot hexadecimal codes, and write each with its control function and microoperation.
  • Trace clear, complement, increment, circulate and skip instructions on given register contents, including the effect on the extended-accumulator bit \(E\).
  • Explain why the input register, output register and the flags \(FGI\) and \(FGO\) exist, and write the programmed-input-output loops that use them.
  • State the exact condition that sets the interrupt flip-flop \(R\) and write the three microoperations of the interrupt cycle.
  • Explain why interrupts are taken only between instructions, why \(IEN\) is cleared during the cycle, and how the service routine returns.
  • Explain why the fetch microoperations become \(R'T_0\), \(R'T_1\), \(R'T_2\) once interrupts exist.

docs.title: 11.1 Instructions that finish in one step
docs.text:
Recall how the 16-bit instruction word is divided. Bit 15 is the mode bit \(I\), bits 14 to 12 are the operation code and bits 11 to 0 hold an address. For opcodes 000 to 110 the address field names a memory word, and the seven memory-reference instructions follow. The eighth opcode, 111, is used differently: it is an escape. The twelve low bits are no longer an address, and the mode bit no longer chooses between direct and indirect addressing. Instead the mode bit separates two classes of instruction.

  • With \(D_7 = 1\) and \(I = 0\) the instruction is a register-reference instruction, whose hexadecimal code has the form 7xxx.
  • With \(D_7 = 1\) and \(I = 1\) the instruction is an input-output instruction, with a code of the form Fxxx.

Here \(D_7\) is the output of the 3 × 8 operation decoder that is 1 when the opcode is 111. At timing step \(T_3\), the point where the control unit has just finished any indirect-address step, the hardware looks at \(D_7\) and \(I\) and sorts the instruction into one of the two classes. It is customary to give the two conditions their own names:

\[r = D_7 I' T_3 \qquad\text{(register-reference)} \qquad\qquad p = D_7 I T_3 \qquad\text{(input-output)}\]

The signal \(r\) is true only at \(T_3\) and only for a register-reference instruction. The signal \(p\) is true only at \(T_3\) and only for an input-output instruction. Because both classes are over after one timing step, each of them contains the common microoperation \(r\!:\ SC \leftarrow 0\) or \(p\!:\ SC \leftarrow 0\), which returns the sequence counter to zero and starts the next fetch. A register-reference or input-output instruction therefore occupies exactly four clock pulses, \(T_0\) to \(T_3\), compared with five to seven for a memory-reference instruction.

docs.title: One bit per instruction
docs.text:
How does the machine know which of the twelve register-reference instructions it has been given? In a memory-reference instruction the three opcode bits are decoded into eight lines, one of which is chosen. The twelve low bits of a 7xxx word work in a different way. Each bit position is wired to one operation, so the instruction is recognised by which single bit is set. Let \(B_i\) denote bit \(i\) of the instruction register. Then each register-reference instruction is a control function of the form \(rB_i\), the control signal \(r\) ANDed with the bit that selects the operation. Think of the twelve bits as a panel of light switches rather than a dial: flip bit 11 and the accumulator is cleared; flip bit 5 and it is incremented. No decoder is needed, because each bit connects directly to its own small control action, and this is also why these instructions can finish in a single step.

The consequence for hexadecimal codes is that every code is a power of two within the low twelve bits. 7800 has bit 11 set, 7020 has bit 5 set and 7001 has bit 0 set. The same idea holds for the input-output class, where the six instructions use bits 11 down to 6.

docs.title: The twelve register-reference instructions
docs.text:
Table 11.1 lists all twelve. Read the control function and the microoperation together: the symbol before the colon is the condition that must be true, and what follows the colon is what happens on the next clock pulse.

Symbol Hex Bit Control function and microoperation Meaning CLA 7800 \(B_{11}\) \(rB_{11}\): AC ← 0 Clear AC CLE 7400 \(B_{10}\) \(rB_{10}\): E ← 0 Clear E CMA 7200 \(B_9\) \(rB_9\): AC ← AC' Complement AC CME 7100 \(B_8\) \(rB_8\): E ← E' Complement E CIR 7080 \(B_7\) \(rB_7\): AC ← shr AC, AC(15) ← E, E ← AC(0) Circulate right through E CIL 7040 \(B_6\) \(rB_6\): AC ← shl AC, AC(0) ← E, E ← AC(15) Circulate left through E INC 7020 \(B_5\) \(rB_5\): AC ← AC + 1 Increment AC SPA 7010 \(B_4\) \(rB_4\): if (AC(15) = 0) then (PC ← PC + 1) Skip if AC positive SNA 7008 \(B_3\) \(rB_3\): if (AC(15) = 1) then (PC ← PC + 1) Skip if AC negative SZA 7004 \(B_2\) \(rB_2\): if (AC = 0) then (PC ← PC + 1) Skip if AC zero SZE 7002 \(B_1\) \(rB_1\): if (E = 0) then (PC ← PC + 1) Skip if E zero HLT 7001 \(B_0\) \(rB_0\): S ← 0 Halt the computer

Table 11.1. The register-reference instructions. Every one of them also performs \(r\!:\ SC \leftarrow 0\), so each ends at \(T_3\).

Notice how the table is organised. The first two rows act on the accumulator and the extended bit \(E\) by clearing them, the next two complement them, the two circulate instructions rotate the pair, INC adds one, four skip instructions test a condition, and HLT stops everything. We now take these groups in turn.

Example 11.1: Decoding register-reference and input-output words

Problem. Identify each word, giving its class and the instruction: (a) 7800, (b) 7100, (c) 7001, (d) F800, (e) F400, (f) F080.

Working. Write the first hexadecimal digit in binary. A leading 7 is 0111, so \(I = 0\) and the opcode is 111: register-reference. A leading F is 1111, so \(I = 1\) and the opcode is 111: input-output. Then find the single set bit among the low twelve.

Word Class Low 12 bits Set bit Instruction 7800 register-reference 1000 0000 0000 \(B_{11}\) CLA 7100 register-reference 0001 0000 0000 \(B_8\) CME 7001 register-reference 0000 0000 0001 \(B_0\) HLT F800 input-output 1000 0000 0000 \(B_{11}\) INP F400 input-output 0100 0000 0000 \(B_{10}\) OUT F080 input-output 0000 1000 0000 \(B_7\) ION

Answer. CLA, CME and HLT are register-reference instructions; INP, OUT and ION are input-output instructions.

Example 11.2: Writing the control function of an instruction

Problem. Write the control function and the microoperations of CLA, INC, SZA and SPA.

Working. Each instruction is selected by \(D_7 I' T_3\) and its own bit \(B_i\), and it ends with \(SC \leftarrow 0\). Using Table 11.1:

D7 I' T3 B11 :  AC ← 0,                       SC ← 0      (CLA)
D7 I' T3 B5  :  AC ← AC + 1,                  SC ← 0      (INC)
D7 I' T3 B2  :  if (AC = 0) then (PC ← PC+1), SC ← 0      (SZA)
D7 I' T3 B4  :  if (AC(15) = 0) then (PC ← PC+1), SC ← 0  (SPA)

Answer. As above. The control function matters as much as the transfer: \(D_7I'T_3B_4\) says that the instruction is register-reference, that it is executed at \(T_3\), and that bit 4 selects it.

docs.title: 11.2 Clear, complement and increment
docs.text:
The five instructions CLA, CLE, CMA, CME and INC are the arithmetic and logic operations of this family. CLA and CLE set the accumulator or the extended bit to zero. CMA and CME replace their register by its one's complement, that is, they invert every bit of AC or the single bit of \(E\). INC adds one to AC. All five take one clock pulse after \(T_3\) begins and none of them touches memory.

A recurrent confusion concerns what each instruction leaves alone. CMA changes only AC. It does not touch \(E\), and \(E\) is the business of CME, a different instruction. INC adds one to AC but does not touch \(E\), even if the addition wraps from FFFF to 0000, and the carry that would have emerged is simply discarded. Finally, no register-reference instruction changes PC, apart from the skips, and no register-reference instruction needs the address that the decode step copied into AR.

Example 11.3: Executing CMA

Problem. The basic computer has AC = A937 and \(E = 1\). The instruction 7200 (CMA) is stored at address 021, and PC = 021. Find AC, \(E\), PC, AR and IR after CMA has executed. All values are hexadecimal.

Working.

Fetch    T0: AR ← PC               AR = 021
         T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC+1 IR = 7200, PC = 022
Decode   T2: AR ← IR(0-11)         AR = 200
             I ← IR(15)            7 = 0111, so I = 0 and opcode = 111: D7 = 1
Execute  T3: D7 I' T3 = r is true. The low 12 bits of 7200 are 0010 0000 0000,
             so B9 is set: this is CMA.  AC ← AC',  SC ← 0

Complement A937 hexadecimal digit by digit, or bit by bit:

A937 = 1010 1001 0011 0111
AC'  = 0101 0110 1100 1000 = 56C8

Answer. AC = 56C8, \(E = 1\) (CMA does not touch \(E\)), PC = 022, AR = 200, IR = 7200.

Common slips. There are three. Complementing \(E\) as well (that is CME, a different instruction). Leaving AR at 021, whereas \(T_2\) copied the twelve low bits of IR into AR even though a register-reference instruction never uses them. And leaving PC at 021, forgetting that PC was incremented at \(T_1\).

Two of these instructions together give the most useful operation in the family. The two's complement of a number is its one's complement plus one, so a CMA followed by an INC negates the accumulator.

Example 11.4: What do CLA, CMA, INC do together?

Problem. What is the effect of the three-instruction sequence CLA, CMA, INC, and of CMA, INC on its own when AC = 0005?

Working. CLA gives AC = 0000. CMA complements it: AC = FFFF. INC adds one: FFFF + 1 = 0000, the carry is discarded (INC does not touch \(E\)), so AC returns to 0000. The sequence is the two's-complement negation of zero, and zero is its own negative.

For AC = 0005: CMA gives FFFA; INC gives FFFB, which is \(-5\) in 16-bit two's complement.

Answer. CLA, CMA, INC leaves AC = 0000. CMA followed by INC negates a number: 0005 becomes FFFB.

docs.title: 11.3 The circulate instructions
docs.text:
The two instructions CIR and CIL rotate the contents of AC one place, using the extended bit \(E\) as a seventeenth bit. We say that the 16 bits of AC together with \(E\) form a ring of 17 bits.

For CIR, circulate right, every bit of AC moves one place towards the least significant end: AC(15) ← E, AC(14) ← AC(15), and so on down to AC(0) ← AC(1). The bit that falls off the right end, AC(0), does not disappear, because it goes into \(E\), and the old \(E\) enters at the left end. In the notation of Table 11.1: AC ← shr AC, AC(15) ← E, E ← AC(0). CIL is the mirror image: AC ← shl AC, AC(0) ← E, E ← AC(15).

CIR:   E → AC(15) → AC(14) → ... → AC(1) → AC(0) → E        (right-moving ring of 17 bits)
CIL:   E ← AC(15) ← AC(14) ← ... ← AC(1) ← AC(0) ← E        (left-moving ring of 17 bits)

Because the ring is closed, nothing is lost. This is what distinguishes a circulate from a plain shift, in which a bit falls off one end and a zero is brought in at the other. A useful check on any trace is that the total number of 1s in \(E\) and AC is the same before and after, and that a CIL followed by a CIR (or the reverse) restores the original values.

Example 11.5: CIR and CIL on AC = 8001

Problem. AC = 8001 and \(E = 0\). Give AC and \(E\) after (a) CIR, (b) then CIL; and say whether SNA would skip in each state.

Working.

(a) 8001 = 1000 0000 0000 0001. CIR moves every bit right. AC(0) = 1 goes into \(E\), and the old \(E\) = 0 enters AC(15). New AC = 0100 0000 0000 0000 = 4000, and \(E = 1\).

(b) CIL moves every bit left. AC(15) = 0 goes into \(E\) and the old \(E\) = 1 enters AC(0). AC = 1000 0000 0000 0001 = 8001, \(E = 0\). We are back where we started, as a left circulation after a right one must be.

(c) SNA skips when AC(15) = 1: it would skip for 8001 and not for 4000.

Answer. (a) AC = 4000, \(E = 1\). (b) AC = 8001, \(E = 0\). (c) SNA skips in the second state only.

Example 11.6: CIL followed by CIR

Problem. AC = B6D1 and \(E = 0\). Apply CIL and then CIR.

Working. B6D1 = 1011 0110 1101 0001. CIL: the old AC(15) = 1 goes to \(E\), all bits move left, and the old \(E\) = 0 enters AC(0). The result is 0110 1101 1010 0010 = 6DA2 with \(E = 1\). CIR on this result: the old AC(0) = 0 goes to \(E\), the bits move right, and the old \(E\) = 1 enters AC(15): 1011 0110 1101 0001 = B6D1, \(E = 0\).

Answer. After CIL, AC = 6DA2 and \(E = 1\); after the following CIR the original AC = B6D1, \(E = 0\) is restored.

Example 11.7: A circular shift on an 8-bit number

Problem. The 8-bit number 0010 1101 is shifted left circularly by 2 positions. Give the result in binary and the hexadecimal value before and after.

Working. 0010 1101 splits into the nibbles 0010 and 1101, which is 2D in hexadecimal. The first circular left shift moves the leading 0 round to the right end: 0010 1101 → 0101 1010. The leading bit is again 0 and wraps round: 0101 1010 → 1011 0100, which is B4 in hexadecimal. As a check, there are four 1s before and four after.

Answer. The result is 1011 0100; the hexadecimal value is 2D before and B4 after.

Circular shift versus logical shift, and when E is involved

A logical left shift feeds zeros in at the right. For the number above it would also give 1011 0100, but only by luck: it gives 1010 1100 for a number with 1s at the top. In a circular shift the bit that leaves the left end re-enters at the right, so count the 1s as a check. Also note that a question that asks for "a left shift by 2 of an 8-bit number" with no mention of \(E\) wants a plain 8-bit circular shift. Bring \(E\) in only when the question is about the basic computer's CIL or CIR instruction, which rotate the 17-bit ring.

Doubling and halving

A shift is also arithmetic. Clearing \(E\) with CLE and then executing CIL doubles an unsigned number in AC, and \(E\) collects the bit that overflowed. CLE followed by CIR halves it, with \(E\) receiving the remainder bit. This is why multiplication and division by powers of two are almost free in hardware, and why shift-and-add is how a simple machine multiplies at all.

docs.title: 11.4 Skip instructions and halt
docs.text:
The basic computer has no if statement. What it has instead are the four skip instructions SPA, SNA, SZA and SZE. Each one tests a condition and, if the condition is true, adds one to PC. Since PC was already incremented to point at the next instruction at \(T_1\), this second increment makes it point at the instruction after that, so the very next instruction is skipped.

Instruction Skips the next instruction when Test performed on SPA AC is positive (or zero) AC(15) = 0 SNA AC is negative AC(15) = 1 SZA AC is zero all 16 bits of AC are 0 SZE E is zero E = 0

Table 11.2. The four skip instructions.

SPA and SNA examine only bit 15. The reason is that signed numbers in the basic computer are held in two's complement, and in that representation bit 15 is the sign: 0 means positive or zero, 1 means negative. "Skip if positive" is therefore literally "skip if the top bit is 0", which costs one gate rather than a comparison. Note also that the name SPA is slightly generous, since 0000 has AC(15) = 0 and so SPA also skips when AC is zero.

docs.title: Skip plus branch is the ancestor of if/else
docs.text:
Programmers use the skip instructions by putting a branch (BUN) in the slot that may be skipped. Then "skip the branch" means "fall through" and "do not skip" means "take the branch". For example,

        SZA              / skip next if AC = 0
        BUN NOTZERO      / AC was not zero: go there
        ...              / AC was zero: this runs

is exactly the same as the high-level statement if (AC == 0) { ... } else goto NOTZERO;. Every branch that you write in C or Python is compiled down, in the end, to a conditional skip or its equivalent plus a jump. You are looking at the great-grandparent of the if/else statement.

Example 11.8: Which skip instructions fire?

Problem. AC = 0000 and \(E = 1\). Which of SPA, SNA, SZA and SZE cause a skip?

Working. Test each condition against the register contents. SPA: AC(15) = 0, so AC is positive (zero counts) and the instruction skips. SNA: AC(15) = 0, not 1, so no skip. SZA: AC = 0, so it skips. SZE: \(E = 1\), not 0, so no skip.

Answer. SPA and SZA skip; SNA and SZE do not.

docs.title: Halting the machine
docs.text: The last instruction, HLT, executes S ← 0. Here \(S\) is the start-stop flip-flop: while \(S = 1\) the sequence counter keeps running and the computer fetches and executes instructions, but when \(S = 0\) the computer halts. HLT is the only way a program stops the machine. A program that lacks one simply runs on into whatever happens to be in memory after it.

docs.title: Composing instructions: subtraction
docs.text:
The basic computer has no subtract instruction, but the instructions we have met are enough to build one. Since \(A - B = A + (-B)\), and CMA followed by INC negates the accumulator, subtraction is a short program. We want \(AC \leftarrow AC - M[X]\).

Example 11.9: Subtracting a memory word

Problem. Using only existing instructions, write a sequence that leaves \(AC - M[X]\) in AC, and trace it for AC = 0030 and \(M[X]\) = 0012. Let TMP be a free memory word.

Working. We must negate the memory word, but that destroys AC, because LDA overwrites the accumulator. So AC is first saved in TMP, and then the negated memory word is added to it.

        STA TMP       / M[TMP] ← AC: save the original AC
        LDA X         / AC ← M[X]
        CMA           / AC ← AC'
        INC           / AC ← AC + 1, so AC = −M[X]
        ADD TMP       / AC ← AC + M[TMP] = −M[X] + original AC

Trace: after STA, TMP = 0030. After LDA, AC = 0012. CMA gives FFED. INC gives FFEE (which is \(-18\)). ADD adds 0030: FFEE + 0030 = 1001E, so AC = 001E and the carry sets \(E = 1\).

Answer. AC = 001E, that is \(48 - 18 = 30\) in decimal, as required. Here \(E = 1\) merely records that a carry came out of the top bit; for a non-zero subtrahend this happens exactly when the true (unsigned) result is not negative.

Why a SUB register-reference instruction cannot simply be added

Suppose you wanted to add a new one-bit register-reference instruction, say a SUB, to this family. You would need a free bit among \(B_{11}\) to \(B_0\), and there is none: all twelve bits are already taken by CLA down to HLT. The 7xxx field is full. A real design would have to widen the field or reuse some other pattern. This is also a first example of why a microprogrammed control unit, which we meet in the next chapter, makes it easy to add instructions: with a control memory the new instruction would be a new routine, not new wiring.

docs.title: 11.5 Talking to slow devices
docs.text: Now we turn to the six input-output instructions. To understand them we must first look at the way a processor and a keyboard or printer exchange data, because the very large difference in their speeds shapes the whole design.

docs.title: The input-output configuration
docs.text:
Figure 11.1 shows the basic computer's connection to a terminal. A keyboard supplies characters and a printer displays them. Each character is an 8-bit code, so the interface uses two small registers, both 8 bits wide, and one flip-flop for each direction.

Figure 11.1. The input-output configuration: the keyboard delivers a character into INPR and sets FGI, the printer takes a character from OUTR and sets FGO when done.
  • Input register, INPR. The keyboard's interface shifts a character into INPR, 8 bits, and sets the input flag \(FGI\) to 1. The flag means "a character has arrived and is waiting in INPR".
  • Output register, OUTR. The computer puts a character into OUTR. The printer takes it, and when it has finished with it, the interface sets the output flag \(FGO\) to 1. The flag means "the printer has finished the last character and can take another".
  • The flags. FGI and FGO are two of the seven flip-flops of the machine (the others are \(I\), \(S\), \(E\), \(R\) and \(IEN\)). They tell the CPU when the slow device is ready.

INPR and OUTR are separate from the accumulator, and character transfers pass through the low eight bits of AC. The computer never has to fit its pace to the device, because the registers and flags decouple the two.

Why are the flags needed at all? A processor that operates at megahertz or gigahertz speeds communicates with a keyboard on which someone taps a few characters per second, which is a mismatch of millions to one. If the CPU simply read INPR whenever it liked, it would read garbage. Think of a diner: the fast cook (CPU) does not stare at the slow customer; he just checks whether the "order up" bell has rung (flag = 1). The flag is the bell. The wasteful part is not the bell but how often the cook walks over to check it, a problem to which the interrupt is the solution.

docs.title: The six input-output instructions
docs.text:
All six are recognised by \(D_7 = 1\) and \(I = 1\), so they are controlled by \(p = D_7IT_3\), and all end with \(p\!:\ SC \leftarrow 0\). As with the register-reference class, each is selected by one bit of IR, which we write \(B_i\).

Symbol Hex Control function and microoperation Meaning INP F800 \(pB_{11}\): AC(0-7) ← INPR, FGI ← 0 Input a character into AC, clear the input flag OUT F400 \(pB_{10}\): OUTR ← AC(0-7), FGO ← 0 Output the character in AC, clear the output flag SKI F200 \(pB_9\): if (FGI = 1) then (PC ← PC + 1) Skip next instruction if the input flag is set SKO F100 \(pB_8\): if (FGO = 1) then (PC ← PC + 1) Skip next instruction if the output flag is set ION F080 \(pB_7\): IEN ← 1 Turn the interrupt system on IOF F040 \(pB_6\): IEN ← 0 Turn the interrupt system off

Table 11.3. The input-output instructions.

INP and OUT move the character and, at the same time, clear the flag, so that the flag always reflects "a new, unread character is waiting" (for input) or "the printer is free" (for output). The device sets the flag; the instruction clears it. SKI and SKO are the skip instructions of the input-output family: they let the program test a flag without any other instruction having to be able to read it. ION and IOF control the interrupt system, which we will meet in Section 11.7.

docs.title: 11.6 Programmed input-output and its price
docs.text:
Without interrupts, a program must find out for itself whether a device is ready. The technique, called programmed input-output or polling, uses the skip instructions together with a branch back. To read a character:

LOOP,  SKI           / skip next if FGI = 1
       BUN LOOP      / flag still 0 - ask again
       INP           / AC(0-7) ← INPR, clear FGI

SKI looks at the input flag. If no character has arrived (FGI = 0), SKI does not skip, the BUN jumps back to SKI, and the pair loops. The moment FGI becomes 1, SKI skips the BUN and execution falls through to INP, which collects the character. The order of the two instructions matters: SKI first, then BUN. This is a skip over a branch, exactly the idiom of Section 11.4: skip the jump when the thing you are waiting for has happened. Written the other way round (BUN first) the program would never test the flag at all.

Sending a character is similar, but the CPU must wait for the output flag, because it must not put a new character into OUTR while the printer is still busy with the old one:

LOUT,  SKO           / skip next if FGO = 1
       BUN LOUT      / printer still busy - ask again
       OUT           / OUTR ← AC(0-7), clear FGO

Example 11.10: Read a character and echo it to the printer

Problem. Write a program fragment that waits for a key to be pressed, reads the character, waits for the printer to be free, and prints it.

Working. Combine the two loops. The character stays in the low eight bits of AC between the INP and the OUT.

LIN,   SKI           / is there a character?  skip if FGI = 1
       BUN LIN       / no: look again
       INP           / yes: AC(0-7) ← INPR, FGI ← 0
LOUT,  SKO           / is the printer ready?  skip if FGO = 1
       BUN LOUT      / no: look again
       OUT           / OUTR ← AC(0-7), FGO ← 0

Answer. The six instructions above. Each skip is followed by a BUN back to the skip, so the processor passes through a loop until the corresponding flag is 1.

docs.title: What programmed input-output costs
docs.text:
The method is correct and simple, but the CPU does nothing useful while it waits. Let us put a number on this.

Example 11.11: How much time does the spin loop waste?

Problem. A typist produces a character every 200 ms. The basic computer's clock period is 1 µs (an assumption chosen only to make the arithmetic simple). How many times does the SKI, BUN pair execute between two characters?

Working. SKI is an input-output instruction, so it takes the four pulses \(T_0\) to \(T_3\). A direct BUN takes five pulses, \(T_0\) to \(T_4\) (at \(T_3\) nothing happens for a direct address, and PC ← AR occurs at \(T_4\)). One pass round the loop when the flag is 0 therefore takes \(4 + 5 = 9\) pulses = 9 µs. In 200 ms = 200 000 µs the loop runs \(200\,000 / 9 \approx 22\,000\) times.

Answer. About 22 000 passes, and only the last one of them finds anything to do. With a much faster clock the number grows into the millions, which is the order of magnitude the "million to one" mismatch implies.

Every pass of that loop is work the CPU could have spent on something else. It is like waiting for a parcel by walking to the front door every ten seconds: you never miss the courier, but you get nothing else done and nearly every trip finds nothing. This waste is the motivation for the interrupt system.

docs.title: 11.7 The idea of an interrupt
docs.text:
An interrupt reverses the roles. Instead of the processor repeatedly asking the device, the device tells the processor when it is ready. The CPU works without interruption on its program; when the courier arrives, the doorbell rings. The CPU finishes whatever it was doing, puts a bookmark in its work, answers the door by running a short service routine, and then goes back to exactly where it left off. This one idea is why a computer can run a game smoothly and still react at the moment you move the mouse.

For this to work, three things are needed.

  1. A way to ask. A device must be able to raise a request. In the basic computer the flags FGI and FGO do this.
  2. A way to be ignored. Sometimes code must not be disturbed. The interrupt-enable flip-flop \(IEN\) is the master switch: it is set by the instruction ION and cleared by IOF, and while it is 0 the flags are ignored.
  3. A way to come back. The place where the program was interrupted must be saved before control goes elsewhere, so that the program can later resume.

Two flip-flops carry the machinery. IEN, the interrupt-enable flip-flop, we have just described. R, the interrupt flip-flop, is the control flip-flop that says "the next cycle is to be an interrupt cycle instead of a fetch". When \(R = 0\) the computer is in an ordinary instruction cycle; when \(R = 1\) it is in an interrupt cycle.

docs.title: When R is set
docs.text:
The interrupt flip-flop is set by

\[T_0'T_1'T_2'\,(IEN)\,(FGI + FGO)\;:\; R \leftarrow 1\]

Each factor of the condition is there for a reason.

Factor Meaning \(T_0'T_1'T_2'\) None of the three fetch-and-decode steps is active: the machine is not in the middle of fetching an instruction \(IEN\) The interrupt system has been switched on (by ION) \(FGI + FGO\) At least one device flag is actually set

If any factor is missing, \(R\) is not set. Note why the first factor is needed. If \(R\) could become 1 while \(T_0\), \(T_1\) or \(T_2\) were active, then a fetch signal such as \(R'T_1\) would stop being true half-way through a fetch, and the machine would be left with a half-fetched instruction. By setting \(R\) only when none of those steps is active, the designers guarantee that an interrupt can begin only after the fetch and decode of an instruction are complete. And since the execute microoperations of the instruction in progress do not depend on \(R\) at all, they run to the end, finishing with \(SC \leftarrow 0\). The effect of \(R = 1\) appears at the start of the next cycle, where \(R'T_0\) is false and \(RT_0\) is true.

Misconception: an interrupt drops whatever the CPU is doing, mid-instruction

It does not. The set condition requires \(T_0'T_1'T_2'\), and the interrupt cycle itself starts only when the sequence counter returns to zero. The current instruction must finish first. Interrupts are therefore checked between instructions, which is what keeps every instruction atomic: you never resume into a half-completed sequence of microoperations, so the machine state is always clean when the service routine runs. If a device raises its flag while an ADD is at \(T_5\), the ADD still runs to its last step, \(SC \leftarrow 0\), and only then does the interrupt cycle begin in place of the next fetch.

docs.title: 11.8 The interrupt cycle
docs.text:
When \(R = 1\) the computer does not fetch the next instruction. It carries out the interrupt cycle, which consists of three microoperations controlled by \(RT_0\), \(RT_1\) and \(RT_2\):

RT0:  AR ← 0,  TR ← PC             / aim at memory word 0; save PC in TR
RT1:  M[AR] ← TR,  PC ← 0          / return address stored at word 0; clear PC
RT2:  PC ← PC + 1,  IEN ← 0,
      R ← 0,  SC ← 0               / PC = 1; interrupts off; back to ordinary timing

The cycle saves the return address (the current value of PC) in memory location 0, jumps to location 1, where the service routine, or a branch to it, is stored, and disables further interrupts. Read the three steps as follows.

  • \(RT_0\) points the address register at word 0 (AR ← 0) and parks PC in the temporary register TR for safety. TR is the scratch register of the control unit; this is one of the places where it is used.
  • \(RT_1\) writes the return address into word 0 (M[AR] ← TR) and clears PC. The saved value is the address of the instruction that would have been fetched next, which is exactly where the program must resume.
  • \(RT_2\) increments PC, which becomes 1, so the next instruction is fetched from location 1 where the service routine begins. It also clears \(IEN\), so that the routine cannot itself be interrupted; it clears \(R\), so that ordinary fetching resumes; and it clears \(SC\), so that the timing restarts at \(T_0\).
Figure 11.2. The interrupt cycle: when the instruction cycle finishes, if IEN is 1 and a device flag is set, R is set; the three steps RT0, RT1, RT2 save PC in word 0 and start the service routine at word 1.
