  • IR (16 bits). Holds the instruction being executed. Its bits are read in three groups: bit 15 is \(I\), bits 12-14 go to a 3-to-8 decoder to produce \(D_0 \dots D_7\), and bits 0-11 are copied into AR as the address.

The other three registers need one line each. TR is scratch space that the hardware keeps for itself and that no instruction names; INPR takes one character arriving from the keyboard; OUTR holds one character on its way to the printer or screen.

docs.title: The seven one-bit flip-flops
docs.text:
Besides the registers, the machine has seven single-bit flip-flops, each of which records one fact.

Flip-flop Meaning when set Set or cleared by I the current instruction uses indirect addressing loaded from IR(15) during decode S the computer is running (S = 0 means halted) cleared by HLT E extended AC bit: the carry out of an addition ADD, CLE, CME, CIR, CIL R an interrupt is pending; the next cycle is the interrupt cycle set by the interrupt condition, cleared at the end of the interrupt cycle IEN interrupts are enabled ION sets, IOF clears FGI input flag: a character is ready in INPR set by the device, cleared by INP FGO output flag: the output device is ready set by the device, cleared by OUT

E deserves a word now, because it appears in the first instruction we meet. When two 16-bit numbers are added the sum can need 17 bits. The seventeenth bit, the carry out, has nowhere to go inside a 16-bit AC, so it is caught in E. You can think of E as the 17th bit of the accumulator. We return to R, IEN, FGI and FGO when we study input-output and interrupts.

docs.title: 9.4 The common bus
docs.text:
Eight registers of 16 bits each: wiring every register to every other one would take hundreds of wires, and most of them would sit idle almost all the time. The basic computer avoids this by letting all the registers and the memory share one set of 16 lines, the common bus. At any moment exactly one unit places its contents on the bus, and any register whose load control LD is enabled copies the bus into itself on the next clock pulse.

The bus is a one-lane bridge. A traffic controller, the three selection lines S2S1S0, lets exactly one vehicle onto the bridge at a time; anyone waiting to receive the value simply opens their gate (LD = 1) and grabs a copy as it passes. The trade is cheap wiring in exchange for a limit of one bus transfer per clock pulse, which is precisely why an instruction takes several timing steps instead of one.

Figure 9.2. The common-bus organisation of the basic computer: memory and six registers are the seven sources, selected by S2S1S0; the adder and logic circuit sits at the input of AC and is not a bus source.

docs.title: The eight selections
docs.text:
Three selection lines give \(2^3 = 8\) codes. Code 0 puts nothing useful on the bus, codes 1 to 6 select the six registers, and code 7 selects the memory output. Figure 9.2 numbers the sources the same way.

S2 S1 S0 Decimal Unit placed on the bus 0 0 0 0 none (nothing useful) 0 0 1 1 AR 0 1 0 2 PC 0 1 1 3 DR 1 0 0 4 AC 1 0 1 5 IR 1 1 0 6 TR 1 1 1 7 Memory, M[AR]

There is nothing to memorise beyond the order: AR, PC, DR, AC, IR, TR, memory are sources 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, and S2S1S0 is just that number written in binary. Want PC on the bus? PC is source 2, so write 2 in binary, 010. Want memory? Memory is 7, so 111. In hardware the selection is made by a set of multiplexers (in Mano's design, sixteen 8-to-1 multiplexers, one per bus line) whose select inputs are S2S1S0.

docs.title: The register controls
docs.text:
Every register has three kinds of control input.

  • LD (load) copies the bus into the register on the next clock pulse.
  • INR (increment) adds 1 to the register, in place.
  • CLR (clear) resets the register to 0.

LD needs the bus; INR and CLR do not, because they act locally inside the register. (AR, PC, DR, AC and TR can be incremented or cleared; SC has only INR and CLR.) Memory has a Read and a Write control: on a read it drives the bus (source 7), and on a write it takes its input from the bus. In both cases it works at the address held in AR. A register transfer on the bus therefore always needs two things: a selection code (who talks) and a load enable (who listens).

docs.title: The adder-and-logic circuit
docs.text:
Two paths do not go through the bus at all, and Figure 9.2 shows the first of them. The inputs of AC come from an adder-and-logic circuit whose own two inputs are AC and DR; a third input, INPR, lets the INP instruction bring a character into AC. The circuit performs AC ∧ DR, AC + DR, a plain transfer of DR, a complement of AC, and the shifts, and its single output goes back into AC. It is not a bus source. This is what makes AC ← AC + DR possible in one clock pulse: AC never has to drive the bus in order to be added to. INPR and OUTR are also off the bus: INPR reaches AC through the adder, and OUTR is loaded from AC.

A 12-bit register (AR, PC) drives or loads only the low 12 of the 16 bus lines, and when it drives the bus its upper four bits read as 0.

docs.title: Three rules that decide what is possible
docs.text:
The wiring just described leaves the basic computer with three rules, and almost every "why is this illegal?" question is one of them.

  1. One source per clock pulse. One talker, any number of listeners. Two microoperations may share a pulse only if at most one of them needs the bus. IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1 is legal because PC increments inside itself and never touches the bus; DR ← AC, IR ← PC is not, because it needs two talkers.
  2. Memory is addressed only through AR. The address input of the memory unit is wired to AR and to nothing else, so M[PC] or M[DR] cannot exist. DR ← M[PC] is illegal; the legal version is AR ← PC followed by DR ← M[AR], in two clock pulses.
  3. AC is loaded only through the adder and logic circuit, whose inputs are AC and DR. No other register reaches it. AC ← AC + IR is illegal; the legal version is DR ← IR followed by AC ← AC + DR.

Check any suspicious register-transfer statement against all three in turn: does it address memory with something other than AR? does it feed the adder with something other than AC and DR? does it need the bus twice in one pulse? If none applies, it is legal.

docs.title: 9.5 From microoperations to control signals
docs.text:
The notation we use to describe the machine is register transfer language (RTL). Its conventions are few.

  • The arrow ← means "is replaced by": AR ← PC copies the contents of PC into AR, and the right-hand side is unchanged.
  • Square brackets denote a memory word: M[AR] is the word whose address is in AR.
  • A comma separates microoperations performed in the same clock pulse: PC ← PC + 1, AR ← 0.
  • A colon separates a control condition from the operation: T0: AR ← PC means "when timing signal T0 is active, perform AR ← PC".

Here we ask what a microoperation turns into in hardware. Take the simplest, AR ← PC, "copy the contents of PC into AR".

  1. Put PC on the bus. Set S2S1S0 = 010 (decimal 2 is PC). PC's 12 bits appear on the low 12 bus lines.
  2. Let AR listen. Enable LD(AR) = 1. Every other register keeps LD = 0.
  3. Clock pulse. On the clock edge the low 12 bus lines are latched into AR. Done, in one clock pulse.

AR is only 12 bits, so it takes just the low 12 of the 16 bus lines and the top four are simply ignored. The width mismatch is harmless: register widths and bus width need not match, because each register takes the slice it needs.

The commonest slip

Students write S2S1S0 = 001 for AR ← PC because they see AR first. The selection code names the source, never the destination. The source is PC, which is number 2, so 010. The destination is set by LD, not by S.

This gives a template for any transfer X ← Y:

  • S2S1S0 = the bus code of Y;
  • LD(X) = 1;
  • Read = 1 if Y is memory; Write = 1 if X is memory.

When a question says "give the control signals", answer in exactly three slots: who drives the bus (S2S1S0), who listens (LD, INR or CLR), and whether memory is involved (Read or Write).

docs.title: Two microoperations in one pulse
docs.text:
The fetch step of the instruction cycle contains the pair IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1. Yet the bus lets only one source drive it per clock pulse. How can two things happen "at once"? The answer is that only IR ← M[AR] uses the bus (memory drives it, IR loads it). PC ← PC + 1 does not travel across the bus at all: PC has its own private increment input INR that adds 1 in place inside the register. The two microoperations therefore do not compete for the single bus, and both finish on the same clock edge. The moral is that transfers between registers use the bus, while a register incrementing or clearing itself does not. This is what allows several microoperations to share one timing step. The table shows which statements need the bus.

Microoperation Uses the bus? Control signals AR ← PC yes: PC drives, AR loads S2S1S0 = 010, LD(AR) IR ← M[AR] yes: memory drives, IR loads S2S1S0 = 111, Read, LD(IR) M[AR] ← AC yes: AC drives, memory writes S2S1S0 = 100, Write PC ← PC + 1 no: local INR INR(PC) AC ← AC + 1 no: local INR INR(AC) AR ← 0 no: local CLR CLR(AR)

Example 9.6: Control signals for a memory read

Problem. Give the bus selection and control signals that realise DR ← M[AR], the read of the word addressed by AR into DR.

Solution. The source is memory, so S2S1S0 = 111 (decimal 7) and the memory Read control is asserted. The destination is DR, so LD(DR) = 1. The address used is whatever is already in AR, because memory always reads from the address in AR.

Answer. S2S1S0 = 111, Read = 1, LD(DR) = 1.

The source decides S; the destination decides LD.

Example 9.7: Three transfers, filling in the signals

Problem. Complete the table of signals for M[AR] ← AC, PC ← AR, IR ← M[AR] and TR ← PC.

Solution. Apply the template: bus code of the source, load of the destination, Read/Write if memory is involved.

Microoperation S2S1S0 Other controls M[AR] ← AC 100 (AC is 4) Write = 1 PC ← AR 001 (AR is 1) LD(PC) = 1 IR ← M[AR] 111 (memory is 7) Read = 1, LD(IR) = 1 TR ← PC 010 (PC is 2) LD(TR) = 1

In the fetch step, PC ← PC + 1 happens in the same clock pulse as IR ← M[AR], via INR(PC), with no bus cycle of its own.

Example 9.8: AC ← AC + DR and the bus

Problem. A student claims that AC ← AC + DR needs S2S1S0 = 100, because AC is involved. Is that right?

Solution. No. AC and DR are the two inputs of the adder-and-logic circuit, which feeds AC directly. Neither register has to be placed on the bus, so the bus is free (and S2S1S0 is irrelevant). The control signals are simply the adder-and-logic function "add" and LD(AC) = 1. AC never has to drive the bus to be added to.

docs.title: Transfers that cannot be written directly
docs.text:
Now apply the three rules.

Example 9.9: Two statements that cannot be executed as written

Problem. Explain why each of the following statements cannot be directly executed in the basic computer, and give the correct sequence of microoperations: (i) IR ← M[PC]; (ii) AC ← AC + TR.

Solution.

(i) The address input of the memory unit is hard-wired to AR. PC cannot address memory: there is no path at all from PC to the address lines. The correct sequence needs two clock pulses, because two bus transfers are needed:

T0: AR ← PC        (put the address where memory can see it)
T1: IR ← M[AR]     (now the read is legal)

(ii) The adder-and-logic circuit has exactly two inputs, AC and DR; TR is not wired to it. The operand must be brought to DR first:

T0: DR ← TR        (TR drives the bus, S2S1S0 = 110; DR loads)
T1: AC ← AC + DR   (legal, and needs no bus cycle)

These are exactly the three rules of Section 9.4 in action: memory only through AR, and AC only through AC and DR. (The timing labels T0, T1 here only number the pulses.)

The same reasoning explains why AC ← M[AR] cannot be a single step either, although PC ← M[AR] can. In the second, memory drives the bus and PC loads from the bus, which is exactly what an indirect branch does. AC, by contrast, does not load from the bus: its input comes from the adder-and-logic circuit, whose operand is DR. The correct sequence is DR ← M[AR] then AC ← DR, which is precisely what the LDA instruction does.

Example 9.10: Swapping AC and DR in one pulse

Problem. Can the basic computer perform DR ← AC and AC ← DR at the same time, exchanging the two registers in one clock pulse?

Solution. Yes, because only one of the two transfers uses the bus. AC is placed on the bus with S2S1S0 = 100 and LD(DR) = 1; at the same time the adder-and-logic circuit presents DR to the input of AC (the transfer function) with LD(AC) = 1. Both loads take place on the same clock edge, so each register receives the other's old value. The exchange works because the second transfer travels through the adder circuit, not over the bus.

docs.title: 9.6 Instruction codes and the 16-bit word
docs.text: An instruction is a binary code, stored in memory like any other word, that tells the processor to perform one specific operation. In the basic computer an instruction is exactly one 16-bit word, and the bit pattern is called the instruction code. Besides the opcode and the address, an instruction format may contain addressing-mode bits (how to interpret the address), register-select fields, and in some machines an immediate-value field or a displacement. The basic computer needs only the first three.

docs.title: How many addresses?
docs.text:
An instruction format defines how the bits of an instruction word are divided into fields. The biggest design decision is how many operand addresses each instruction names, and this is how machines are classified.

Format Typical instruction Meaning Where the result goes Seen in Three-address ADD X, A, B add the contents of A and B into a third named place X RISC machines with register operands Two-address ADD A, B add B into A into one of the two operands x86 and most CISC machines One-address ADD A add A to the accumulator always into AC (implied) the basic computer Zero-address ADD add the top two stack items back onto the stack stack machines; the Java VM

Every memory-reference instruction of the basic computer works on the accumulator: "AC ← AC + M[EA]". Because AC is implied, it never has to be named in the instruction, so the format needs just one 12-bit address. That is exactly what leaves room for three opcode bits and the mode bit inside 16 bits. The trade-off is the usual one: fewer address fields mean shorter instructions, but you need more of them to get the same work done.

Example 9.11: X = (A + B) × (C + D) in four formats

Problem. Write the computation of \(X = (A+B)\times(C+D)\) for a three-, two-, one- and zero-address machine, and count the instructions.

Solution.

Three-address (3) Two-address (6) One-address (7) Zero-address (8) ADD R1, A, B MOV R1, A LOAD A PUSH A ADD R2, C, D ADD R1, B ADD B PUSH B MUL X, R1, R2 MOV R2, C STORE T ADD ADD R2, D LOAD C PUSH C MUL R1, R2 ADD D PUSH D MOV X, R1 MUL T ADD STORE X MUL POP X

Reading the trend. As the number of address fields falls, the number of instructions rises (3, 6, 7, 8), but each instruction is shorter because it names fewer things. Three-address names everything; two-address reuses one operand as the destination; one-address hides the destination in AC; zero-address hides both operands on the stack, so the instruction says only what to do, never to what. The basic computer is the one-address column, with LOAD = LDA, ADD = ADD and STORE = STA.

docs.title: Sizing the fields of a format
docs.text:
The same reasoning is used for any machine. Three fields are determined by the data in the question, and the opcode takes whatever bits remain.

  1. Address field = \(\lceil\log_2(\text{number of memory words})\rceil\).
  2. Mode field = \(\lceil\log_2(\text{number of addressing modes})\rceil\).
  3. Register field = \(\lceil\log_2(\text{number of registers})\rceil\).
  4. Opcode field = word length minus the other three.
  5. Finish by adding the fields back up: the total must equal the word length. This free check catches every arithmetic slip.

Never try to compute the opcode first, and always round up.

Example 9.12: Instruction-format field widths

Problem. A computer has a memory of 64 K words, each 32 bits wide. One memory word stores a single instruction. The instruction contains four fields: an addressing-mode field (to select one of 4 addressing modes), an opcode field, a register code (to select one of 30 registers) and an address field. Specify the number of bits required for each field.

Solution.

  • Mode: 4 modes need \(\log_2 4 = 2\) bits.
  • Register: 30 registers need \(\log_2 30 \approx 4.9\), so 5 bits (\(2^4 = 16\) is too few; \(2^5 = 32\) is enough, with two codes spare).
  • Address: \(64\text{K} = 2^{16}\) words, so 16 bits.
  • Opcode: \(32 - 2 - 5 - 16 = 9\) bits.

Answer. Mode 2, opcode 9, register 5, address 16, and \(2 + 9 + 5 + 16 = 32\).

| mode 2 | opcode 9 | register 5 | address 16 |

Example 9.13: The same question, a larger machine

Problem. A computer uses a memory unit with 256 K words of 32 bits each. A binary instruction code is stored in one word. The instruction has four parts: a mode field to specify one of 16 addressing modes, an operation code, a register code part to specify one of 60 registers, and an address part. (i) How many bits are there in each part? (ii) Draw the instruction word format. (iii) How many bits are there in the data and address inputs of memory?

Solution.

(i) 16 modes need 4 bits. 60 registers need \(\log_2 60 \approx 5.9\), so 6 bits (\(2^5 = 32\) is too few, \(2^6 = 64\) is enough). \(256\text{K} = 2^{18}\) words, so the address is 18 bits. The opcode is \(32 - 4 - 6 - 18 = 4\) bits.

(ii) One row of four boxes, widths marked, total 32:

| MODE 4 | OPCODE 4 | REGISTER 6 | ADDRESS 18 |

(iii) The memory has \(2^{18}\) words, so 18 address inputs; each word is 32 bits, so 32 data inputs.

Check. \(4 + 4 + 6 + 18 = 32\).

docs.title: 9.7 Direct and indirect addressing
docs.text:
In the basic computer the 16-bit instruction word has three fields.

Bit 15 Bits 14-12 Bits 11-0 I (mode) opcode (3 bits) address (12 bits) or operation bits

The opcode has three bits, so there are eight codes 000 to 111; codes 000-110 are the seven memory-reference operations, and code 111 is shared by two other formats. The address field is 12 bits, enough to name any of the 4096 memory words. An instruction is a tiny sentence: a verb (the opcode: "add", "load", "store"), a noun that tells you where to find it (the 12-bit address) and a one-bit adverb (the \(I\) bit: "use this address directly" or "the real address is written over there"). "LDA 350" is just "load what is at 350".

The address field never changes; what changes is what you do with it. The effective address (EA) is the address of the operand that the instruction will actually use, and the mode bit \(I\) decides how it is obtained.

  • Direct (\(I = 0\)): the address field is the address of the operand: \(EA = \text{address field}\). One memory read fetches the operand. Direct addressing is a friend's home address: go straight there.
  • Indirect (\(I = 1\)): the address field points to a memory word that holds the address of the operand: \(EA = M[\text{address field}]\). One extra memory read fetches the pointer, then another fetches the operand. Indirect addressing is a mail-forwarding slip: the address you were given holds a note saying "they actually live at 135", so you make one extra hop.

Figure 9.3 shows both cases for the same address field 300.

Figure 9.3. Direct and indirect addressing: with I = 0 the address field itself locates the operand; with I = 1 it locates a pointer, and one further read locates the operand.

Indirect addressing costs a second memory read, but it is what makes pointers possible: change the note in one place and every instruction that follows it reaches the new operand, without editing the instructions themselves. It is the seed of the whole family of addressing modes (indexed, relative, base-register) that later instruction sets provide.

Indirection is single-level

In the basic computer indirection happens exactly once. The hardware does not keep following pointers until it hits real data, even if the fetched word looks like another address. In LDA I 040 with M[040] = 0100 and M[100] = 0250, AC receives 0250, not the contents of address 250. One \(I\) bit, one extra hop.

Counting memory accesses for an instruction that reads its operand, including the one that fetches the instruction itself: an immediate operand (carried inside the instruction, which the basic computer does not use for memory-reference instructions but is part of the general vocabulary) needs 1 access; direct needs 2 (instruction, operand); indirect needs 3 (instruction, pointer, operand).

Example 9.14: Effective address, direct and indirect

Problem. Location 250 (hex) holds the instruction, and the address field of the instruction is 300 (hex). Memory word 300 contains 0135, and word 135 contains 2468. Find the effective address and the operand for (a) direct addressing, (b) indirect addressing.

Solution.

(a) Direct (\(I = 0\)): \(EA\) = address field = 300. Operand = M[300] = 0135.

(b) Indirect (\(I = 1\)): \(EA = M[300] = 0135\), so \(EA\) = 135. Operand = M[135] = 2468.

Answer. Direct: EA = 300, operand = 0135. Indirect: EA = 135, operand = 2468.

The three-step recipe for every EA question: (1) read the leading hex digit to find whether \(I\) is 0 or 1; (2) if \(I = 0\), EA is the address field, full stop; (3) if \(I = 1\), look up memory at the address field once and whatever is there is the EA.

Example 9.15: Indirect store, and the effective address

Problem. Word 400 holds B7A0 (STA, indirect, field 7A0). M[7A0] = 0245, M[245] = 00FF, AC = ABCD. What is the EA, and what value ends up where?

Solution. B is 1011, so \(I = 1\) and the opcode is 011 (STA). The address field is 7A0. Indirect: \(EA = M[7A0] = 0245\), i.e. 245. STA stores AC at the effective address: M[245] ← AC.

Answer. EA = 245; location 245 changes from 00FF to ABCD. Location 7A0 is untouched.

Example 9.16: Direct and indirect with the same operand values

Problem. M[300] = 0500 and M[500] = 0800. What does ADD 300 add to AC when (i) \(I = 0\) and (ii) \(I = 1\)?

Solution. (i) Direct: EA = 300, and the operand added is M[300] = 0500. (ii) Indirect: the address field 300 locates a pointer, so EA = M[300] = 0500, and the operand added is M[500] = 0800. The effective address and the operand are two different answers: the address field is where the operand lives, not the operand itself.

docs.title: 9.8 The three instruction formats and the 25 instructions
docs.text:
Three opcode bits allow only eight codes, yet the basic computer has 25 instructions. The trick is that opcode 111 is not an instruction at all: it is an escape code meaning "the operation is spelled out in the low 12 bits instead". The two classes of instruction that use it are told apart by the mode bit \(I\). This gives three formats, summarised in Figure 9.4, and one 16-bit word can be read in three different ways.

Figure 9.4. One 16-bit word read three ways: memory-reference (opcode 000-110), register-reference (opcode 111, I = 0) and input-output (opcode 111, I = 1). Format Opcode (bits 14-12) I Hex range How many Memory-reference 000-110 0 or 1 0xxx-6xxx (\(I=0\)), 8xxx-Exxx (\(I=1\)) 7 Register-reference 111 0 7xxx 12 Input-output 111 1 Fxxx 6
  • In the memory-reference format bits 11-0 are an address and \(I\) selects direct (0) or indirect (1) addressing.
  • In the register-reference format (opcode 111, \(I = 0\)) there is no memory operand; exactly one bit of the low 12 selects an operation on AC or E.
  • In the input-output format (opcode 111, \(I = 1\)) again exactly one bit of the low 12 selects an operation, this time on the input-output devices and the interrupt system.

The opcode 111 therefore serves two formats, and the hardware tells them apart with the \(I\) bit alone. "7000 and F000 are the same instruction" is a classic error: the \(I\) bit differs, so 7xxx is register-reference and Fxxx is input-output. Twelve one-hot bits with \(I = 0\) give twelve register-reference instructions; with \(I = 1\) the same trick gives six input-output ones, and \(7 + 12 + 6 = 25\).

docs.title: The memory-reference instructions
docs.text:
The seven memory-reference instructions are listed below, with the hex code for \(I=0\) (direct) and \(I=1\) (indirect); the low three hex digits are the address. Their microoperations are the subject of the next chapter.

Symbol Opcode Hex (\(I=0\)) Hex (\(I=1\)) Operation In plain English AND 000 0xxx 8xxx AC ← AC ∧ M[EA] bitwise AND of a memory word into AC ADD 001 1xxx 9xxx AC ← AC + M[EA], E ← Cout add a memory word to AC, carry into E LDA 010 2xxx Axxx AC ← M[EA] load a memory word into AC STA 011 3xxx Bxxx M[EA] ← AC store AC into memory BUN 100 4xxx Cxxx PC ← EA jump: branch unconditionally BSA 101 5xxx Dxxx M[EA] ← PC, PC ← EA + 1 call a subroutine, saving the return address ISZ 110 6xxx Exxx M[EA] ← M[EA] + 1, skip if 0 increment memory, skip the next instruction if it became zero

There is a pattern in the hex codes: setting \(I = 1\) adds 8 to the leading hex digit (0→8, 1→9, 2→A, 3→B, 4→C, 5→D, 6→E), because that is simply bit 15 turning on. AND, ADD, LDA and STA are the "do work" instructions; BUN, BSA and ISZ are control flow: go there, call a routine, count and maybe skip. Every program you have written is these two groups.

docs.title: The register-reference and input-output instructions
docs.text:
Register-reference (opcode 111, \(I=0\)) Input-output (opcode 111, \(I=1\)) CLA 7800 clear AC INP F800 input a character into AC(0-7), clear FGI CLE 7400 clear E OUT F400 output the character in AC(0-7), clear FGO CMA 7200 complement AC SKI F200 skip next instruction if FGI = 1 CME 7100 complement E SKO F100 skip next instruction if FGO = 1 CIR 7080 circulate right AC and E ION F080 interrupt enable on (IEN ← 1) CIL 7040 circulate left AC and E IOF F040 interrupt enable off (IEN ← 0) INC 7020 increment AC SPA 7010 skip if AC positive SNA 7008 skip if AC negative SZA 7004 skip if AC = 0 SZE 7002 skip if E = 0 HLT 7001 halt the computer (S ← 0)

The micro-operation of each of these is covered in the chapters on register-reference and input-output instructions; here we need only their encoding.

docs.title: Why the codes are powers of two
docs.text:
In the register-reference and I-O formats each low bit position selects one operation. That is why the hex codes are powers of two within the low 12 bits.

Bit B11 B10 B9 B8 B7 B6 B5 B4 B3 B2 B1 B0 Register-reference CLA CLE CMA CME CIR CIL INC SPA SNA SZA SZE HLT Hex (7xxx) 7800 7400 7200 7100 7080 7040 7020 7010 7008 7004 7002 7001 Input-output INP OUT SKI SKO ION IOF Hex (Fxxx) F800 F400 F200 F100 F080 F040

For example, CLA = 0111 1000 0000 0000 = 7800: only bit 11 of the low twelve is set. One-hot is a row of light switches. A memory-reference opcode is a multiplexer dial (pick one of eight), but the 12 low bits of a 7xxx instruction are a light-switch panel: flip bit 11 and AC clears; flip bit 5 and AC increments. This layout means the hardware needs no decoder here, since each bit wires straight to its own control action, which is why these instructions finish in a single timing step (see the next chapter).

Exactly one bit

Two register-reference bits set at once (for example 7801) is not a legal instruction of the basic computer: the microoperations would fire simultaneously. Exactly one bit of the low twelve should be on.

docs.title: Classifying the same 25 instructions by function
docs.text:
There are two ways to classify the 25 instructions. By format (how the bits are laid out): memory-reference, register-reference, input-output. By function (what they achieve): the six types below. Read the question carefully, because either may be asked.

Type What instructions of this type do General examples In the basic computer Data transfer Move data between memory, registers and I/O devices; nothing is computed LOAD, STORE, MOV, PUSH, POP, IN, OUT LDA, STA, INP, OUT Arithmetic Compute with numbers ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, INC, DEC, NEG ADD, INC Logical and bit manipulation Operate bit by bit: set, clear, complement, shift or rotate AND, OR, XOR, NOT, CLR, SHL, SHR, ROL, ROR AND, CMA, CLA, CLE, CME, CIR, CIL Program control Change which instruction runs next: jump, call, return, conditional skip JMP, CALL, RET, BEQ, BNE BUN, BSA, ISZ, SPA, SNA, SZA, SZE Input-output Transfer a character to or from a device and test its flags IN, OUT, test-flag, enable/disable interrupt INP, OUT, SKI, SKO, ION, IOF Machine control Control the processor itself rather than data HALT, NOP, WAIT HLT

What is missing tells you a lot. There is no SUB, MUL or DIV. You build them from what exists: subtraction is CMA + INC + ADD (add the two's complement), and multiplication is a loop of ADD and CIL. A small instruction set does not mean a limited machine: it means more work for the programmer, which is precisely the RISC bargain.

A set of instructions is complete if it lets the user write a program for any computable function. The basic computer's set is complete because it contains all four necessary groups: arithmetic, logical and shift instructions (ADD, CMA, INC, CIR, CIL, AND, CLA); instructions that move data between memory and registers (LDA, STA); program control and status checking (BUN, BSA, ISZ and the skip instructions); and input and output (INP, OUT).

docs.title: 9.9 Reading a hexadecimal instruction
docs.text:
Hex is used only because 16 bits are four hex digits. The fields do not line up with the digits, so convert first. The first hex digit carries both the mode bit and the opcode (it is \(I\) followed by the three opcode bits); the last three are the address. Decoding is like splitting a phone number: split, look up, done.

  1. Write the word as four nibbles of binary.
  2. Split off bit 15 (I) and bits 14-12 (the opcode).
  3. Classify. Opcode 000-110: memory-reference, and the remaining 12 bits are an address. Opcode 111: look at \(I\); 0 means register-reference, 1 means input-output, and the remaining 12 bits are one-hot.
  4. Name it. For a memory-reference instruction the opcode number gives the name (0 AND, 1 ADD, 2 LDA, 3 STA, 4 BUN, 5 BSA, 6 ISZ). Otherwise, find which single bit of the low 12 is set.

There is a shortcut. Look at the leading hex digit: 0-6 is a direct memory-reference instruction; 8-E is an indirect memory-reference instruction (the same instruction with \(I=1\)); 7 is register-reference; F is input-output. The digits 7 and F are the only two that are not addresses.

Example 9.17: Identify the type and meaning of four words

Problem. Decode (a) 2350, (b) B064, (c) 7800, (d) F200.

Solution.

  • (a) 2350: leading hex 2 = 0010, so \(I=0\) and the opcode is 010 = 2. LDA, direct, address 350: "load M[350] into AC."
  • (b) B064: hex B = 1011, so \(I=1\) and the opcode is 011 = 3. STA, indirect, address field 064: "store AC into memory at EA = M[064]."
  • (c) 7800: opcode 111 with \(I=0\), so register-reference; bit 11 is set. CLA: clear AC.
  • (d) F200: opcode 111 with \(I=1\), so input-output; 200 = 0010 0000 0000, bit 9 is set. SKI: skip the next instruction if FGI = 1.

Example 9.18: Decoding words from the instruction set

Problem. Decode (a) 6A12, (b) C400, (c) 7040, (d) F040, (e) 0FFF, (f) 2A05, (g) 8123, (h) 7020.

Solution.

  • (a) 6A12: leading digit 6, opcode 110, \(I=0\): ISZ direct, address A12; increment M[A12] and skip the next instruction if it becomes 0.
  • (b) C400: C = 1100, so \(I=1\), opcode 100: BUN indirect, field 400; jump to EA = M[400].
  • (c) 7040: register-reference; the low 12 bits 040 = 0000 0100 0000, bit 6: CIL, circulate AC and E left.
  • (d) F040: input-output, bit 6: IOF, turn the interrupt system off.
  • (e) 0FFF: opcode 000, \(I=0\): AND direct, address FFF; AC ← AC ∧ M[FFF].
  • (f) 2A05: opcode 010, \(I=0\): LDA direct, address A05.
  • (g) 8123: 8 = 1000, \(I=1\), opcode 000: AND indirect, address field 123, EA = M[123].
  • (h) 7020: register-reference; 020 = 0000 0010 0000, bit 5: INC, increment AC.

Example 9.19: The same instruction in both modes

Problem. Write the 16-bit hex code for "ADD the word at 45C to AC" (a) directly and (b) indirectly. What changes?

Solution. ADD has opcode 001. With \(I=0\) the leading four bits are 0001 = hex 1, so the word is 145C. With \(I=1\) they are 1001 = hex 9, giving 945C.

Answer. 145C (direct) and 945C (indirect). Only the leading hex digit changes, by exactly 8.

Example 9.20: Decoding the assignment words

Problem. Decode (a) 1BAF, (b) C123, (c) 7100, (d) F800, (e) 6045, (f) A700: give the class, the mode where relevant, the operation and the address field.

Solution. Convert the leading digit to bits and read off \(I\) and the opcode.

Word Leading digit \(I\) Opcode Result 1BAF 1 = 0001 0 001 memory-reference: ADD direct, address BAF C123 C = 1100 1 100 memory-reference: BUN indirect, address field 123 7100 7 0 111 register-reference; 100 has only bit 8: CME F800 F 1 111 input-output; bit 11: INP 6045 6 = 0110 0 110 memory-reference: ISZ direct, address 045 A700 A = 1010 1 010 memory-reference: LDA indirect, address field 700

Encoding is the same method run backwards, and it makes the leading-digit pattern plain: the digit is the mode bit followed by the opcode.

Example 9.21: Encoding instructions

Problem. Write the hexadecimal machine code for (a) ADD indirect, address 3F0; (b) STA direct, address 020; (c) BSA direct, address 100; (d) CLA; (e) SKO.

Solution.

  • (a) ADD is opcode 001 and indirect sets \(I=1\): leading bits 1001 = 9. Word: 93F0.
  • (b) STA is 011, direct: 0011 = 3. Word: 3020.
  • (c) BSA is 101, direct: 0101 = 5. Word: 5100.
  • (d) CLA is register-reference with bit 11 set: 7800.
  • (e) SKO is input-output with bit 8 set: F100.

docs.title: 9.10 Summary
docs.text:
Key points

  • The basic computer is a stored-program machine: instructions and data share one 4096 × 16 memory, and a word is an instruction only because the control unit fetches it as one.
  • Instruction word: bit 15 = I, bits 14-12 = opcode, bits 11-0 = address; \(1 + 3 + 12 = 16\). The 12-bit address is forced by \(2^{12} = 4096\); the opcode gets what is left.
  • Eight registers: AR and PC are 12 bits (addresses), DR, AC, IR, TR are 16 bits (words), INPR and OUTR are 8 bits (characters); seven flip-flops I, S, E, R, IEN, FGI, FGO.
  • Eight units share one 16-line bus. S2S1S0 selects the source (1 AR, 2 PC, 3 DR, 4 AC, 5 IR, 6 TR, 7 memory); the load line of the destination says who listens; INR and CLR act locally and need no bus.
  • Three rules: one bus source per pulse; memory is addressed only through AR; AC is loaded only through the adder-and-logic circuit with inputs AC and DR.
  • Control-signal template for X ← Y: S2S1S0 = code of Y, LD(X) = 1, Read if Y is memory, Write if X is memory.
  • Direct: EA = address field. Indirect: EA = M[address field], exactly once, at the cost of one extra memory read.
  • Opcode 111 is an escape: with \(I=0\) it is a register-reference instruction (7xxx), with \(I=1\) an input-output instruction (Fxxx), one-hot in the low 12 bits. \(7 + 12 + 6 = 25\) instructions.
  • To decode a hex word, look at the leading digit: 0-6 direct memory-reference, 8-E indirect, 7 register-reference, F input-output.
Item Value Memory 4096 × 16 (12 address lines, 16 data lines, 8 KB) Instruction word I (bit 15), opcode (14-12), address (11-0) Registers AR 12, PC 12, DR 16, AC 16, IR 16, TR 16, INPR 8, OUTR 8 Bus codes S2S1S0 000 none, 001 AR, 010 PC, 011 DR, 100 AC, 101 IR, 110 TR, 111 memory Memory-reference (I=0 / I=1) AND 0xxx/8xxx, ADD 1xxx/9xxx, LDA 2xxx/Axxx, STA 3xxx/Bxxx, BUN 4xxx/Cxxx, BSA 5xxx/Dxxx, ISZ 6xxx/Exxx Register-reference 7xxx, one of 12 bits: CLA 7800 ... HLT 7001 Input-output Fxxx, one of 6 bits: INP F800 ... IOF F040 Field sizing address = \(\lceil\log_2 \text{words}\rceil\), mode = \(\lceil\log_2 \text{modes}\rceil\), register = \(\lceil\log_2 \text{registers}\rceil\), opcode = remainder

docs.title: 9.11 Exercises
docs.text:
Exercise 9.1. List all eight registers of the basic computer with their bit widths, and state the function of each in one line.

Answer

AR (12 bits): holds the address for memory. PC (12): holds the address of the next instruction. DR (16): holds the operand read from or to be written to memory. AC (16): accumulator, where arithmetic and logic results are formed. IR (16): holds the instruction being executed. TR (16): the control unit's temporary scratch register. INPR (8): one character from the input device. OUTR (8): one character for the output device. AR and PC are 12 bits because they hold addresses into 4096 words; INPR and OUTR are 8 bits because they hold a character; the others hold a full 16-bit word.

Exercise 9.2. (a) Why does the basic computer use a common bus instead of point-to-point connections? (b) Give the S2S1S0 code and the unit it selects for all eight codes. (c) State the bus selection and load signals needed to perform PC ← AR.

Answer

(a) Giving every register its own wire to every other register would need a very large number of connections, most idle at any moment. A common bus needs one set of 16 lines; the price is one transfer per clock pulse. (b) 000 none, 001 AR, 010 PC, 011 DR, 100 AC, 101 IR, 110 TR, 111 memory M[AR]. (c) The source is AR, so S2S1S0 = 001; the destination is PC, so LD(PC) = 1.

Exercise 9.3. (a) How many address lines and data lines does the basic computer's memory have? (b) If the memory were expanded to 65 536 words, how many address bits would each instruction need, and what problem would that create for the current 16-bit instruction format?

Answer

(a) 12 address lines and 16 data lines (4096 × 16). (b) \(65\,536 = 2^{16}\), so 16 address bits are needed. That would use up the whole 16-bit word, leaving no room for the opcode and mode bit; a wider word or multi-word instructions would be required.

Exercise 9.4. A memory has 1024 words of 8 bits. How wide are AR and DR if the machine is organised like the basic computer? If the opcode were 4 bits instead of 3, how many opcodes would there be, and how many memory-reference instructions could be kept if one opcode is reserved for the register-reference and input-output escape? (Assume the word grows to 17 bits, or the address shrinks, so that the fields still fit.)

Answer

\(1024 = 2^{10}\), so AR is 10 bits; the word is 8 bits, so DR is 8 bits. A 4-bit opcode gives \(2^4 = 16\) codes. Keeping one as the escape leaves 15 memory-reference instructions.

Exercise 9.5. A memory unit has 1 M words of 16 bits. State the number of address lines, data lines, and the total number of bits stored.

Answer

\(1\text{M} = 2^{20}\) words: 20 address lines. 16 data lines. Capacity \(2^{20} \times 16 = 16\,777\,216\) bits \(= 2\) MB.

Exercise 9.6. Decode each word: give the class (memory-reference, register-reference or I-O), the mode where relevant, the operation and the address field. (a) 1BAF (b) C123 (c) 7100 (d) F800 (e) 6045 (f) A700.

Answer

(a) ADD direct, address BAF. (b) BUN indirect, address field 123. (c) register-reference, CME (bit 8). (d) input-output, INP. (e) ISZ direct, address 045. (f) LDA indirect, address field 700. Method: leading digit 1 = 0001 (\(I=0\), opcode 001), C = 1100 (\(I=1\), 100), 7 register-reference, F input-output, 6 = 0110, A = 1010.

Exercise 9.7. An instruction is stored at address 0AC. Its mode bit is \(I=1\) and its address field is 250. Memory word 250 contains 07F0, and word 7F0 contains 1234. (a) What is the effective address? (b) What is the operand? (c) Repeat both parts if \(I=0\).

Answer

(a) \(I=1\): \(EA = M[250] = 07F0\), so EA = 7F0. (b) Operand \(= M[7F0] = 1234\). (c) \(I=0\): EA = 250, operand \(= M[250] = 07F0\).

Exercise 9.8. Explain, with the bit layout, why opcode 111 is used for both register-reference and input-output instructions, and how the hardware tells the two apart. Give one example hex code of each.

Answer

Three opcode bits give only eight codes, but the machine has 25 instructions. Opcode 111 is an escape meaning that the operation is selected by one bit of the low 12 bits (one-hot) instead of by the opcode. The bit layout is I 111 b11...b0; the mode bit \(I\) is 0 for register-reference and 1 for input-output. Examples: 7800 (CLA, \(I=0\)) and F800 (INP, \(I=1\)). Twelve one-hot bits with \(I=0\) give 12 register-reference instructions, six with \(I=1\) give six I-O instructions.

Exercise 9.9. Write the hexadecimal machine code for (a) ADD indirect, address 3F0; (b) STA direct, address 020; (c) BSA direct, address 100; (d) CLA; (e) SKO.

Answer

(a) 93F0 (b) 3020 (c) 5100 (d) 7800 (e) F100. For memory-reference words the first digit is \(I\) followed by the opcode: 1001 = 9 for ADD indirect, 0011 = 3, 0101 = 5.

Exercise 9.10. Multiple choice.

  1. The memory of the basic computer is organised as: (A) 256 × 8, (B) 4096 × 16, (C) 1024 × 32, (D) 65536 × 8.
  2. When S2S1S0 = 111, the unit placed on the bus is: (A) AC, (B) PC, (C) memory, (D) TR.
  3. An instruction has \(I=1\) and opcode 010. It is: (A) LDA, indirect, (B) LDA, direct, (C) a register-reference instruction, (D) an I-O instruction.
  4. To realise AR ← DR in one clock pulse, the control settings are: (A) S2S1S0 = 011, LD(AR) = 1; (B) S2S1S0 = 001, LD(DR) = 1; (C) S2S1S0 = 111, LD(AR) = 1; (D) S2S1S0 = 011, LD(DR) = 1.
  5. Compared with the direct version, an indirect LDA needs: (A) fewer memory accesses, (B) exactly one additional memory read, (C) two additional reads, (D) no change.
Answer
  1. B: 4096 × 16, giving 12 address bits and 16-bit words. 2. C: code 7 selects memory. 3. A: \(I=1\) means indirect and 010 is LDA. 4. A: the source DR is code 3 (011), the destination AR is selected by its load line. 5. B: one extra read to fetch the pointer.

Exercise 9.11. True or false, with a one-line reason. (a) The program counter of the basic computer is 16 bits wide. (b) The same 16-bit pattern in memory can be treated as an instruction or as data, depending only on how and when the CPU fetches it. (c) 7000 and F000 encode the same instruction. (d) In the basic computer indirect addressing follows a chain of pointers until it reaches the operand.

Answer

(a) False: PC is 12 bits because it holds a memory address. (b) True: instructions and data share one memory and are just binary words. (c) False: the \(I\) bit differs, so one is register-reference and the other input-output. (d) False: indirection is single-level, EA = M[address field] exactly once.

Exercise 9.12. Fill in the blanks. (a) When the mode bit \(I = 0\) a memory-reference instruction uses __ addressing. (b) In the transfer X ← Y, the bus selection code names the _, while the load line LD names the . (c) Instructions 7xxx are instructions and instructions Fxxx are ___ instructions.

Answer

(a) direct. (b) source (Y); destination (X). (c) register-reference; input-output.

Exercise 9.13. Explain why PC ← M[AR] can be executed in one clock pulse but AC ← M[AR] cannot. Give the correct sequence for the second.

Answer

PC ← M[AR] is legal: memory drives the bus and PC loads from the bus (an indirect branch does exactly this). AC ← M[AR] is not: AC does not load from the bus; its input comes from the adder-and-logic circuit, whose operand is DR. The correct sequence is DR ← M[AR] followed by AC ← DR, which is precisely what LDA does.

Exercise 9.14. Describe the function of TR, and give one microoperation in which the basic computer actually uses it.

Answer

TR is a 16-bit temporary register that the hardware uses for itself; no instruction names it. The interrupt cycle uses it: RT0: AR ← 0, TR ← PC, so that PC can be cleared in the next step while its old value is kept safe in TR, ready to be written to memory.

Exercise 9.15. A computer has 512 K words of 64 bits. An instruction has a mode field for 8 modes, an opcode, a register field for one of 100 registers, and an address field. Give the width of every field.

Answer

8 modes need 3 bits. 100 registers need \(\lceil\log_2 100\rceil = 7\) bits (\(2^7 = 128\)). \(512\text{K} = 2^{19}\) words, so 19 address bits. Opcode \(= 64 - 3 - 7 - 19 = 35\) bits. Check: \(3 + 35 + 7 + 19 = 64\). (A 35-bit opcode is absurdly generous, but the leftover is what it is.)

Exercise 9.16. Word 040 contains 0100, word 100 contains 0250 and word 250 contains 1234. LDA I 040 is executed. What is the effective address, what is loaded into AC, and how many memory reads does the whole instruction take?

Answer

\(I=1\), so \(EA = M[040] = 0100\), i.e. 100. The operand is M[100] = 0250, and that is what LDA puts in AC, not 1234 (indirection is single-level). Memory reads: fetch the instruction (1) + the indirect look-up (2) + the operand (3) = three.

Exercise 9.17. For each of the following write the bus selection code and the other control signals: (a) TR ← PC; (b) M[AR] ← AC; (c) IR ← M[AR]. (d) Which of AR ← AR + 1, PC ← PC + 1, AC ← 0 need the bus?

Answer

(a) S2S1S0 = 010, LD(TR) = 1. (b) S2S1S0 = 100, Write = 1. (c) S2S1S0 = 111, Read = 1, LD(IR) = 1. (d) None: increment and clear act locally through INR and CLR; INR(AR), INR(PC), CLR(AC).

Exercise 9.18. Write the four steps of a general method for sizing the fields of an instruction format, and say what check you should always make. Why is log2 30 rounded to 5 and not to 4?

Answer

Mode field \(= \lceil\log_2(\text{modes})\rceil\); register field \(= \lceil\log_2(\text{registers})\rceil\); address field \(= \lceil\log_2(\text{memory words})\rceil\); opcode \(=\) word length minus the other three. Always add the fields back up to confirm that they equal the word length. \(\log_2 30 \approx 4.9\) must be rounded up, because 4 bits can name only 16 things, while 5 bits name 32.

Exercise 9.19. Why is the register-reference instruction 7801 not a legal instruction of the basic computer? Name the two operations whose bits it contains.

Answer

7801 = 0111 1000 0000 0001 has bit 11 (CLA) and bit 0 (HLT) both set. The register-reference format is one-hot: each bit selects one operation, and two set at once would make two microoperations fire in the same step, which the machine does not define. Exactly one of the low twelve bits must be set.

docs.title: Chapter 10: Timing, Control and the Instruction Cycle
docs.text:
How a counter and two decoders turn a stored word into a timed sequence of register transfers, and how the seven memory-reference instructions are carried out microoperation by microoperation.

The previous chapter described the basic computer as a static object: a memory, eight registers, a shared bus and a 16-bit instruction word. A circuit diagram of that machine, however, does not move. Nothing in it says when PC should be copied into AR, when the memory should be read, or which of the 25 instructions is being obeyed. This chapter supplies the heartbeat. A small counter, called the sequence counter, steps through timing signals T0, T1, T2, and so on; a decoder watching the instruction register announces which operation has been fetched; and a block of logic gates combines the two to say, at every clock pulse, exactly which register drives the bus and which register listens.

Once the timing is in place we can follow the loop that the processor never leaves: fetch an instruction, decode it, find its operand and execute it. We study the fetch and decode steps, the fork at time T3 that sorts every instruction into one of four cases, and then the execution of the seven memory-reference instructions AND, ADD, LDA, STA, BUN, BSA and ISZ, each written out exactly. The chapter closes with a collection of full traces, where every register is tracked through every timing step, because this is the kind of question that tests whether you understand the machine rather than having memorised it.

What you will learn

  • Distinguish program, instruction, microoperation and control signal, and name the four categories of microoperation.
  • Explain how the sequence counter, the 4-to-16 decoder and the 3-to-8 decoder generate the timing signals T0 to T15 and the operation signals D0 to D7, and read a control function such as D3T4.
  • Write the fetch and decode microoperations, with the bus signals each one uses, and explain why PC is incremented at T1.
  • Describe the four mutually exclusive cases at T3 and say what each does.
  • Write the microoperations of AND, ADD, LDA, STA, BUN, BSA and ISZ, and explain the design reasons behind them.
  • Trace any instruction through the instruction cycle with a table of register contents after each timing signal.

docs.title: 10.1 Programs, instructions and microoperations
docs.text:
Four levels of description are used for a computer, and it helps to be exact about where each word belongs.

  1. A program is a sequence of instructions that performs a task. You write it. For example, X = A + B might become LDA A, ADD B, STA X.
  2. A machine instruction is one binary word that the processor fetches, decodes and executes. It takes several clock pulses. 2350 is the instruction LDA 350.
  3. A microoperation is one elementary register transfer, completed in one clock pulse. It is the atom of the machine: AR ← PC is a microoperation.
  4. A control signal is an actual wire that makes a microoperation happen: for AR ← PC, S2S1S0 = 010 and LD(AR) = 1.

In a hardwired machine there are only these four levels: gates produce the control signals directly. In a microprogrammed machine one extra level sits between microoperations and control signals, the microinstruction, a control word read from a control memory whose bits are the control signals for one clock pulse; the whole collection of such words is the microprogram. We open that box in the chapter on control-unit design. For now, say it in one line: a program is made of instructions; an instruction is carried out as a sequence of microoperations; each microoperation is one clock pulse of control signals.

Example 10.1: One instruction is a sequence of clock pulses

Problem. List the microoperations by which LDA 350 (direct, hex 2350) is carried out.

Solution. Fetch, decode and execute together take six clock pulses:

T0:   AR ← PC
T1:   IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1
T2:   D0..D7 ← decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)
T3:   (direct: nothing to do)
D2T4: DR ← M[AR]
D2T5: AC ← DR, SC ← 0

One instruction, six clock pulses, organised by the six timing signals T0 to T5.

docs.title: The four categories of microoperation
docs.text:
A microoperation is an elementary operation performed on data stored in registers, completed within one clock pulse. Every machine, however complex, is built from just four kinds.

Category What it does RTL examples Where it appears in the basic computer Register transfer Copies the contents of one register into another; no data is changed R2 ← R1, AR ← PC every LD on the common bus; the whole fetch phase Arithmetic Add, subtract, increment, decrement, complement AC ← AC + DR, DR ← DR + 1 ADD, INC, ISZ, and PC ← PC + 1 in every fetch Logic Bit-by-bit AND, OR, XOR, complement; each bit independent of its neighbours AC ← AC ∧ DR, AC ← AC' AND, CMA, CME, CLA, CLE Shift Move bits sideways: logical, circular or arithmetic AC ← shr AC, AC ← shl AC CIR and CIL (circular, through E)

A microoperation is defined by how long it takes, not by how simple it looks: whatever the hardware can finish between two clock edges. That is why AR ← PC and PC ← PC + 1 fit in one step (different hardware paths) but two bus transfers never can, since they would need the single bus twice. The conventions for reading register transfer language were given in the previous chapter; the one new feature is the control function, a Boolean condition written before a colon, so that D3T4 : SC ← 0 means "when the instruction is STA (D3) and the timing signal is T4, clear the sequence counter".

docs.title: 10.2 The control unit's clock: SC, decoders and timing signals
docs.text:
All flip-flops and registers, including those inside the control unit, are driven by a common master clock. A clock pulse changes the state of a register only if its control inputs (LD, INR, CLR) are enabled, and the control unit's job is to generate those control signals at the right moments. For the basic computer the control unit is hardwired: its signals are produced by decoders, gates and flip-flops, with the logic fixed in the wiring.

Its components are three.

The instruction register. Bits 12-14 of IR go to a 3-to-8 decoder, which produces eight operation signals \(D_0, D_1, \dots, D_7\), exactly one of which is 1. The signal that is high is the identity of the instruction. Bit 15 of IR is stored in the flip-flop I. Bits 0-11 are the address part: they go to AR, and (for register-reference and input-output instructions) also into the control logic, where they select the individual operations.

Signal Opcode Instruction \(D_0\) 000 AND \(D_1\) 001 ADD \(D_2\) 010 LDA \(D_3\) 011 STA \(D_4\) 100 BUN \(D_5\) 101 BSA \(D_6\) 110 ISZ \(D_7\) 111 register-reference or input-output (the escape code)

The sequence counter SC. A 4-bit counter that is incremented on every clock pulse unless it is cleared. Its output goes to a 4-to-16 decoder, whose outputs are the timing signals \(T_0, T_1, \dots, T_{15}\). Exactly one timing signal is 1 at a time. The sequence counter is a metronome that also numbers the beats: on beat T0 one microoperation fires, on T1 the next, and the whole orchestra of registers plays strictly in time. The clever part is the ending. Instead of counting all the way to T15, an instruction that finishes early simply executes SC ← 0, which snaps the counter back to zero so that T0 comes round again and the next instruction begins. That is why a simple instruction such as BUN is fast and a complex one such as ISZ takes more beats: each uses only as many timing signals as it needs. The basic computer never needs more than T6.

The control logic gates. A combinational circuit whose inputs are the \(D\) and \(T\) signals, the flip-flop I, bits of IR, and status bits (E, bits of AC, DR = 0, the flags), and whose outputs are all the control inputs of the machine: the LD, INR and CLR of every register, the memory Read and Write, the bus selection S2S1S0, and the control of the adder-and-logic circuit. Its outputs also feed the INR and CLR inputs of SC, ending a timing sequence.

Figure 10.1. The control unit of the basic computer: the instruction register supplies what to do (I and D0 to D7), the sequence counter supplies when (T0 to T15), and the control logic gates combine them into control signals.

Figure 10.1 puts the pieces together. It is worth reading as two feeds and one block. What to do comes from the instruction register: bit 15 becomes the flip-flop I, and bits 12-14 are decoded into \(D_0 \dots D_7\), one line per opcode. When to do it comes from the sequence counter, decoded into \(T_0 \dots T_{15}\). The control logic gates AND those two together, which is literally what a control function such as \(D_3T_4\) means.

Why both decoders are needed

One decoder alone cannot control anything. \(D_3\) says "this is an STA" but not when to act; \(T_4\) says "beat four" but not of what. Only the AND of the two, \(D_3T_4\), is a usable order: "on beat four of an STA, write AC into memory." The control logic gates are nothing more than an array of such AND gates, ORed together one per control line. A primed symbol means NOT: \(D_7'IT_3\) means "not opcode 111, indirect, at T3".

docs.title: Reading the timing diagram
docs.text:
Figure 10.2 shows the timing signals for an STA instruction (D3). The clock ticks continuously; each rising edge increments SC, so T0, T1, T2 and so on follow one another, one per pulse. D3 rises once the opcode has been decoded (the decode step is T2), and stays high while the instruction is executed. At D3T4 the counter is cleared, which is the signal marked CLR SC, so T0 follows T4 and the next instruction cycle begins. Note that a register loaded on a clock edge changes at that edge: a transfer written for T0 is complete when T1 begins.

Figure 10.2. Timing signals for an STA instruction (opcode 011): the counter walks T0, T1, T2, ... until D3T4 clears it, so T0 follows T4.

docs.title: 10.3 The instruction cycle: fetch and decode
docs.text:
A program is executed by going through a cycle for each instruction. Each instruction cycle consists of four phases:

  1. Fetch an instruction from memory into IR.
  2. Decode the instruction: work out the opcode (\(D_0 \dots D_7\)) and the mode bit I, and move the address field into AR.
  3. Read the effective address from memory if the instruction has an indirect address: replace AR with the pointer it names.
  4. Execute the instruction, as a sequence of microoperations ending in SC ← 0.

On completion of step 4, control returns to step 1 for the next instruction, and this continues until a halt is encountered. The cycle is the picture to keep in your head: everything in this unit is one loop, fetch, decode, execute, repeat, running over a program that is itself stored in memory.

docs.title: The fetch and decode microoperations
docs.text:
SC is initially 0, so the timing signal T0 is active and PC holds the address of the first instruction. The first three timing steps are the same for every instruction.

T0: AR ← PC
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1
T2: D0, ..., D7 ← decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)
  • T0: AR ← PC. The address of the next instruction is copied into AR, because memory can be addressed only through AR. Signals: place PC on the bus (S2S1S0 = 010) and enable LD(AR).
  • T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1. The instruction is read into IR (memory read, source 111, LD(IR)) and PC is incremented to point at the next instruction (INR(PC)). Both happen in one pulse because PC's increment does not use the bus.
  • T2: decode. The opcode bits IR(12-14) go to the 3-to-8 decoder, raising one of \(D_0 \dots D_7\); the 12-bit address IR(0-11) is placed in AR (source 101, LD(AR)); and the mode bit IR(15) is stored in I.

Why must AR ← PC come before M[AR] can be read? The address input of the memory unit is connected to AR alone. PC holds the address we want to read, but memory cannot see PC, so the address is first copied into AR; only then is M[AR] the word we meant. Note also the hand-over of AR: it holds the instruction's own address during fetch, but at T2 it is overwritten with the address field and from then on holds the operand's address. Tracking that hand-over is what many examination questions are really testing.

PC is incremented at T1, not after the instruction

A common misconception is that PC is bumped when the instruction finishes. In fact PC ← PC + 1 happens at T1, during fetch, before the processor even knows what the instruction is. This is exactly why a branch works by overwriting PC at execution time: the default "next" address has already been loaded, and a jump simply replaces it. It is also why BSA can save PC as the return address: PC already points at the instruction after the call. Fetch always assumes "straight ahead"; only branches change their mind later. Consequently, after any instruction, PC is one past the instruction (or has been overwritten by a branch), not equal to the instruction's own address.

Example 10.2: Write the fetch and decode microoperations and explain the order

Problem. Write the microoperations of the fetch and decode phases of the basic computer, state which of them need the bus, and explain why AR ← PC must come before M[AR] can be read.

Solution.

T0: AR ← PC
T1: IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1
T2: D0..D7 ← decode IR(12-14), AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15)

T0 needs the bus (PC talks, AR listens). At T1, IR ← M[AR] uses the bus (memory talks, IR listens) while PC ← PC + 1 uses PC's own increment input and never touches the bus; so there is no conflict and one clock pulse does both. At T2 the AR load from IR(0-11) uses the bus. AR ← PC comes first because the memory's address input is wired to AR alone: PC must be copied into AR before the word M[AR] is the one we want.

The increment PC ← PC + 1 belongs at T1, together with the load of IR; writing it at T0 or T2 is a common mistake.

docs.title: 10.4 The fork at T3: four mutually exclusive cases
docs.text:
After decoding, the timing signal T3 uses \(D_7\) (is the opcode 111?) and I to choose the class of instruction. There are two yes/no questions: "is this one of my seven memory jobs, or an opcode-111 job?" (that is \(D_7\)) and "direct or indirect?" (that is I). Two yes/no questions sort every instruction in the machine into one of four queues, and exactly one branch is taken.

Condition Meaning What happens at T3 D7'IT3 memory-reference, indirect AR ← M[AR]: fetch the effective address D7'I'T3 memory-reference, direct nothing: AR already holds the effective address D7I'T3 register-reference execute it now; SC ← 0 D7IT3 input-output execute it now; SC ← 0 Figure 10.3. The instruction cycle: every instruction starts with the same three steps T0, T1, T2; at T3 the four cases separate.

Figure 10.3 shows the whole picture: every instruction starts the same way, and T3 is where the four paths part.

For the two opcode-111 classes the whole operation completes at T3 and then SC ← 0: they need no operand from memory, so there is nothing left to do, and they never reach T4. For memory-reference instructions (\(D_7 = 0\)) execution proper begins at T4, with the effective address in AR. The indirect step D7'IT3: AR ← M[AR] is shared by all seven memory-reference instructions: it belongs to the cycle, before the execute phase, and not to any particular instruction. That is why it is written \(D_7'IT_3\) and not \(D_2IT_3\).

What D7 means

\(D_7\) means "opcode = 111", not "instruction number 7". It is the decoder output for the escape code, so it marks the two non-memory formats. \(D_7'\) ("not 111") therefore means a memory-reference instruction.

Indirect addressing costs a memory read, not a clock pulse

When I = 1 the T3 slot is spent on the extra memory read AR ← M[AR]. When I = 0 the slot is not skipped: SC still counts through T3, which simply passes with nothing to do. So a direct and an indirect instruction take the same number of clock pulses; what differs is that the indirect one performs one additional memory access (the signals are S2S1S0 = 111, Read, LD(AR)).

Effective-address resolution is thus completely described by the fork. Direct: after T2, AR already holds the effective address. Indirect: after T3, AR holds M[address field], and that is the effective address.

docs.title: Tracing the fetch cycle
docs.text:
The best habit when answering a trace question is to write the answer as a table: timing signal, microoperation, resulting register values. Markers look for the microoperation column, not prose.

Example 10.3: Fetch-cycle trace, direct instruction

Problem. PC = 021 and memory word 021 contains the instruction 2350 (LDA, direct, 350). Trace the register contents through T0-T3.

Solution. 2350 = 0010 0011 0101 0000, so I = 0 and the opcode is 010.

Step Microoperation Result T0 AR ← PC AR = 021 T1 IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1 IR = 2350, PC = 022 T2 decode opcode 010; AR ← IR(0-11); I ← IR(15) D2 = 1, AR = 350, I = 0 T3 D7'I'T3 is true: do nothing AR = 350 is already the effective address

Answer. After T3: PC = 022, IR = 2350, AR = 350 (= EA), D2 = 1, I = 0. Execution of LDA continues at T4.

The same trace, one timing signal at a time, with the registers, the bus and the memory word that is read:

1Before T0: PC holds 021 and memory word 021 is 2350, the instruction LDA 350.

2T0, AR ← PC. The address of the instruction is copied into AR, the only register that addresses memory.

3T1, IR ← M[AR] and PC ← PC + 1. The instruction is read into IR while PC moves on to 022.

4T2, decode. Opcode 010 raises D2, I is 0, and the address field 350 is loaded into AR.

5T3, direct addressing. Nothing to do: AR already holds the effective address.

6T4, DR ← M[AR]. The operand 07B0 is read from word 350 into DR.

7T5, AC ← DR and SC ← 0. LDA is complete and the next cycle starts at T0 with PC = 022.

Figure 10.3a One instruction, step by step. The instruction cycle of LDA 350

Example 10.4: Fetch-cycle trace, indirect instruction

Problem. PC = 021, M[021] = A350 (LDA indirect, field 350) and M[350] = 07B0. Trace T0-T3.

Solution. A = 1010, so I = 1 and the opcode is 010 (LDA).

Step Microoperation Result T0 AR ← PC AR = 021 T1 IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1 IR = A350, PC = 022 T2 decode; AR ← IR(0-11); I ← IR(15) D2 = 1, AR = 350, I = 1 T3 D7'IT3 is true: AR ← M[AR] AR = M[350] = 07B0, i.e. 7B0, the real EA

Answer. The effective address is 7B0. Indirect addressing used the T3 slot for one extra memory read.

Example 10.5: A fetch with real numbers

Problem. PC contains 021 and memory word 021 contains 0083 (all hex). Give the contents of AR, IR and PC after T0, after T1 and after T2.

Solution.

  • After T0 (AR ← PC): AR = 021. PC is still 021, IR unchanged.
  • After T1 (IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1): M[021] = 0083, so IR = 0083 and PC = 022. AR is still 021.
  • After T2 (decode): IR = 0083 = 0000 0000 1000 0011. Bit 15 = I = 0. Bits 14-12 = 000, so D0 = 1, an AND. Bits 11-0 = 083 are copied into AR. So AR = 083, IR = 0083, PC = 022, I = 0.

The usual error is to leave AR at 021 after T2: AR is reused, and it now holds the operand's address.

docs.title: 10.5 The seven memory-reference instructions
docs.text:
Every memory-reference instruction is decoded to one of \(D_0 \dots D_6\) and executes starting at T4, once the effective address is in AR. DR is the buffer that holds the memory operand, and every sequence ends with SC ← 0, which returns control to T0 for the next fetch.

Instruction (\(D_k\)) Microoperations (execute phase) AND (\(D_0\)) D0T4: DR ← M[AR]; D0T5: AC ← AC ∧ DR, SC ← 0 ADD (\(D_1\)) D1T4: DR ← M[AR]; D1T5: AC ← AC + DR, E ← Cout, SC ← 0 LDA (\(D_2\)) D2T4: DR ← M[AR]; D2T5: AC ← DR, SC ← 0 STA (\(D_3\)) D3T4: M[AR] ← AC, SC ← 0 BUN (\(D_4\)) D4T4: PC ← AR, SC ← 0 BSA (\(D_5\)) D5T4: M[AR] ← PC, AR ← AR + 1; D5T5: PC ← AR, SC ← 0 ISZ (\(D_6\)) D6T4: DR ← M[AR]; D6T5: DR ← DR + 1; D6T6: M[AR] ← DR, if (DR = 0) then (PC ← PC + 1), SC ← 0

Learn this table and roughly a third of the unit is in your pocket; better still, learn to read it as a story. Notice a rhythm. Instructions that use a memory value (AND, ADD, LDA, ISZ) all start with the same line, DR ← M[AR]: "first go and fetch the operand". They then differ only in what they do with it: AND combines it, ADD sums it, LDA just copies it, ISZ bumps it and writes it back. STA and the two branches skip the read entirely, because they have nothing to read. If you can tell which instructions need to read memory first, half the table writes itself.

Common mistake

Students often forget that STA, BUN and BSA do not need to read the operand, so they have no DR ← M[AR] step. Only AND, ADD, LDA and ISZ fetch the memory word into DR first. After any memory-reference instruction: PC has advanced by 1 (or been overwritten by a branch), SC is back at 0, and AR holds the effective address that was used.

docs.title: AND, ADD and LDA
docs.text:
These three need an operand from memory, so all three begin at T4 by reading it into DR: DR is the only register connected to the second input of the adder-and-logic circuit. At T5 the circuit forms AC ∧ DR (AND, a bitwise operation), AC + DR with the carry out of bit 15 going to E (ADD), or simply passes DR through to AC (LDA). LDA could not be done as AC ← M[AR] directly, because AC has no path from the bus.

The flip-flop E is the seventeenth bit of AC: the place a carry has to go when two 16-bit numbers add to more than 16 bits. It is cleared when no carry occurs, so after an ADD it always shows the carry out of that addition. E is also what CIR and CIL rotate through, and what SZE tests.

Example 10.6: ADD with no carry

Problem. AC = 000A, the memory word at the effective address (AR = 350) contains 0007, and E = 0. Trace the execute phase of ADD (D1) and give the final AC and E (hex).

Solution.

D1T4: DR ← M[AR]            DR = 0007
D1T5: AC ← AC + DR, E ← Cout  000A + 0007 = 0011; no carry out of bit 15, so E ← 0
      SC ← 0

Answer. AC = 0011, E = 0.

Example 10.7: ADD that overflows into E

Problem. AC = FFFF, M[EA] = 0003, E = 0. What are AC and E after ADD?

Solution. FFFF + 0003 = 1 0002 in 17 bits. The low 16 bits stay in AC; the seventeenth bit, the carry out, is loaded into E.

Answer. AC = 0002, E = 1. E is the extended-AC bit: think of it as the 17th bit that catches what will not fit.

docs.title: STA
docs.text: STA stores AC in memory. No operand needs to be read, so it completes in one step: AC is placed on the bus (S2S1S0 = 100) and the memory writes it at the address in AR. STA is the only instruction that writes memory without first reading it, and it is the shortest memory-reference instruction together with BUN. It is the mirror image of LDA: it puts AC into memory and needs no DR at all. Because there is no DR ← M[AR] step, STA is exactly one timing step shorter than LDA, which must read at T4 and copy at T5.

docs.title: BUN
docs.text: D4T4: PC ← AR, SC ← 0. The effective address becomes the address of the next instruction. A branch is nothing more than a load into PC: AR drives the bus (S2S1S0 = 001) and LD(PC) is asserted. There is no magic to a jump: you overwrite the bookmark and the machine carries on from the new place. It works precisely because fetch already advanced PC: the default "next" address is simply replaced.

docs.title: BSA: subroutine call with no stack
docs.text:
The basic computer has no stack, and BSA (branch and save return address) is how it calls a subroutine. Before jumping into the subroutine, it writes down where it came from, in the word just before the subroutine starts, and then jumps to the word after that.

D5T4: M[AR] ← PC, AR ← AR + 1     (save the return address; step past it)
D5T5: PC ← AR, SC ← 0             (jump to the first real instruction)

PC is the right thing to save. It was incremented during fetch, so it already points at the instruction after the call, which is precisely the address from which execution must resume. Figure 10.4 shows the effect for BSA 470 stored at location 30: after fetch PC = 31; 31 is written into word 470, and PC becomes 471, the first word of the subroutine body.

Figure 10.4. BSA 470 stored at location 30: the return address 31 is saved in word 470 and execution continues at 471.

The subroutine returns with an indirect branch through its own first word. The last instruction of the routine is BUN 470 with I = 1 (hex C470): at T3 it performs AR ← M[470] = 31, and at D4T4 it loads PC ← AR = 31, exactly where the caller left off. A plain BUN 470 would jump to the word holding the return address itself and execute the stored number as an instruction, which is why the return must be indirect.

BSA takes two timesteps because M[AR] ← PC and PC ← AR both use the bus (PC is the source in the first, AR in the second) and so cannot share a pulse; the increment of AR is local (INR(AR)) and can share the first. A limitation is that the return address sits at a fixed place, so a subroutine cannot call itself recursively.

Example 10.8: BSA 135 stored at 021

Problem. PC = 021, M[021] = 5135 (BSA 135, direct), M[135] = 0000. Trace the whole instruction and give PC, AR and M[135] at the end.

Solution. 5 = 0101, so I = 0 and the opcode is 101 (BSA).

Step Microoperation Result T0 AR ← PC AR = 021 T1 IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1 IR = 5135, PC = 022 T2 decode D5 = 1, AR = 135, I = 0 T3 direct: nothing D5T4 M[AR] ← PC, AR ← AR + 1 M[135] = 022, AR = 136 D5T5 PC ← AR, SC ← 0 PC = 136

Answer. PC = 136, AR = 136, M[135] = 0022. The subroutine body starts at 136; the last instruction of the routine is BUN 135 with I = 1 (hex C135), which reads M[135] = 022 and loads PC with it.

Example 10.9: BSA 470 stored at location 30

Problem. Write the microoperations for BSA. If BSA 470, stored at location 30, is executed, answer: (i) at which location is the return address saved? (ii) to which location does control transfer? (iii) which instruction is used at the end of the subroutine to return? (iv) what value is loaded into PC when the return instruction executes?

Solution. The microoperations are D5T4: M[AR] ← PC, AR ← AR + 1 and D5T5: PC ← AR, SC ← 0. The instruction sits at 30, so fetch set PC = 31 before the execute phase began; 31 is the return address.

  • D5T4: M[AR] ← PC with AR = 470 gives M[470] = 31; then AR ← AR + 1 gives AR = 471.
  • D5T5: PC ← AR gives PC = 471. The next instruction fetched is the one at 471, the first line of the subroutine.
  • Return: the last instruction of the subroutine is an indirect branch, BUN I 470. Indirect means AR ← M[470] = 31, then PC ← AR.

Answer. (i) The return address is saved at 470. (ii) Control transfers to 471. (iii) An indirect BUN, written BUN I 470, hex C470. (iv) PC is loaded with 31, the address just after the call.

Do not swap (i) and (ii): the return address goes in 470 and execution starts at 471.

docs.title: ISZ: increment and skip if zero
docs.text:
ISZ increments a memory word and skips the next instruction if the result is zero.

D6T4: DR ← M[AR]                                   (read the counter)
D6T5: DR ← DR + 1                                  (bump it)
D6T6: M[AR] ← DR, if (DR = 0) then (PC ← PC + 1), SC ← 0   (write back; maybe skip)

Memory cannot increment a word in place, so the word has to come out into DR, be incremented there (with INR(DR), which needs no bus), and be written back (S2S1S0 = 011, Write). That takes three separate steps, and ISZ is the longest instruction in the set. The skip is done by an extra increment of PC, which already points at the instruction following ISZ; incrementing it once more steps over that instruction.

What everyday construct is this one instruction secretly implementing? A counted loop. Put ISZ just before a BUN that jumps back to the top of the loop body. Initialise the counter to \(-N\); ISZ ticks it up towards zero, and on the tick that reaches zero the skip jumps over the BUN and the loop exits.

        ORG 100
LOOP,   ...           / loop body
        ISZ CTR       / bump the counter; skip the next instruction when it reaches 0
        BUN LOOP      / not finished: go again
        HLT           / finished
CTR,    DEC -3        / the loop body runs 3 times

Example 10.10: ISZ as a loop counter

Problem. A count is kept in memory location 040, currently holding FFFE (= \(-2\) in 16-bit two's complement). The instruction ISZ 040 sits just before a BUN that jumps back to the top of a loop. Trace the two ISZ executions and explain what construct this builds.

Solution.

First ISZ:

D6T4: DR ← M[040] = FFFE
D6T5: DR ← DR + 1 = FFFF
D6T6: M[040] ← FFFF;  FFFF ≠ 0, so no skip

The following BUN runs and the loop repeats.

Second ISZ:

D6T4: DR ← FFFF
D6T5: DR ← 0000        (FFFF + 1 wraps to 0000)
D6T6: M[040] ← 0000;  DR = 0, so PC ← PC + 1: the BUN is skipped

The loop exits. Because the counter started at \(-2\), the loop body ran exactly twice.

Answer. ISZ takes 040 from FFFE to FFFF (no skip), then from FFFF to 0000 (skip): a loop that executes its body twice. ISZ is the basic computer's for-loop primitive.

Example 10.11: Counting loop passes

Problem. M[040] = FFFD and the instruction ISZ 040 sits before a BUN back to the loop top (the loop body comes before the ISZ). How many times does the body run in total?

Solution. FFFD is \(-3\) in two's complement. Pass 1: body, then ISZ gives FFFE, not zero, so BUN repeats. Pass 2: body, ISZ gives FFFF, BUN repeats. Pass 3: body, ISZ gives 0000, the BUN is skipped.

Answer. The body runs 3 times, because the counter needed three increments to reach zero.

docs.title: How many clock pulses does each instruction take?
docs.text:
Counting timing signals from T0 up to and including the one that clears SC, we get the length of each instruction in clock pulses.

Instruction Last timing signal Clock pulses Reads operand into DR? STA, BUN T4 5 no AND, ADD, LDA, BSA T5 6 AND, ADD, LDA yes; BSA no ISZ T6 7 yes register-reference, input-output T3 4 no

These counts hold for both direct and indirect instructions, for the reason given earlier: T3 is spent either way. Different instructions take different numbers of pulses because each clears the sequence counter as soon as its own work is done; the thing that ends every one of them is SC ← 0, which sends the timing back to T0 for the next fetch. Forgetting SC ← 0 on the last microoperation of an instruction is a classic error.

docs.title: 10.6 Full instruction traces
docs.text:
The questions that carry the most marks ask for a whole instruction, from fetch to the last execute step. The method is the same every time.

  1. Build the instruction word from I, the opcode and the address: the question rarely hands it to you.
  2. Fetch: AR ← PC, then IR ← M[AR] and PC ← PC + 1. Write the new PC down now and do not touch it again unless the instruction is a branch.
  3. Decode: AR ← IR(0-11), I ← IR(15), and note which \(D\) is set.
  4. Indirect? If I = 1, AR ← M[AR] once.
  5. Execute the microoperations of that instruction, then SC ← 0.
  6. Keep a table with one row per timing step, and write a value only where it changes.

The two marks lost every year: PC was already incremented during fetch, so it is one past the instruction, not equal to it; and AR is overwritten at T2 with the address field, so it no longer holds the instruction's own address.

The first trace follows an instruction in motion, through every state of the machine. Figure 10.5 shows the machine at time T1 of this run: memory drives the bus with A083, which is being latched into IR while PC increments. Study the picture, then the table.

Figure 10.5. The basic computer at T1 of LDA I 083: memory is read onto the bus (source 111) and the word A083 is loaded into IR while PC moves on to 022.

Example 10.12: LDA indirect, end to end

Problem. The instruction LDA I 083 is stored at address 021. PC = 021, AC = A137, M[021] = A083, M[083] = 0AC5 and M[AC5] = 8562. Trace the whole instruction, the longest ordinary path through the machine: fetch, decode, resolve the pointer, fetch the operand, land it in AC. A dash means "not yet written by this instruction".

Solution. A083: A = 1010, so I = 1, opcode 010 (LDA), address field 083.

Step Microoperation Control signals AR PC IR DR AC I start - 021 - 0000 A137 - T0 AR ← PC S=010, LD(AR) 021 021 - 0000 A137 - T1 IR ← M[AR], PC ← PC + 1 S=111, LD(IR), INR(PC) 021 022 A083 0000 A137 - T2 decode; AR ← IR(0-11); I ← IR(15) S=101, LD(AR) 083 022 A083 0000 A137 1 T3 D7'IT3: AR ← M[AR] S=111, LD(AR) AC5 022 A083 0000 A137 1 T4 D2T4: DR ← M[AR] S=111, LD(DR) AC5 022 A083 8562 A137 1 T5 D2T5: AC ← DR, SC ← 0 transfer DR, LD(AC), CLR(SC) AC5 022 A083 8562 8562 1

At T2, D2 = 1: the decoder raises the single wire that tells the whole machine this is an LDA. At T3 the 16-bit word 0AC5 read from M[083] is loaded into the 12-bit AR through its low 12 bits, giving AC5.

Answer. AC = 8562; final PC = 022, AR = AC5, IR = A083, DR = 8562. Three rules were obeyed at every step: memory was addressed only through AR; AC was fed only through the adder-and-logic circuit; and no two values crossed the bus in the same pulse.

Example 10.13: AND at address 021
